title: Smells and Refactorings for Software Environmental Sustainability: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Context: The environmental impact of ICT is constantly growing. Enhancing its environmental sustainability requires dealing with energy-hungry software systems, by possibly reducing their footprint. Objective: To better frame the problem and its persistent nature, software can be viewed as carrying structural inefficiencies regardless of how advanced its functionality may be. Identifying these inefficiencies as "green smells" provides a basis for refactoring code to mitigate its ecological impact. We aim at identifying well-known green smells impacting environmental sustainable software and map them to corresponding refactoring aimed at reducing the impact therein. Method: In this article, we conduct a systematic literature review on the articles that discuss green smells and their possible refactorings. We analyse and classify 66 primary studies published up to March 2026. Results: We identify 20 smells impacting environmental sustainability of software. Each smell is associated with one or more refactoring techniques known to mitigate their negative effects on the environmental sustainability of software. Conclusions: The literature witnesses the interest in resolving the green smells affecting software systems. The catalogued green smells and the corresponding refactorings can provide pragmatic value for practitioners in their daily development workflows, while also offering researchers a starting point to establish new research directions in sustainable software engineering.

AI.tldr: This systematic literature review identifies 20 "green smells" (code-level inefficiencies affecting environmental sustainability) and maps them to corresponding refactoring techniques. The study analyzes 66 primary studies published up to March 2026.
AI.motivation: The environmental impact of ICT is growing, and software systems contribute significantly to this footprint. The authors argue that software contains structural inefficiencies ("green smells") regardless of functionality advancement, and identifying these provides a basis for refactoring to reduce ecological impact.
AI.method: Systematic literature review analyzing 66 primary studies discussing green smells and their refactorings, published up to March 2026.
AI.result: Identified 20 green smells impacting environmental sustainability, with each smell associated with one or more refactoring techniques to mitigate negative effects.
AI.conclusion: The literature shows growing interest in resolving green smells. The catalog provides pragmatic value for practitioners in development workflows and offers researchers a foundation for new directions in sustainable software engineering.

title: Characterizing Open-Source Video Games from a Software Engineering Perspective
summary: Video games hold a prominent role in the entertainment industry, which constitutes a multibillion-dollar global market. Within this ecosystem, independent studios, small teams, and solo developers operate with constrained budgets while making their games available through platforms such as itch.io, where many projects are also available as open-source. Where even if the project is fully released, other developers can still have access to the development process through the source code, helping other developers to develop their own games. These open-source games also constitute a valuable corpus for empirical software engineering research, offering transparent access to development artifacts that are typically inaccessible in commercial projects. This study characterizes open-source video games from a Software Engineering standpoint, focusing on their genres, popularity, repository activity, implementation characteristics, and testing practices. To this end, we extracted metadata from 491 video games from itch.io, published as open-source projects in GitHub. The results indicate that open-source games predominantly fall within limited genres (Puzzle, Action, and Platformer), that player ratings, when available, tend to be high, bringing a perception that the community receives well those kind of games, that repositories are largely dormant or minimally maintained, that the majority of these projects adopt either Godot or Unity as their game engine, and that documentation of testing-related practices is seldom included. The results offer insights into the development of open-source video games and may contribute to advancing software engineering practices and tools designed for small teams and independent game developers.

AI.tldr: This study characterizes 491 open-source video games from itch.io (published on GitHub) from a software engineering perspective, examining genres, popularity, repository activity, implementation characteristics, and testing practices.
AI.motivation: Independent game developers often work with constrained budgets and release games on platforms like itch.io, many as open-source. These open-source games constitute a valuable corpus for empirical software engineering research, offering transparent access to development artifacts typically inaccessible in commercial projects.
AI.method: Extracted metadata from 491 video games from itch.io published as open-source projects on GitHub, analyzing genres, popularity (player ratings), repository activity, implementation characteristics (game engines), and testing practices.
AI.result: Open-source games predominantly fall within limited genres (Puzzle, Action, and Platformer). Player ratings tend to be high, suggesting the community receives these games well. Repositories are largely dormant or minimally maintained. The majority adopt either Godot or Unity as their game engine. Documentation of testing-related practices is seldom included.
AI.conclusion: The results offer insights into open-source game development and may contribute to advancing software engineering practices and tools designed for small teams and independent game developers.

title: How Do Coding Agents Optimize Software and Report Performance Validation? A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Open-Source Pull Requests
comment: 46 pages, 11 figures. Extends our MSR 2026 Mining Challenge paper. Huiyun Peng and Ricardo Calvo contributed equally. Replication package: https://github.com/PurdueDualityLab/EMSE-perf-pr-study
summary: Software performance optimization requires identifying bottlenecks and improvement opportunities, and empirically evaluating the effects and trade-offs across performance objectives. Autonomous AI coding agents submit performance-oriented pull requests (PRs) to open-source projects, yet it remains unclear whether these changes reflect established optimization practices and adequately substantiate their claimed value. Extending our MSR 2026 Mining Challenge pilot study of 407 performance PRs, we analyze a sample of 1,130 agentic and 1,130 human-authored performance PRs collected through June 2026. We compare adoption outcomes and patch characteristics between the two groups, and examine their optimization practices and validation behaviors. The results show that agentic PRs are merged less often than human-authored PRs (54.4% vs. 73.3%), but the two groups use similar optimization strategies and report validation at comparable rates. Agentic PRs rely more on static reasoning and less on benchmarks (46.1% vs. 57.2%), although benchmark use converges by the end of the study period. Agentic PRs also report validation for code-smell refactorings as often as for resource-targeting changes, whereas human-authored PRs do so less often. Across both groups, about half of validated PRs report no quantitative performance metric, and relevant trade-offs are rarely quantified. Agentic optimization practice has become increasingly similar to human practice, but the supporting evidence remains incomplete. Establishing whether agent-proposed optimizations are supported by rigorous, quantitative, and multidimensional evidence remains an important challenge. These findings motivate evaluation infrastructure and review criteria that measure intended effects and relevant costs rather than treating the presence of validation alone as sufficient.

AI.tldr: This study compares AI agent-authored vs human-authored performance PRs in open-source projects, finding agentic PRs have lower merge rates (54.4% vs 73.3%) but similar optimization strategies. Agentic PRs rely more on static reasoning than benchmarks, and both groups often lack quantitative performance metrics and trade-off analysis in their validation.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether AI coding agents' performance optimization pull requests (PRs) reflect established optimization practices and adequately substantiate their claimed value, compared to human-authored PRs in open-source projects.
AI.method: Extended empirical study analyzing 1,130 agentic and 1,130 human-authored performance PRs collected through June 2026. Compared adoption outcomes, patch characteristics, optimization practices, and validation behaviors between the two groups.
AI.result: Agentic PRs have lower merge rates than human-authored PRs (54.4% vs 73.3%). Both groups use similar optimization strategies and report validation at comparable rates. However, agentic PRs rely more on static reasoning (54.4% use benchmarks vs 57.2% for human PRs), though benchmark use converges over time. Agentic PRs report validation for code-smell refactorings as often as resource-targeting changes, while human-authored PRs do so less often. About half of validated PRs across both groups report no quantitative performance metric, and relevant trade-offs are rarely quantified.
AI.conclusion: Agentic optimization practice has become increasingly similar to human practice, but supporting evidence remains incomplete. Establishing whether agent-proposed optimizations are supported by rigorous, quantitative, and multidimensional evidence remains an important challenge. The study motivates evaluation infrastructure and review criteria that measure intended effects and relevant costs rather than treating validation presence alone as sufficient.

title: World Requirement Model: Learning Requirement-Change Consequences from Typed Artifact Graphs
summary: Requirement changes can affect connected stakeholders, constraints, components, and tests. We present World Requirement Model (WRM), which encodes this engineering context as a typed artifact graph and predicts consequences at shared artifact identifiers. Relation-aware attention and typed propagation contextualize nodes; world and decision representations support learned dynamics. Shared readouts score impact, conflict, violation, and defect risk; auxiliary objectives supervise successor adjacency and latent prediction. On 28 scored cases from 282 synthetic cases in six domains, WRM obtains impact mean average precision (MAP) of 0.724 versus 0.623 for a hashed-text multilayer perceptron (MLP), a 16.2\% relative gain and paired difference of 0.101 (conditional 95\% interval [0.044,0.159]). Lowest-quarter mean AP improves by 32.4\%, and equal-domain MAP by 13.3\%. Four 47-case comparisons on an expanded corpus show MAP gains of 15.6--29.1\% and higher means on all five reported metrics. The recorded advantage thus extends across score summaries and annotation/training settings. Checkpoints were selected on scored cases, and backbones are unmatched, so these results characterize selected systems. Our analysis establishes candidate-coverage bounds and shows that the current linear impact head cannot rerank a fixed world's artifacts across decisions. WRM contributes an artifact-addressed world-model formulation, comparative evidence for contextual consequence scoring, and explicit conditions for evaluating requirement-world prediction.

AI.tldr: World Requirement Model (WRM) is a novel approach that encodes engineering context as a typed artifact graph to predict consequences of requirement changes. It uses relation-aware attention and typed propagation to contextualize nodes, achieving 16.2% relative improvement in impact prediction over baseline MLP on 28 scored cases from 282 synthetic cases.
AI.motivation: Requirement changes in engineering systems affect multiple connected elements including stakeholders, constraints, components, and tests. Currently, there is no effective way to predict the consequences of these changes across the entire engineering context. This paper addresses the need for a model that can predict impact, conflict, violation, and defect risk at shared artifact identifiers.
AI.method: WRM encodes engineering context as a typed artifact graph. It uses relation-aware attention and typed propagation to contextualize nodes. World and decision representations support learned dynamics. Shared readouts score impact, conflict, violation, and defect risk. Auxiliary objectives supervise successor adjacency and latent prediction. The model is evaluated against a hashed-text MLP baseline.
AI.result: On 28 scored cases from 282 synthetic cases in six domains, WRM achieves impact mean average precision (MAP) of 0.724 versus 0.623 for the baseline, representing a 16.2% relative gain (paired difference 0.101, 95% CI [0.044,0.159]). Lowest-quarter mean AP improves by 32.4%, and equal-domain MAP by 13.3%. Four 47-case comparisons on an expanded corpus show MAP gains of 15.6-29.1% with higher means on all five reported metrics.
AI.conclusion: WRM contributes an artifact-addressed world-model formulation for requirement change prediction. The approach demonstrates contextual consequence scoring through comparative evidence. However, the current linear impact head cannot rerank a fixed world's artifacts across decisions. The study establishes candidate-coverage bounds and provides explicit conditions for evaluating requirement-world prediction. Note: Results are based on selected checkpoints and unmatched backbones.

title: HelixWorld: A Real-time Interactive Audio-Visual World Model
summary: World simulation is inherently multisensory, demanding synchronized visual and acoustic dynamics in real time. Yet prevailing interactive world models remain strictly silent, focusing exclusively on visual rendering and control while overlooking the acoustic dimension. We present HelixWorld, a real-time interactive audio-visual world model where visual scenes and camera-grounded spatial stereo sound co-evolve natively under user interaction. We curate a high-fidelity spatial audio-visual dataset with true stereo acoustics and metric camera poses, upon which we pre-train a bidirectional teacher conditioned on 6-DoF camera trajectories and user actions. To enable low-latency causal interaction, we distill the teacher into a few-step streaming student via an online trajectory distillation loss, sustaining drift-free joint audio-visual rollouts at 24 FPS on a single GPU. Furthermore, we formalize spatial-acoustic consistency and introduce HelixBench to evaluate whether synthesized sound fields faithfully track dynamic viewpoint motion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HelixWorld matches state-of-the-art silent world models in visual fidelity and responsiveness, while significantly surpassing existing baselines in camera-aligned spatial-acoustic immersion.

AI.tldr: HelixWorld is a real-time interactive audio-visual world model that generates synchronized visual scenes and camera-grounded spatial stereo sound under user interaction. It uses a bidirectional teacher-student architecture with online trajectory distillation to achieve low-latency joint audio-visual rollouts at 24 FPS on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Current interactive world models are "strictly silent" - they focus exclusively on visual rendering while overlooking the acoustic dimension, despite world simulation being inherently multisensory requiring synchronized visual and acoustic dynamics in real time.
AI.method:
1) Curated a high-fidelity spatial audio-visual dataset with true stereo acoustics and metric camera poses
2) Pre-trained a bidirectional teacher conditioned on 6-DoF camera trajectories and user actions
3) Distilled the teacher into a few-step streaming student via online trajectory distillation loss
4) Formalized spatial-acoustic consistency metrics
5) Introduced HelixBench benchmark for evaluation
AI.result: HelixWorld matches state-of-the-art silent world models in visual fidelity and responsiveness, while significantly surpassing existing baselines in camera-aligned spatial-acoustic immersion. Achieves drift-free joint audio-visual rollouts at 24 FPS on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that real-time synchronized audio-visual world modeling is feasible, bridging the gap between visual-only world models and true multisensory simulation. The approach enables immersive interactive experiences with spatially consistent audio that tracks dynamic viewpoint motion.

title: CurveCodec 2: Skeleton-agnostic animation compression with a learned entropy model
summary: Skeletal motion is stored as every joint's transform at every frame, yet most of it is implied by the body rather than by what the motion is about. Compression is one way to ask what a motion must still say once the body is known, and a production codec must answer it for any skeleton with a stated error bound. Our earlier codec, CurveCodec, matched the mean error of ACL, the production library of modern game engines, with a learned prior over sparse anchors, but not ACL's worst case, and it counted its payload as floats rather than bits. Here we ask where the redundancy of skeletal motion lies and which part of a codec a learned model should take over. Measurements give three answers. At production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each quantized curve from its own past, the second from choosing per joint, in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples not to code. On the gaps such an encoder leaves, a nearest-neighbour oracle over millions of training samples is no better than linear interpolation, and no learned in-betweener we tried paid for itself. What a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals the codec must send. CurveCodec 2 codes every sub-track as a curve in the log map, quantized in closed loop and thinned to rate-distortion-selected keys, with residuals entropy-coded under a small learned model whose integer inference is bit-exact across platforms. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL's own worst case per joint within a stated tolerance, or ACL's mean error per clip. On a held-out test side of 4,472 clips from 33 datasets, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37x ACL's bytes at ACL's default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract and 0.22x at 0.1 cm under the mean contract, decodes on one CPU core, and transfers without retraining to a species absent from training. Project page: https://rubbly.cn/publications/curvecodec/

AI.tldr: CurveCodec 2 is a production motion capture compression algorithm that achieves 0.37x ACL's byte size at default precision (0.01 cm) and 0.22x at 0.1 cm precision, by combining predictive coding, rate-distortion key selection, and learned entropy coding of residuals. It verified worst-case and mean error contracts and transfers to unseen skeletal species without retraining.
AI.motivation: Skeletal motion data contains significant redundancy - most motion is implied by the body itself rather than the motion's intent. Current production codecs like ACL (the standard in game engines) don't fully exploit this redundancy. The goal was to create a compression codec that achieves better compression ratios while maintaining ACL's precision guarantees.
AI.method: The authors first measured where redundancy exists in skeletal motion through three key findings: (1) predicting each quantized curve from its past provides the largest savings at production precision, (2) per-joint hierarchical closed-loop selection of which samples not to code provides secondary savings, and (3) learned interpolation models (neural networks) don't outperform linear interpolation for remaining gaps. The final codec combines: curve coding in log map space, closed-loop quantization and thinning to rate-distortion-selected keys, and entropy coding of residuals using a small learned model with integer inference that is bit-exact across platforms.
AI.result: On a held-out test set of 4,472 clips from 33 datasets, CurveCodec 2 achieves 0.37x ACL's bytes at ACL's default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract, and 0.22x at 0.1 cm under the mean contract. It decodes on a single CPU core and transfers without retraining to a species absent from training (demonstrating generalization).
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that the primary value of learned models in motion compression is modeling residual distributions for entropy coding, not as interpolators. The codec maintains bit-exactness across platforms while achieving significant compression improvements over ACL, with verified contracts on both worst-case per-joint error and mean error per clip. The ability to transfer to unseen skeletal topologies suggests the approach learns general motion characteristics rather than skeleton-specific patterns.

title: Bayes-Sufficient Compression Is Not Enough: How Does Communication Help Multi-Agent Systems?
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems pair a sender with broad context and an executor with a limited local view. We study when a short message improves the executor's next decision, when raw context is preferable, and when a stronger sender helps. Our framework, \emph{receiver-relative bounded coordination}, expresses message utility as receiver gain minus protocol tax. Compression beats raw context when tax savings exceed losses from omitted information and decoder mismatch. Even \emph{Bayes-sufficient} compression can fail when a bounded executor cannot use its surface form. A three-stage decomposition separates externalization, absorption, and \emph{action closure}, explaining how errors remain after the correct content reaches the receiver. Under a single-crossing condition, sender upgrades help above a receiver-burden threshold. Across six benchmarks, the same Qwen protocol raises ContextBench joint accuracy from $0.633$ to $0.775$ but lowers ToolSandbox from $0.889$ to $0.653$. Fixed-message replay reveals closure failures despite correct artifact recovery. These results guide an inference-time selector that improves the accuracy-cost frontier on the evaluated communication regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "receiver-relative bounded coordination" as a framework for analyzing communication between sender and executor agents in multi-agent LLM systems. It identifies when short messages outperform raw context, introduces a three-stage decomposition (externalization, absorption, action closure), and demonstrates an inference-time selector that improves accuracy-cost tradeoffs across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems need to coordinate between a sender with broad context and an executor with limited local view. The key question is: when does a short message improve the executor's decision versus when is raw context preferable? The authors aim to understand the fundamental tradeoffs in communication protocols for these systems.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework expressing message utility as "receiver gain minus protocol tax." They analyze when compression beats raw context (when tax savings exceed losses from omitted information and decoder mismatch), even when compression is Bayes-sufficient. They introduce a three-stage decomposition separating externalization, absorption, and action closure to explain how errors persist despite correct content delivery. Under a single-crossing condition, they analyze when sender upgrades help. The method includes experiments on six benchmarks and an inference-time selector.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks, the same Qwen protocol shows starkly different results: ContextBench joint accuracy rises from 0.633 to 0.775, but ToolSandbox accuracy drops from 0.889 to 0.653. Fixed-message replay reveals "closure failures" despite correct artifact recovery. The inference-time selector improves the accuracy-cost frontier on evaluated communication regimes.
AI.conclusion: The receiver-relative bounded coordination framework provides a principled way to choose between short messages and raw context. The three-stage decomposition (especially action closure) explains why errors persist even when content is correctly transmitted. Sender upgrades help only above a receiver-burden threshold. The inference-time selector can navigate these tradeoffs to improve performance across different communication regimes.

title: Training Numerical Intelligence via Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery
summary: AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of generating scientific code, but generating code is not the same as improving the algorithms behind it. For numerical solvers, execution feedback can expose poor performance, but rarely reveals its underlying cause and how to address it. We introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), a framework that links numerical diagnosis to reusable solver self-improvement. ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm that first explains why a solver performs poorly, then uses this diagnosis to guide the discovery of appropriate numerical methods. The resulting knowledge is packaged into reusable solver skills, turning solver improvement from trial-and-error editing into a structured process of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation. Across four challenging numerical domains--power flow equation, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ordinary differential equations, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs--ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. On GOC-500 power flow, for example, ADSD reduces mean solver error by nearly $71\times$, with improvements further transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.

AI.tldr: Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD) is a framework that enables numerical solvers to self-improve by linking numerical diagnosis to reusable solver skills. It follows a diagnosis-first paradigm that explains poor solver performance and guides the discovery of appropriate numerical methods, packaging the resulting knowledge into reusable solver skills.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents can generate scientific code but struggle to improve the algorithms behind it. For numerical solvers, execution feedback can expose poor performance but rarely reveals the underlying cause or how to address it. The authors aim to turn solver improvement from trial-and-error editing into a structured process.
AI.method: ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm with three stages: (1) diagnosis - explaining why a solver performs poorly, (2) discovery - using the diagnosis to guide discovery of appropriate numerical methods, and (3) implementation - packaging the resulting knowledge into reusable solver skills.
AI.result: ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency across four challenging numerical domains: power flow equations, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ordinary differential equations, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs. On GOC-500 power flow, ADSD reduces mean solver error by nearly 71×, with improvements transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.
AI.conclusion: ADSD successfully demonstrates that linking numerical diagnosis to reusable solver skills can transform solver improvement from trial-and-error into a structured, systematic process. The framework shows consistent improvements across diverse numerical domains and transfers well to unseen scenarios.

title: Fractal Cross Product: Theory, Differentiable Implementation and Application to Medical Image Analysis
summary: The magnitude of the generalized Euclidean cross product is a Gram volume whose degree under common scaling is fixed by the integer dimension of the spanning frame. We formulate a generalized Fractal Cross Product (FCP) as a nonlinear radial deformation with a prescribed positive degree $D$, which may be non-integer. The scalar construction applies in any ambient dimension $m\geq k$, while its canonically oriented vector form requires codimension one. It recovers the classical generalized cross product exactly at $D=k$ and retains orthogonality, alternation, rotation equivariance, and $D$-homogeneity, but is generally not multilinear. For exact self-similar frame systems, the construction also obeys a scale-balance law at the similarity dimension. We derive a differentiable, dimensionless image response and a non-circular empirical accumulation exponent obtained by regressing raw angular Gram responses across patch widths. Binary64 calculations recover the finite-frame identities to roundoff, while raster experiments recover the Sierpiński-triangle value 1.5849625 at three resolutions. In five-seed medical-imaging comparisons, FCP-centered fusion increased mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.7264 to 0.8135 and from 0.5843 to 0.6765 on the random and hospital-separated Retinal Image Database for Optic Nerve Evaluation partitions, respectively, and from 0.7403 to 0.7475 on FracAtlas. On FracAtlas, balanced accuracy increased from 0.6186 to 0.6721 and the harmonic mean of precision and sensitivity from 0.3669 to 0.4457. These results support the utility of the complete fusion framework, but do not isolate the effect of FCP from that of its complementary descriptors and fusion head.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Generalized Fractal Cross Product (FCP) - a nonlinear radial deformation extending the classical Euclidean cross product to arbitrary degree D (including non-integer values). The method is applied to medical image fusion, showing improved performance in retinal image analysis and FracAtlas datasets.
AI.motivation: The classical Euclidean cross product is limited to specific dimensions and lacks flexibility for fractal-based frame systems. The authors seek to generalize the cross product to handle arbitrary positive degrees D and support self-similar frame systems commonly found in fractal structures, while maintaining key properties like orthogonality and rotation equivariance.
AI.method: The authors formulate FCP as a nonlinear radial deformation with prescribed positive degree D. They derive a differentiable dimensionless image response and a non-circular empirical accumulation exponent via regression of angular Gram responses across patch widths. Binary64 calculations verify finite-frame identities, while raster experiments test the Sierpiński triangle (recovering value 1.5849625). For medical imaging, they implement FCP-centered fusion using five-seed configurations on Retinal Image Database for Optic Nerve Evaluation and FracAtlas datasets.
AI.result: Binary64 calculations recover finite-frame identities to roundoff precision. Raster experiments recover the Sierpiński-triangle value 1.5849625 at three resolutions. In medical imaging: Retinal Image Database - AUC increased from 0.7264 to 0.8135 (random partition) and 0.5843 to 0.6765 (hospital-separated); FracAtlas - AUC from 0.7403 to 0.7475, balanced accuracy from 0.6186 to 0.6721, F1 measure from 0.3669 to 0.4457.
AI.conclusion: The complete fusion framework demonstrates utility in medical imaging tasks, particularly for retinal image analysis and fractal atlas applications. However, the authors note that the results do not isolate the effect of FCP alone from complementary descriptors and fusion head, indicating that future work should isolate the specific contribution of the FCP methodology.

title: Hallucination Reduction for LLM-Based Audio Understanding via Multimodal Direct Preference Optimization
summary: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) are prone to hallucinating and over-relying on text priors when simultaneously presented with audio and text inputs. To mitigate these hallucinations, we propose utilizing the multimodal Direct Preference Optimization (mDPO) objective, which forces the model to ground its generation in the acoustic input by contrasting intact and distorted audio counterparts. We extend this preference learning framework to the audio domain by applying a variety of acoustic perturbations. Evaluating the Qwen2-Audio backbone across the DCASE 2025 Challenge and AH Existence datasets, we demonstrate that extending mDPO to LALMs significantly enhances temporal reasoning in the complex DCASE dataset, and improves performance on basic existence verification in the AH benchmark. We identify temporal reversal, frequency masking, and random noise as the most effective perturbations. Ultimately, our approach achieves an absolute accuracy improvement of 14.0% on the DCASE 2025 dataset and 27.4% on AH Existence.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes extending multimodal Direct Preference Optimization (mDPO) to Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) to reduce hallucinations caused by over-reliance on text priors. The approach contrasts intact audio with acoustically perturbed versions to force model grounding in acoustic inputs. Evaluating on Qwen2-Audio across DCASE 2025 and AH Existence datasets, the method achieves 14.0% and 27.4% absolute accuracy improvements respectively.
AI.motivation: Large Audio Language Models tend to hallucinate and over-rely on text priors when processing simultaneous audio and text inputs, leading to unreliable outputs that don't properly ground generation in acoustic information.
AI.method: The researchers extended the mDPO framework to the audio domain by applying acoustic perturbations (temporal reversal, frequency masking, and random noise) to create preference pairs contrasting intact versus distorted audio. The Qwen2-Audio backbone was fine-tuned using this approach and evaluated on DCASE 2025 Challenge and AH Existence datasets.
AI.result: The approach achieved significant improvements: 14.0% absolute accuracy improvement on the DCASE 2025 temporal reasoning dataset and 27.4% improvement on the AH Existence benchmark. Temporal reversal, frequency masking, and random noise were identified as the most effective perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Extending mDPO to LALMs through acoustic perturbations effectively reduces hallucinations by forcing models to ground their generation in acoustic inputs rather than text priors. The method particularly excels at temporal reasoning and basic existence verification tasks.

title: Noise-Resilient Testing of Quantum Programs Based on Output Dominance
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) is a central quality-assurance activity for checking whether quantum programs conform to their specifications. In the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, gate, decoherence, and measurement errors distort observed outputs, making it difficult to distinguish program defects from noise. The existing noise-aware QST literature typically mitigates or models noise before applying a test oracle. However, these strategies can incur substantial cost and depend on calibration data, model training, or backend-specific information, limiting their applicability. We present Qomino, a dominance-guided QST approach for judging tests from noisy samples without a separate noise-estimation or mitigation phase. The approach combines decomposition-aware inverse construction, comparison of the expected outcome with the strongest observed competitor, and bounded retries for inconclusive decisions. We evaluate Qomino on 30 controlled buggy variants from six Qiskit programs and six simulated noisy backends, comparing it with six baselines spanning statistical, quantum-specific, and learning-based methods. Qomino achieves 85.65% accuracy over all six programs and 99.95% in the restricted two-program evaluation, significantly outperforming the corresponding baselines. Across the evaluated programs and backends under the stated settings, Qomino is faster than the compared quantum-specific and learning-based methods. Ablation and retry analyses support the contributions of its main components.

AI.tldr: Qomino is a dominance-guided quantum software testing approach that judges tests from noisy samples without separate noise-estimation or mitigation phases. It combines decomposition-aware inverse construction, comparison of expected outcomes with strongest observed competitors, and bounded retries for inconclusive decisions.
AI.motivation: In the NISQ era, gate, decoherence, and measurement errors distort observed outputs, making it difficult to distinguish program defects from noise. Existing noise-aware QST approaches require costly mitigation/modeling, calibration data, model training, or backend-specific information, limiting their practical applicability.
AI.method: Qomino uses three main techniques: (1) decomposition-aware inverse construction, (2) comparison of expected outcome with the strongest observed competitor, and (3) bounded retries for inconclusive decisions. It evaluates on 30 controlled buggy variants from six Qiskit programs across six simulated noisy backends.
AI.result: Qomino achieves 85.65% accuracy over all six programs and 99.95% in the restricted two-program evaluation, significantly outperforming six baselines (statistical, quantum-specific, and learning-based methods). It is faster than quantum-specific and learning-based methods across evaluated programs and backends.
AI.conclusion: Qomino successfully addresses the challenge of testing quantum programs in noisy environments without requiring separate noise estimation or mitigation. Its dominance-guided approach, combined with decomposition-aware inverse construction and bounded retry mechanisms, provides an effective and efficient solution for quantum software testing in NISQ era.

title: DABACO: A Multi-Camera Dataset and Benchmark for Screen Localization and Pointing Estimation
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22797835. Code and toolkit: https://domondo.github.io/dabaco-dataset-toolkit/
summary:
Screen localization and pointing estimation are key to low-cost interactive devices. Yet developing and evaluating these algorithms requires realistic data: synthetic captures cannot fully reproduce the optical distortion, rolling shutter, motion blur, and display processing of a physical acquisition, and most existing datasets provide static images rather than the video needed to assess continuous pointing. In this paper, we introduce the DABACO Dataset. Developed within the DABACO (Dispositivo Apuntador de BAjo COste, or Low-Cost Pointing Device) project, this dataset supports the development and evaluation of screen detection and camera-based pointing algorithms for embedded systems. It comprises video sequences captured with multiple low-cost camera sensors, including monochrome global-shutter and color rolling-shutter modules, on embedded platforms such as the Raspberry Pi 4B and ESP32-S3.
  We present a systematic annotation pipeline combining temporary visual watermarking, optical-flow tracking, manual verification, and marker removal. Both the original marked captures and the marker-free images, together with explicit corner annotations and modification masks, are released to support auditing and the study of potential reconstruction bias.
  In addition, we release an open-source evaluation toolkit with two reference baselines: a classical screen-detection pipeline based on edge and contour geometry, and a closed-vocabulary, off-the-shelf YOLOv8 segmentation model evaluated without dataset-specific training. Both are evaluated on a general-purpose computer using Intersection over Union, corner error, and pointing error, establishing initial reference results for future embedded implementations. Overall, DABACO addresses a gap in existing resources and is intended to support the development and evaluation of new low-cost screen-localization and pointing systems.

AI.tldr: The DABACO Dataset is introduced for developing and evaluating screen localization and camera-based pointing algorithms for low-cost embedded devices. It comprises video sequences from multiple low-cost camera sensors (monochrome global-shutter and color rolling-shutter) on embedded platforms like Raspberry Pi 4B and ESP32-S3. The dataset includes original marked captures, marker-free images, corner annotations, and modification masks, along with an open-source evaluation toolkit with two reference baselines.
AI.motivation: Developing and evaluating screen localization and pointing algorithms for low-cost interactive devices requires realistic data. Synthetic captures cannot fully reproduce optical distortion, rolling shutter, motion blur, and display processing. Existing datasets provide static images rather than video needed to assess continuous pointing.
AI.method: The authors developed a systematic annotation pipeline combining: (1) temporary visual watermarking, (2) optical-flow tracking, (3) manual verification, and (4) marker removal. Two reference baselines were evaluated: (1) classical screen-detection pipeline using edge and contour geometry, and (2) off-the-shelf YOLOv8 segmentation model without dataset-specific training. Evaluation metrics include Intersection over Union (IoU), corner error, and pointing error.
AI.result: The dataset provides video sequences from multiple low-cost camera sensors on embedded platforms, with both marked and marker-free images, explicit corner annotations, and modification masks. Initial reference results were established using IoU, corner error, and pointing error metrics on a general-purpose computer.
AI.conclusion: DABACO addresses a gap in existing resources for low-cost screen-localization and pointing systems. It supports the development and evaluation of new algorithms for embedded implementations, with released data and toolkit for future research.

title: Neuroll: Real-Time Neural Strand-Based Hair Simulation via Simulator-in-the-Loop Unrolling
summary: Time integration has been the cornerstone of physics-based animation that enables the simulation of complex interactions between rigid and deformable objects, including the motion of hair. Despite recent advances with optimized time integration that enabled thousands of hair strands to be simulated in real time, achieving the same performance on commodity hardware remains infeasible due to the computational demands of resolving complex dynamics and interactions between thousands of individual strands. With the rise of learning-based techniques, the offload of time integration to neural networks helps to achieve significant performance gains, making these approaches suitable for real-time applications such as gaming and virtual avatars. However, state-of-the-art neural techniques tend to produce less physically plausible motion and oftentimes fail to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. Inspired by classical time integrators, we design a neural counterpart that mirrors their input-output formulation -- taking previous hair states, material stiffness, and collision geometry as the inputs for the neural time integrator, which is then trained via a self-supervised, simulator-in-the-loop method with randomized unrolling horizons. By formulating training in each strand's local coordinate frame, we obtain a network that generalizes across multiple dimensions, including hairstyle, material property, body motion, and body type. Our method inherits the benefits of a strand-based neural simulator, and hence is density-independent, lightweight, memory-efficient, and performant. Our neural hair integrator produces stable long-horizon rollouts and can be naturally extended to support quasi-static simulation simply by resetting hair states.

AI.tldr: A neural network time integrator for hair simulation that takes previous hair states, material stiffness, and collision geometry as inputs, trained via self-supervised simulator-in-the-loop with randomized unrolling horizons. The method generalizes across hairstyles, material properties, body motion, and body types by using a strand-based local coordinate frame formulation.
AI.motivation: Traditional physics-based hair simulation is computationally expensive, making real-time applications on commodity hardware challenging. While learning-based techniques offer performance gains, they often lack physical plausibility and fail to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios.
AI.method: The method designs a neural counterpart to classical time integrators, taking previous hair states, material stiffness, and collision geometry as inputs. Training uses a self-supervised, simulator-in-the-loop approach with randomized unrolling horizons. By formulating training in each strand's local coordinate frame, the network achieves generalization across multiple dimensions.
AI.result: The neural hair integrator produces stable long-horizon rollouts, is density-independent, lightweight, memory-efficient, and performant. It can be naturally extended to support quasi-static simulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neural time integrator successfully bridges classical physics-based simulation and learning-based approaches, achieving real-time performance while maintaining physical plausibility and generalization capabilities across diverse scenarios.

title: Least Squares for Time Series Forecasting
summary: A time-series forecast is scored on a future value of the series. A representation loss that regresses the next latent, as in LeNEPA, is a different least-squares problem on the same bottleneck. We write both programs down. The forecast program minimizes the error of a decoded latent on the coordinate that will be reported. For a scalar target and a linear decoder, every latent rank of at least one matches ordinary least squares, and an isotropy constraint is only a rescaling: after the decoder is refit, the forecast does not move. The other program fits the whole next vector at a fixed rank, then freezes the encoder and attaches a head. On a four-dimensional series whose last three coordinates are the same autoregression, that rank-1 fit puts mass $0.9998$ on the repeated coordinate and forecasts the remaining signal at the marginal variance $2.794$. The forecast program puts mass $1$ on the signal and matches the innovation variance $0.992$. Rank $2$ gives the vector fit a second direction, and the two programs agree. Iterating the fitted one-step coefficient $0.803$ raises the open-loop error from $0.992$ at one step to $2.700$ at eight steps.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two optimization programs for time-series forecasting with latent variable models: (1) a forecast program that minimizes decoded latent error on a specific target coordinate, and (2) a representation loss (LeNEPA) that fits the entire next vector at a fixed rank. The author shows that for scalar targets with linear decoders, both approaches are equivalent at rank ≥1, but differ at rank-1 on a specific 4D autoregressive example where the forecast program achieves the correct innovation variance (0.992) while the vector fit approach yields marginal variance (2.794).
AI.motivation: To understand the relationship between representation learning and forecasting in latent variable models, specifically whether training to predict the full next latent state differs from training to forecast a specific target coordinate.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of two optimization programs (forecast vs representation loss) with linear decoders, plus empirical validation on a 4D synthetic series where last 3 coordinates follow the same autoregression.
AI.result: At rank-1, the forecast program correctly captures innovation variance (0.992) while the representation loss puts 99.98% mass on the repeated coordinate, yielding marginal variance (2.794). At rank-2, both programs agree. Iterating the rank-1 coefficient (0.803) shows error accumulation from 0.992 at 1 step to 2.700 at 8 steps.
AI.conclusion: The two programs are not equivalent at rank-1; the representation loss can fail to capture the true signal structure while the forecast program correctly identifies the innovation variance. Rank-2 or higher is needed for the programs to agree. This demonstrates the importance of matching the training objective to the forecasting task in latent variable models.

title: REACT: Physically and Chemically Consistent Reconstruction of Marine Active Tracers
summary: Reconstructing global sea surface pH from sparse observations is critical for monitoring ocean acidification and understanding marine carbon cycling. Traditional assimilation and inverse models are physically grounded but costly for large-scale reconstruction. Recent black-box and physics-guided AI models improve efficiency, but are mainly designed for passive tracers, where the reconstructed variable is also the transported inventory. In contrast, pH is an active carbonate tracer: it is the prediction target, while dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is the conserved carbon inventory. This mismatch can produce low pH error while violating carbonate closure and source-free carbon conservation. To address this, we introduce \textbf{REACT}, a carbon-first reconstruction framework that decouples transport, active correction, and chemical decoding. REACT transports a latent carbonate state with a conservative advection--diffusion solver, captures non-conservative carbon-cycle variations with a source module, decodes the corrected state into pH, and constrains the output through carbonate equilibrium. This design keeps pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state. On simulation data, REACT reduces pH NRMSE by (14.7%) and chemical consistency error by (24.0%) over the best baseline. Cross-temporal-scale evaluations show robustness against error accumulation from coarse to fine temporal scales, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component.

AI.tldr: REACT is a carbon-first deep learning framework for reconstructing global sea surface pH from sparse observations. It addresses the fundamental mismatch in existing AI models that treat pH as a passive tracer when it's actually an active carbonate tracer. The framework decouples transport, active correction, and chemical decoding to enforce carbon conservation while accurately predicting pH.
AI.motivation: Traditional ocean acidification monitoring requires reconstructing sea surface pH from sparse observations. Existing methods have critical limitations: (1) traditional assimilation/inverse models are computationally expensive, (2) AI models are designed for passive tracers but pH is an active carbonate tracer where pH is the target while DIC is the conserved inventory. This mismatch causes low pH errors but violates carbonate closure and carbon conservation. A carbon-first approach is needed that maintains pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state.
AI.method: REACT introduces a carbon-first reconstruction framework with four key components: (1) A conservative advection-diffusion solver transports a latent carbonate state, (2) A source module captures non-conservative carbon-cycle variations, (3) A decoder transforms the corrected state into pH, (4) Carbonate equilibrium constraints are applied to the output. This design decouples transport, active correction, and chemical decoding to keep pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state.
AI.result: On simulation data, REACT reduces pH NRMSE by 14.7% and chemical consistency error by 24.0% over the best baseline. Cross-temporal-scale evaluations demonstrate robustness against error accumulation from coarse to fine temporal scales. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component.
AI.conclusion: REACT successfully addresses the fundamental challenge of reconstructing active carbonate tracers like pH by introducing a carbon-first framework that maintains prediction accuracy while enforcing physical consistency. The framework shows significant improvements in both pH accuracy and chemical consistency, with robustness across different temporal scales. This approach represents a paradigm shift from passive tracer reconstruction to active carbonate tracer modeling, with potential applications in ocean carbon cycle monitoring and climate modeling.

title: Do Motion Tokenizers for Co-Speech Gesture Generation Encode Gesture Semantics?
summary: Discrete motion tokenizers encode motion as atomic units and are widely used for co-speech gesture generation. It remains unclear which motion properties, especially those relevant to gesture semantics, are recoverable from these codebooks. We probe a reconstruction-trained codebook using 19 co-speech gesture descriptors spanning from raw motion to abstract communicative function. Results show that geometry and handedness are readily decodable from token embeddings, while motion category is only weakly decoded despite showing systematic differences in discrete code usage. This gap between reconstruction quality and descriptor decodability suggests that reconstruction objectives alone do not guarantee that gesture semantics are captured, and that evaluating codebooks on such properties can guide the design of more semantic motion tokenizers.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates what motion properties (especially gesture semantics) are recoverable from discrete motion tokenizers used for co-speech gesture generation. Using 19 gesture descriptors, the study finds that geometry and handedness are readily decodable from token embeddings, while motion category is only weakly decoded despite showing systematic differences in discrete code usage.
AI.motivation: Discrete motion tokenizers are widely used for co-speech gesture generation, but it remains unclear which motion properties relevant to gesture semantics are actually captured in these codebooks. The researchers aim to understand what information is preserved when motion is encoded into discrete tokens.
AI.method: The researchers probe a reconstruction-trained codebook using 19 co-speech gesture descriptors spanning from raw motion to abstract communicative function. They investigate decodability of various properties from the token embeddings.
AI.result: Geometry and handedness are readily decodable from token embeddings. However, motion category is only weakly decoded despite showing systematic differences in discrete code usage. This reveals a gap between reconstruction quality and descriptor decodability.
AI.conclusion: Reconstruction objectives alone do not guarantee that gesture semantics are captured in motion tokenizers. Evaluating codebooks on semantic properties can guide the design of more semantic motion tokenizers for gesture generation.

title: Temporal Anchors and Editing Sensitivity in Partial Speech Spoofing: A Controlled Study
summary: Partial-spoof detectors must reject synthetic content while accepting benign edits. We diagnose temporal anchors and boundary-consistency training using frozen WavLM features, nonlinguistic unit controls, and source-locked evaluation. Genuine-genuine and genuine-fake splices contrast editing false alarms with synthetic-content misses; they do not isolate a unique causal artifact. With layer-6 features, phone units have higher PartialSpoof evaluation frame EER than soft frames (11.18% versus 9.59%). In 500 retrospective PS-eval cases, augmentation reduces genuine-splice false alarms; synthetic-core misses increase at 5% PS-development FPR but not demonstrably at 1%. A 200-case Llama A follow-up retains the false-alarm reduction but does not establish a miss-rate increase. Constructed-case ranking can improve while fixed-threshold misses rise. Consistency gives no uniform gain, and encoder-layer rankings change across corpora. We report frame and event localization with three seeds, including word units, and treat PS evaluation as retrospective. Audit code, selected training scripts, and result summaries are available at https://github.com/mysxs/partial-spoof-diagnostics.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses partial-spoof detection systems by examining temporal anchors, boundary-consistency training, and feature layer effectiveness. The study finds that layer-6 features with phone units yield higher EER (11.18%) than soft frames (9.59%), augmentation reduces false alarms but may increase synthetic-core misses, and encoder-layer rankings vary across corpora. The work provides frame/event localization results and open-source code.
AI.motivation: Partial-spoof detectors must balance rejecting synthetic content while accepting benign edits. The authors aim to diagnose why current methods fail to isolate unique causal artifacts and understand the trade-offs between false alarms and misses.
AI.method: The study uses frozen WavLM features with nonlinguistic unit controls and source-locked evaluation. It contrasts genuine-genuine and genuine-fake splices, evaluates different encoder layers (particularly layer-6), tests augmentation strategies, and conducts retrospective analysis on PS-eval cases and a Llama A follow-up.
AI.result: Layer-6 phone units show higher EER (11.18%) than soft frames (9.59%). Augmentation reduces genuine-splice false alarms but increases synthetic-core misses at 5% PS-development FPR. Consistency training provides no uniform gain, and encoder-layer rankings change across corpora.
AI.conclusion: Partial-spoof detection faces fundamental trade-offs between false alarms and misses. The diagnosis reveals that no single causal artifact can be isolated, and performance varies significantly across corpora and evaluation settings. The approach treats PS evaluation as retrospective and provides open-source audit code.

title: DreamTest: World-Model Surrogates for Search-Based Testing of Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
summary:
Testing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents in cyber-physical systems aims to uncover diverse failures before deployment, but each execution can be expensive. Surrogate-assisted testing reduces this cost by learning to predict which test configurations are likely to fail. Prior surrogates treat the system as a black box and predict pass or fail outcomes directly; we instead model how a test unfolds and estimate failure from an imagined episode.
  We introduce DreamTest, a world-model surrogate for testing DRL agents. DreamTest adapts a recurrent state-space model to learn agent behaviour and environment dynamics from the agent's training log. Given a candidate configuration, imagined rollouts produce a failure score that guides search without executing every candidate in a simulator or real system.
  We evaluate DreamTest for failure prediction, test generation, and failure diversity on Parking, Humanoid, and DonkeyCar. Mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) exceeds the strongest baseline by 97%, 12%, and 39%, respectively, and gains on five out-of-distribution test sets reach 145%, 29%, and 44%. Under the same simulator-validation budget, the best "DreamTest + search" combinations find 29%, 22%, and 79% more novel failures on average. Across clusterings with k = 2-40, failures generated with DreamTest cover the most behavioural clusters for almost all k, indicating that DreamTest consistently discovers behaviourally diverse failures.

AI.tldr: DreamTest is a world-model surrogate for testing DRL agents in cyber-physical systems. It uses a recurrent state-space model learned from agent training logs to generate imagined rollouts that predict failure scores, guiding test search without requiring full simulator execution.
AI.motivation: Testing DRL agents in cyber-physical systems is expensive, and each execution costs significantly. Prior surrogate-assisted testing approaches treat the system as a black box and predict pass/fail outcomes directly. The authors sought a more effective approach that models how tests unfold rather than simply classifying outcomes.
AI.method: DreamTest adapts a recurrent state-space model (world model) to learn agent behavior and environment dynamics from the agent's training log. Given a candidate test configuration, it generates imagined rollouts to produce a failure score that guides search, without executing every candidate in a simulator or real system.
AI.result: Mean AUPRC exceeds the strongest baseline by 97% (Parking), 12% (Humanoid), and 39% (DonkeyCar). Gains on five out-of-distribution test sets reach 145%, 29%, and 44%. Under the same simulator-validation budget, "DreamTest + search" combinations find 29%, 22%, and 79% more novel failures. Failures generated with DreamTest cover the most behavioral clusters for almost all k values (2-40).
AI.conclusion: DreamTest consistently discovers behaviorally diverse failures and significantly improves testing efficiency for DRL agents in cyber-physical systems, outperforming black-box surrogate approaches across multiple metrics including failure prediction accuracy, test generation, and failure diversity.

title: Computational Design of Free-Form Lampshades
comment: To appear in Proceedings of ACM SCF 2026
summary: Conventional lampshades are predominantly restricted to simple geometries, owing to the difficulty of controlling optical functions across complex shapes. We present a computational design method that enables 3D-printable lampshades with complex free-form shapes to achieve controlled illumination, such as uniform luminance. Given an arbitrary shape, our method determines the internal cavity geometry and the number and placement of lights in two stages: an initialization stage fixes the number of lights and establishes their initial positions and the initial cavity geometry, after which gradient-based optimization jointly refines the cavity geometry and light positions via differentiable rendering subject to geometric constraints. We calibrate the material parameters of the translucent shade material prior to optimization to improve the agreement between simulation and the fabricated result. We validate our approach by 3D-printing five lampshade designs of varying geometric complexity and demonstrate that the fabricated lampshades achieve reasonably uniform luminance.

AI.tldr: A computational design method enables 3D-printed lampshades with complex free-form shapes to achieve controlled illumination (uniform luminance). Given an arbitrary shape, the method determines internal cavity geometry and light placement through a two-stage process: initialization followed by gradient-based optimization using differentiable rendering.
AI.motivation: Conventional lampshades are restricted to simple geometries due to the difficulty of controlling optical functions across complex shapes. This limits design freedom and functional performance.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) Initialization stage fixes the number of lights and establishes initial positions and cavity geometry; (2) Gradient-based optimization jointly refines cavity geometry and light positions via differentiable rendering subject to geometric constraints. Material parameters of the translucent shade material are calibrated prior to optimization to improve simulation-fabrication agreement.
AI.result: Validated by 3D-printing five lampshade designs of varying geometric complexity. The fabricated lampshades achieve reasonably uniform luminance.
AI.conclusion: The computational design method enables 3D-printable lampshades with complex free-form shapes to achieve controlled illumination such as uniform luminance, bridging the gap between complex geometry and optical functionality.

title: Memory-State Critic for Asymmetric Actor-Critic with Application to Vision-Based Pursuit-Evasion
comment: Accepted at the 19th European Workshop on Reinforcement Learning (EWRL 2026), Lille, France. Non-archival workshop
summary: In partially observable Markov decision processes, the optimal policy generally depends on the history of observations and past actions. Asymmetric actor-critic methods have become popular to learn such policies when additional information, such as the true state of the environment, is available during training. The critic, which is not needed at execution, is given access to the state. A critic conditioned on the state alone is generally ill-defined and yields biased policy gradients. Conditioning on the state and the history, the history-state critic restores both. In this paper, we show that conditioning the critic on the state and the policy's own memory, i.e., the internal representation of the history through which the policy selects its actions, is already well-defined and gives unbiased policy gradients, removing the need for a second recurrent approximator of the history. We call it the memory state critic. It follows that a critic based on the policy's memory need not backpropagate its loss into that memory, even though the memory is a lossy encoding of the history. We evaluate the memory-state critic in a vision-based pursuit-evasion environment between two quadrotors across two arena types. The pursuer is the learning agent, and the evader is sampled per episode from a fixed pool of heuristic behaviours. The results show that the memory-state critic outperforms the history-state critic and converges faster. In addition to being unbiased compared to the state-only critic, it maintains a slight edge in the wall arena, where the actor's history carries information that the privileged state alone does not.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of biased policy gradients in asymmetric actor-critic methods for partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). The authors propose a "memory state critic" that conditions on the policy's internal memory (rather than the full history) combined with the state, eliminating the need for a second recurrent approximator while maintaining unbiased gradients.
AI.motivation: In POMDPs, optimal policies depend on observation and action history. Asymmetric actor-critic methods use privileged state information during training but face bias when the critic is conditioned on state alone. The history-state critic solves this but requires a second recurrent network, adding complexity. The authors seek a simpler solution that maintains unbiased gradients.
AI.method: The authors propose conditioning the critic on the state and the policy's own internal memory (the internal representation of history used for action selection) rather than the full history. They theoretically show this yields unbiased policy gradients without requiring backpropagation of the critic's loss into the policy's memory. The method is evaluated in a vision-based pursuit-evasion task with quadrotors across two arena types.
AI.result: The memory-state critic outperforms the history-state critic in terms of convergence speed and final performance. It maintains an advantage in the wall arena where the actor's history carries information not present in the state alone. The method is unbiased compared to the state-only critic while achieving better performance.
AI.conclusion: The memory-state critic provides a theoretically sound and practically effective solution for asymmetric actor-critic in POMDPs. By leveraging the policy's own memory representation, it achieves unbiased gradients without requiring a second recurrent approximator, resulting in faster convergence and better performance than history-state critics, especially in scenarios where historical information is valuable.

title: Proxy Confidence: Auditing Black-Box LLM Agents with a Surrogate's Log-Probabilities
summary:
A deployed LLM agent emits tool calls, queries, and code that can be silently wrong -- by the time the error surfaces, the action has run. Frontier chat APIs hide the model's token probabilities; the agent's stated confidence barely beats chance on the mistakes that matter; and resampling does not help, since frontier models are highly repetitive, reproducing the same call across samples.
  We recover the missing signal from a low-cost open-weight surrogate run in parallel. It reads the same context, schema, and proposed action as the agent, then scores the call from its own log-probabilities through a family of complementary readouts: teacher forcing and request-PMI weigh the likelihood of each argument value, a discriminative verdict judges the call as a whole, and tool-choice competition tests the function against its siblings. One principle says which to trust: a generative likelihood localizes wrong argument values, while the verdict catches holistically wrong calls. When the error type is unknown, an ensemble is the low-regret default. The readout is training-free, needs no access to the agent's internals, and costs one prefill pass alongside the tool call.
  On difficult coding tasks it reaches AUROC 0.825 where the actor's stated confidence is near chance (0.598), and the generative readouts beat it by +0.07 to +0.28 across three further actors. Against self-consistency it gains +0.14 to +0.19 on near-deterministic actors, at 1/K the cost. The signal drives two deployment modes: a real-time gate escalating the least-trustworthy calls for review (+0.05 to +0.30 accepted-action accuracy at 50% coverage), and confidence feedback, returning the tool result with the score so the agent adapts its next step -- lifting task success on live-execution benchmarks (+0.119 and +0.137, p <= 1e-4) and beating a random-value control where step errors are silent (+0.078, p = 0.003).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free method to detect errors in LLM agent tool calls by running a parallel open-weight surrogate model that scores the proposed actions using multiple complementary readouts (teacher forcing, request-PMI, discriminative verdict, and tool-choice competition). This method achieves AUROC 0.825 on difficult coding tasks, significantly outperforming the agent's stated confidence (0.598), and enables two deployment modes: real-time gating and confidence feedback that improves task success rates.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can emit silently wrong tool calls, queries, and code. Existing safeguards (frontier chat API token probabilities, stated confidence, resampling) fail because: 1) APIs hide token probabilities, 2) stated confidence barely beats chance on critical errors, and 3) frontier models are highly repetitive, reproducing the same mistake across samples.
AI.method: The method runs a low-cost open-weight surrogate model in parallel that reads the same context, schema, and proposed action as the agent. It scores the tool call using four complementary readouts: (1) teacher forcing and request-PMI weigh the likelihood of each argument value, (2) a discriminative verdict judges the call as a whole, and (3) tool-choice competition tests the function against its siblings. The key principle is that generative likelihood localizes wrong argument values while verdict catches holistically wrong calls. An ensemble is used when error type is unknown. The approach is training-free, requires no access to agent internals, and costs only one prefill pass alongside the tool call.
AI.result: On difficult coding tasks, the method achieves AUROC 0.825 where the actor's stated confidence is near chance (0.598). Generative readouts beat the baseline by +0.07 to +0.28 across three further actors. Against self-consistency, it gains +0.14 to +0.19 on near-deterministic actors at 1/K the cost. For real-time gate deployment (50% coverage), it improves accepted-action accuracy by +0.05 to +0.30. For confidence feedback, it improves task success on live-execution benchmarks by +0.119 and +0.137 (p ≤ 1e-4) and beats a random-value control by +0.078 (p = 0.003).
AI.conclusion: The missing signal for detecting LLM agent errors can be recovered from a low-cost open-weight surrogate model using complementary readouts. The method significantly outperforms the agent's stated confidence, self-consistency, and random baselines. It enables two practical deployment modes: escalating uncertain calls for human review and providing confidence feedback to the agent for adaptive planning, both of which improve overall task success rates.

title: LoRA Direction Extraction for Controllable Light Toggling in FLUX.1 Kontext
summary: We propose a fine-tuning method for flow-matching diffusion models aimed at realistic artificial light modeling without the need for a large training dataset. We address the task of controllable interior image editing, where the goal is to turn artificial light sources on or off while preserving the scene geometry, object placement, materials, and visual identity of the original image. To achieve this, we decompose the task into two independent formulations. We introduce the LoRA Direction Training Method, which extracts the pure direction of the LoRA adapter effect in the diffusion model flow field, and we also introduce specialized loss functions to ensure the realism of the inverse transformation. Additionally, the resulting increment map is used for more precise adjustment of the lighting color and temperature.

AI.tldr: A fine-tuning method for flow-matching diffusion models that enables controllable interior image editing (turning artificial lights on/off) while preserving scene properties, using LoRA Direction Training and specialized loss functions without requiring large training datasets.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of realistic artificial light modeling in interior images. Existing methods likely require large training datasets or fail to preserve scene geometry, object placement, materials, and visual identity when editing lighting. The key motivation is to achieve controllable light switching without extensive data requirements.
AI.method: The method decomposes the task into two independent formulations. (1) LoRA Direction Training Method: Extracts the pure direction of LoRA adapter effect in the diffusion model flow field. (2) Specialized loss functions ensure realism of the inverse transformation (light on→off and off→on). The resulting increment map enables precise adjustment of lighting color and temperature.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide quantitative results or comparative metrics. The method appears to enable realistic light editing while preserving scene properties, with precise color/temperature control through the increment map.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables controllable interior image editing for artificial light manipulation without requiring large training datasets, preserving scene geometry and visual identity while offering fine-grained lighting control.

title: Can LLM Agents Automate Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-Speech?
summary: Although reinforcement learning (RL) post-training repairs the localized segmental errors of zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS), arriving at a working recipe still relies on tedious manual tuning, and whether LLM agents can take over this research pipeline is unclear. We investigate this question with AgenticTTS-Forge, a collaborative workflow that structures human guidance and agentic execution around a shared workspace, applied to CosyVoice2-0.5B. To measure what the agent automates, we audit its trajectory stage by stage against the published recipe. To measure what it exploits, we score its policies with held-out observers hidden from the agent. Our results show that the agent recovers an underspecified recipe, improves it, and, when gains stall, surveys the literature unprompted and pivots from the LM carrier to the flow carrier, halving Bad cases. However, its autonomy exposes three traps across the data, proxy, and algorithm axes: the held-out set leaks through a channel the contract never reads, a self-shaped reward inflates the proxy where it is scored, and separately tuned policies do not compose additively. These findings show that the binding constraint is measurement rather than reasoning, and can inform the design of harnesses whose contracts read every channel the agent does.

AI.tldr: LLM agents can automate TTS post-training repair, improving recipes and even pivoting to better approaches, but face three traps: data leakage through unread channels, reward inflation, and non-additive policy composition—indicating measurement, not reasoning, is the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot TTS produces segmental errors requiring RL post-training, but manual recipe tuning is tedious. The authors investigate whether LLM agents can automate this research pipeline.
AI.method: AgenticTTS-Forge: a collaborative human-agent workflow applied to CosyVoice2-0.5B. Trajectory audited against published recipe; policies scored by held-out observers hidden from the agent.
AI.result: Agent recovers and improves underspecified recipe, surveys literature unprompted, pivots from LM to flow carrier (halving Bad cases). However, three traps: data leakage via unread contract channel, self-shaped reward inflation, and non-additive policy composition.
AI.conclusion: The binding constraint is measurement rather than reasoning. Design implication: contracts should read every channel the agent accesses to prevent leakage.

title: Practical Runtime Enforcement of First-Order Temporal Requirements
summary:
Runtime enforcers observe a system's behavior and exert control over it to ensure that the system always adheres to its requirements. Many natural requirements not only formulate restrictions on the system's present behavior, but also impose obligations on its future behavior; for instance, agentic security may require personal data collected during a run to be erased by some deadline. In an ever-growing compliance landscape, real-world systems may be subject to hundreds of such requirements. However, existing enforcement mechanisms supporting complex policies are often too slow for production software; instead, developers may resort to non-temporal access control mechanisms and ad-hoc instrumentation, but these scale poorly with requirement complexity.
  To address this problem, we introduce an efficient algorithm and tool for enforcing complex temporal requirements and demonstrate its performance. Specifically, we identify a fragment of Metric First-Order Temporal Logic (MFOTL) that can be enforced with low runtime complexity while supporting a rich family of practically relevant requirements, including obligations. We then design an enforcement algorithm for this fragment and implement it in EnfFlash, a novel tool that enforces requirements with latency up to 44x lower than EnfGuard, the previous state-of-the-art enforcer, on standard benchmarks, and up to three orders of magnitude lower on security policies for LLM agents. This performance is achieved by compiling requirements into imperative programs that we efficiently interpret. We evaluate EnfFlash both standalone, on existing benchmarks, and integrated in web applications as an enforcement backend. We demonstrate that it can enforce a substantial 400-line MFOTL formula specifying the GDPR on a social network while adding under 15 ms to each page view, which is sufficient for most interactive and real-time applications.

AI.tldr: EnfFlash is a novel runtime enforcement tool that efficiently enforces complex temporal requirements written in a fragment of Metric First-Order Temporal Logic (MFOTL). It compiles requirements into imperative programs for efficient interpretation, achieving 44x lower latency than prior state-of-the-art and can enforce a 400-line GDPR formula with under 15ms overhead.
