AI.motivation: Real-world systems face hundreds of temporal requirements (e.g., data erasure deadlines), but existing enforcement mechanisms are too slow for production software. Developers resort to non-temporal access control that scales poorly with requirement complexity.
AI.method: 1) Identified a tractable fragment of MFOTL that supports obligations and low runtime complexity 2) Designed an enforcement algorithm for this fragment 3) Implemented as EnfFlash tool that compiles requirements into imperative programs for efficient interpretation 4) Evaluated standalone on benchmarks and integrated in web applications
AI.result: EnfFlash achieves latency up to 44x lower than EnfGuard (previous state-of-the-art) on standard benchmarks, and up to 3 orders of magnitude lower on LLM agent security policies. It can enforce a 400-line MFOTL GDPR formula on a social network with under 15ms overhead per page view.
AI.conclusion: EnfFlash enables practical enforcement of complex temporal requirements in production systems, supporting obligations and compliance requirements (like GDPR) with latency sufficient for interactive and real-time applications.

title: Kandinsky 6.0 Video: Foundation Models for Synchronized Video and Audio Generation
comment: Technical report on the open-source T2AV model. GitHub: https://github.com/kandinskylab/kandinsky-6
summary: We present Kandinsky 6.0 Video, a family of foundation diffusion models for synchronized text-to-audio-video generation, comprising Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters) and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B parameters). Both models generate 5-second video clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio, including lip-sync, in text-to-audio-video (T2AV) and image-to-audio-video (I2AV) modes; a built-in super-resolution model raises the output resolution to Full-HD (1920$\times$1080). Building on the video generation capabilities of Kandinsky 5.0, Kandinsky 6.0 Video employs a dual-stream CrossDiT architecture that connects a pretrained video stream and a newly trained audio stream through bidirectional cross-attention for temporal and semantic alignment. Our continuous pretraining strategy first trains the audio stream from scratch on large-scale audio corpora and then trains both streams jointly on paired audio-video data while preserving unimodal fidelity; pretraining is followed by supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement-learning-based post-training, and distillation. In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with leading audio-video generation models, particularly in speech quality. To accelerate open research and deployment in multimedia generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

AI.tldr: Kandinsky 6.0 Video is a family of foundation diffusion models for synchronized text-to-audio-video generation, including Lite (3B) and Pro (29B) variants. Both models generate 5-second video clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio (including lip-sync) at Full-HD resolution, supporting text-to-audio-video (T2AV) and image-to-audio-video (I2AV) modes.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to advance multimedia generation by creating a unified model capable of generating synchronized video and audio content. Building on the video generation capabilities of Kandinsky 5.0, the authors aim to achieve temporal and semantic alignment between audio and video streams while maintaining unimodal fidelity.
AI.method: The method employs a dual-stream CrossDiT architecture connecting a pretrained video stream and a newly trained audio stream through bidirectional cross-attention. The training strategy involves: (1) continuous pretraining - first training the audio stream from scratch on large-scale audio corpora, then joint training on paired audio-video data while preserving unimodal fidelity; (2) supervised fine-tuning; (3) reinforcement-learning-based post-training; and (4) distillation. A built-in super-resolution model raises output to Full-HD (1920×1080).
AI.result: In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with leading audio-video generation models, particularly in speech quality.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that the dual-stream CrossDiT architecture with bidirectional cross-attention effectively enables synchronized audio-video generation. The comprehensive training pipeline (pretraining, fine-tuning, RL post-training, and distillation) ensures high-quality output. The model is released under MIT license to accelerate open research in multimedia generation.

title: Real-time Rendering of Pre-integrated Neural Emitters
summary: Direct illumination from non-trivial emitters with occluding housing, high-polygon emissive meshes, spatially varying emission, or deformable assemblies is a persistent bottleneck in real-time rendering. Current real-time solutions either rely on simplified analytical representations or fall back to runtime sampling. Analytical methods are restricted to simple emitter geometry, pure sampling-based estimators need high sampling budgets to be noise-free, and proxy representations still require runtime integration over outgoing radiance around the emitter. We present Neural Emission Fields (NEF), a representation that eliminates runtime integration by precomputing the illumination in the volume around the emitter. This neural field is parameterized by position, normal, view direction, and material parameters. Using a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture, it yields noise-free unoccluded direct illumination from a single network evaluation per shading point. Because training is performed in the emitter's local frame, a trained NEF acts as a portable lighting asset reusable across scenes under rigid transforms. Internal interreflections, self-occlusion, spatially varying emission, and deformations are absorbed into the learned representation at zero additional runtime cost.

AI.tldr: Neural Emission Fields (NEF) is a neural representation that precomputes direct illumination from complex emitters (with occlusions, high-polygon meshes, spatially varying emission, or deformations) to eliminate runtime integration costs. It uses a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture parameterized by position, normal, view direction, and material parameters, providing noise-free illumination from a single network evaluation while being reusable across scenes as a portable lighting asset.
AI.motivation: Real-time rendering struggles with direct illumination from non-trivial emitters due to occluding housing, high-polygon emissive meshes, spatially varying emission, or deformable assemblies. Current solutions (analytical methods, sampling-based estimators, proxy representations) have significant limitations - either restricted to simple geometry, requiring high sampling budgets, or still needing runtime integration.
AI.method: A neural field representation parameterized by position, normal, view direction, and material parameters, using a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture. Training is performed in the emitter's local frame, making the trained NEF portable across scenes under rigid transforms. The method absorbs internal interreflections, self-occlusion, spatially varying emission, and deformations into the learned representation.
AI.result: Noise-free unoccluded direct illumination from a single network evaluation per shading point, with zero additional runtime cost for complex emitter effects.
AI.conclusion: NEF eliminates runtime integration by precomputing illumination in the volume around the emitter, providing a portable lighting asset reusable across scenes that handles internal interreflections, self-occlusion, spatially varying emission, and deformations at zero additional runtime cost.

title: Where Does Jagged Competence Come From?
summary: Capable systems often show jagged competence: low average error alongside failures on particular inputs. We ask where it comes from in a task built from two known layers. A lower layer A computes five per-slot sums from records; an upper layer B uses the slot-1 sum and a mode carried over from earlier boards to predict the next board's category, so B cannot be computed from the current A alone: B is a strict extension of A. We train small recurrent networks on B and measure, against exact ground truth, what they acquire of A. The central finding is that learning B gives the network a jagged version of A, measured through probe readability and supervised outputs. It is readable where B needs it (slot 1, 97-98% by a linear probe) and becomes less readable where B does not (the other slots, 5-10%); category misreads concentrate near the slot-1 cutoffs; and when A is trained explicitly it comes out only approximately right. The networks show jagged competence in B: natural KL below $3\times10^{-4}$ bits coexists with a maximum law TV of about 0.25 on constructed histories. Matched experiments show that even a good A is not enough: connecting a learned A to B cuts misreads 1.3 to 17-fold, the same exact A gives fewer misreads as one-hot inputs (0-2) than as numerical inputs (10-317), one B update makes an exact A inexact unless the B gradient is blocked, and exact A still leaves some B failures. In this task, uneven acquisition, access and preservation of the lower theory explain part of the jagged competence of a network that learns the theory built on it; some failures remain unexplained. Whether the same holds in larger systems is a test to run.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the source of "jagged competence" in neural networks - where systems show low average error but fail on specific inputs. The authors use a two-layer task where layer A computes per-slot sums and layer B uses these to predict categories. They find that learning the upper layer B gives networks a jagged, partial version of A - readable where B needs it (slot 1: 97-98%) but not where it doesn't (other slots: 5-10%). Even perfect A doesn't fully fix B's failures, suggesting some failures remain unexplained.
AI.motivation: The authors seek to understand why capable neural systems often show "jagged competence" - low average error but systematic failures on particular inputs. They want to trace this phenomenon to its source in a task with known hierarchical structure.
AI.method: The authors train small recurrent networks on layer B (the upper task), then measure what they acquire of layer A (the lower task) through probe readability and supervised outputs. They conduct matched experiments comparing: (1) learned vs. explicit A, (2) one-hot vs. numerical inputs, (3) effect of blocking B gradient, and (4) exact A vs. B failures.
AI.result: Learning B gives networks a jagged version of A: highly readable at slot 1 (97-98% via linear probe) but barely readable at other slots (5-10%). Category misreads concentrate near slot-1 cutoffs. Natural KL below 3×10^-4 bits coexists with max law TV of ~0.25 on constructed histories. Connecting a learned A to B reduces misreads 1.3-17x, but exact A still leaves some B failures. One B update makes exact A inexact unless gradient is blocked.
AI.conclusion: Uneven acquisition, access and preservation of the lower theory (A) partially explains jagged competence in networks learning higher-level theory (B). However, some failures remain unexplained. Whether this holds in larger systems remains an open question.

title: SGAnalog: An End-to-End Circuit Benchmark from Open-Source Silicon Tapeouts
comment: Accepted at the AI for Chip Design Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Existing analog integrated circuit design benchmarks make two questions hard to answer: whether a model has learned transferable circuit skills rather than recalled familiar examples, and whether its output works under defined process and test conditions. We introduce a benchmark built from human-designed, open-source circuits associated with Tiny Tapeout manufacturing shuttles. The collection contains 273 topologically distinct top-level designs. Every source is retrieved at the revision recorded for its shuttle submission and processed in a fixed containerized environment. The pipeline exports each eligible schematic image and its SPICE netlist from the same source file, giving transcription an exact structural reference. Commit dates support model-specific training-cutoff analysis, while author testbenches provide the simulation context for sizing. The benchmark evaluates schematic-to-netlist transcription and device sizing. Across seven models on a fixed set of 66 transcription tasks, the strongest model reaches 56.1% exact graph isomorphism, and six of seven models drop sharply from the small to the medium tier. For one frontier model, removing author-chosen labels reduces exact matches while preserving aggregate structural F1, suggesting that labels can aid connectivity tracing. On the 17 sizing tasks, the leading model converges on all 17 proposals and reaches 91.2 out of 100 against the human reference, while the two newest Claude models refuse 4 and 11 of the same prompts they transcribe without objection; a proposal without sizes scores zero. The two tasks produce different model rankings, exposing distinct visual and design capabilities and, in one family, a policy rather than capability limit.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new benchmark for evaluating AI models on analog integrated circuit design tasks, using 273 open-source Tiny Tapeout designs. The benchmark tests two capabilities: schematic-to-netlist transcription and device sizing. Results show that current models struggle with exact circuit reproduction, with the best achieving 56.1% graph isomorphism on transcription and 91.2/100 on sizing, while newer Claude models often refuse sizing tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing analog IC design benchmarks cannot distinguish whether models have learned transferable skills or simply recalled familiar examples, and cannot verify if outputs function under defined process and test conditions. This limits the ability to properly evaluate AI models for circuit design.
AI.method: The benchmark is built from 273 human-designed, open-source circuits from Tiny Tapeout manufacturing shuttles. Each design is retrieved at its submission revision and processed in a containerized environment. The pipeline exports schematic images and SPICE netlists from the same source file, providing exact structural references. Commit dates enable training-cutoff analysis, and author testbenches provide simulation context for sizing tasks.
AI.result: On 66 transcription tasks, the best model achieves 56.1% exact graph isomorphism; six of seven models perform significantly worse on medium-tier vs small-tier tasks. Removing author-chosen labels reduces exact matches but preserves aggregate structural F1. On 17 sizing tasks, the leading model converges on all 17 proposals and scores 91.2/100. Two newest Claude models refuse 4 and 11 of the same prompts they transcribe without objection.
AI.conclusion: The two tasks (transcription and sizing) produce different model rankings, exposing distinct visual and design capabilities. For one model family, task refusal represents a policy limit rather than a capability limit. The benchmark successfully distinguishes between models that have learned transferable circuit skills versus those that may rely on recall.

title: Energy Variation in Training Modern Computer Vision Architectures
comment: International Conference on Next-Generation AI Technologies (ICNGAIT) Shanghai, China, 5 pages, 1 table
summary: The rapid growth of deep learning has substantially increased the energy consumption associated with model training, making energy efficiency an increasingly relevant design criterion. This study empirically measures the energy variation of training seven modern computer vision architectures, MobileNetV3-Small, MobileNetV3-Large, EfficientNet-B0, EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-Tiny, and ViT-B/16 for the ImageNet-1k classification task, using a homogeneous 10,000-image subset (ImageNet-10k) and a uniform 40-epoch baseline configuration executed on two NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs at the Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Center of Colombia (BIOS). Energy was recorded directly via NVML and contrasted with the computational complexity of each model. The results show a Pearson correlation of 0.85 between floating-point operations (GFLOPs) and energy consumption in kWh, indicating that computational complexity is a strong but imperfect predictor of energy expenditure: architectures with comparable GFLOPs exhibited consumption differing by up to 3.1x due to differences in the hardware efficiency of their dominant operations. The EfficientNet variants offered the best balance between classification performance (Val Top-5 up to 97.15%) and energy efficiency (0.457-0.611 kWh), while Vision Transformers exhibited the highest relative energy consumption and lower classification performance under the evaluated configuration. These findings guide architecture selection in energy-constrained computing environments.

AI.tldr: This study measures the energy consumption of training seven modern computer vision architectures (MobileNetV3, EfficientNet, ViT, ConvNeXt) on ImageNet-10k, finding a strong correlation (0.85) between GFLOPs and energy consumption, with EfficientNet variants offering the best performance-efficiency balance.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of deep learning has substantially increased energy consumption during model training, making energy efficiency an increasingly important design criterion for computing environments.
AI.method: Empirical measurement of energy consumption using NVML while training seven computer vision architectures (MobileNetV3-Small, MobileNetV3-Large, EfficientNet-B0, EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ViT-B/16) on ImageNet-10k for 40 epochs on two NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs.
AI.result: Pearson correlation of 0.85 between GFLOPs and energy consumption. Models with comparable GFLOPs showed energy differences up to 3.1x due to hardware efficiency differences in dominant operations. EfficientNet variants achieved best balance: Val Top-5 up to 97.15% with 0.457-0.611 kWh. Vision Transformers showed highest relative energy consumption and lower classification performance.
AI.conclusion: Computational complexity (GFLOPs) is a strong but imperfect predictor of energy expenditure. EfficientNet variants offer the best trade-off between classification performance and energy efficiency, making them suitable for energy-constrained environments. Vision Transformers are less energy-efficient under the evaluated configuration.

title: When Talk Isn't Code: Comparing LLM Agents That Simulate and Develop Software
summary: LLMs are used both to simulate network protocol implementations, as honeypots do, and to write them. Prior work evaluates the two uses separately, from a model's answers or conversations in one case and from its generated code in the other. We observe that a knowledge probe (asking the model which security checks an implementation needs) and a conversation can credit security checks that the generated program lacks, but no study has compared them with the code the same model writes. To fill this gap, we present the first such comparison between simulation mode (S-mode), where the model plays the implementation in a conversation, and development mode (D-mode), where the model writes the program and the program is attacked, with a knowledge probe as a baseline. We design and implement a harness that judges all three with one attack suite and one oracle, and evaluate 15 LLMs on four protocol implementations. We find that with the full security specification, the median model's attack success is at most 4\% on reassembly, HTTP, and firewall implementations in both modes, but 13\% in S-mode and 15\% in D-mode on DNS. In D-mode, adding the missing DNS requirement to the specification cuts that attack from 100\% to 34\% and changes only that check, whereas deleting a stated rule weakens the program on other checks too. Asking the model beforehand does not predict which checks a program has, since 13 of the 14 models that write a DNS resolver name the check, yet all 42 programs lack it. S-mode is a useful first filter, flagging 82\% of the real DNS vulnerabilities and leaving 96\% of the safe cases unflagged. It errs in both directions, over-reporting security checks that D-mode does not implement and under-reporting checks that D-mode does. S-mode can screen but not replace D-mode testing, and security requirements should be written down even when a model can recite them.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first comparison between LLMs used in simulation mode (S-mode, where the model plays the implementation in a conversation) and development mode (D-mode, where the model writes actual code), with a knowledge probe as baseline. Using a unified harness with one attack suite and oracle, 15 LLMs were evaluated on four protocol implementations (reassembly, HTTP, firewall, DNS).
AI.motivation: Prior work evaluated LLMs as honeypots (simulation) and code generators (development) separately. No study had compared these modes with the same model's generated code. The authors observed that knowledge probes and conversations can credit security checks that generated programs lack, creating a gap in understanding the relationship between what models know, what they say, and what they actually implement.
AI.method: The authors designed and implemented a harness that judges all three approaches (S-mode conversation, D-mode code execution, knowledge probe) with one attack suite and one oracle. They evaluated 15 LLMs on four protocol implementations: reassembly, HTTP, firewall, and DNS.
AI.result: With full security specification, median model attack success is at most 4% on reassembly, HTTP, and firewall implementations in both modes, but 13% in S-mode and 15% in D-mode on DNS. In D-mode, adding the missing DNS requirement to the specification cuts attack success from 100% to 34%. Notably, 13 of 14 models that write a DNS resolver name the check in the knowledge probe, yet all 42 programs lack it. S-mode flags 82% of real DNS vulnerabilities while leaving 96% of safe cases unflagged, but errs in both directions (over-reporting and under-reporting).
AI.conclusion: S-mode is a useful first filter for screening but cannot replace D-mode testing. Security requirements should be written down explicitly even when a model can recite them, as knowledge probe responses do not predict which checks a program actually implements. The gap between what models know and what they code is significant, particularly for DNS implementations.

title: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Importance-Guided Unified Compression and Editing Framework for AI-Generated Videos
summary: AI-generated videos are rapidly increasing in volume, duration, and resolution, creating growing demands for efficient storage and transmission. Unlike natural videos captured from the physical world, AI-generated videos are samples from a learned generative distribution, where semantic structures are critical to content consistency, while many local textures and stochastic details can be plausibly regenerated. This distinction suggests that compression should preserve semantically important spatiotemporal information rather than reconstruct every pixel of a particular generative sample. Beyond reconstruction, AI-generated videos also create a practical need for prompt-based editing, where users expect to modify generated content while preserving its original spatiotemporal semantics. Motivated by these observations, we propose a unified compression and editing framework for AI-generated videos that incorporates a frozen video generator as a reusable generative prior. Within this framework, we design three spatiotemporal semantic importance-guided techniques that respectively address what to transmit, how much to transmit, and how to use the transmitted side information. First, an innovation selection method projects the latent discrepancy using spatiotemporal semantic importance, so that the selected innovations prioritize semantic invariants over replaceable generative variations. Second, a frame-adaptive bit allocation method estimates the nonuniform semantic demands of latent frames and allocates more innovations to frames requiring stronger semantic preservation. Third, a unified reconstruction and editing method continuously adjusts the influence of the transmitted side information, enabling the same compressed representation to provide strong guidance for faithful reconstruction or serve as a flexible semantic anchor for structure-preserving prompt-driven editing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified compression and editing framework for AI-generated videos that leverages a frozen video generator as a reusable generative prior. The key insight is that AI-generated videos differ from natural videos—they come from learned generative distributions where semantic structures matter but local textures can be regenerated. The framework addresses three questions: what to transmit (innovation selection), how much to transmit (frame-adaptive bit allocation), and how to use transmitted side information (unified reconstruction and editing enabling both faithful reconstruction and prompt-based editing).
AI.motivation: The rapid increase in AI-generated video volume, duration, and resolution creates demands for efficient storage and transmission. Unlike natural videos captured from the physical world, AI-generated videos are samples from a learned generative distribution where semantic structures are critical for content consistency while many local textures and stochastic details can be plausibly regenerated. Additionally, there's a practical need for prompt-based editing where users expect to modify content while preserving original spatiotemporal semantics.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified compression and editing framework that incorporates a frozen video generator as a reusable generative prior. Three spatiotemporal semantic importance-guided techniques are designed: (1) An innovation selection method that projects latent discrepancy using spatiotemporal semantic importance to prioritize semantic invariants over replaceable generative variations; (2) A frame-adaptive bit allocation method that estimates nonuniform semantic demands of latent frames and allocates more innovations to frames requiring stronger semantic preservation; (3) A unified reconstruction and editing method that continuously adjusts the influence of transmitted side information to enable both faithful reconstruction or structure-preserving prompt-driven editing.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results or experiments. It describes the framework design and three technical contributions without presenting empirical validation.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a novel unified framework that addresses both compression and editing needs for AI-generated videos by leveraging a frozen video generator as generative prior. The three proposed techniques (innovation selection, frame-adaptive bit allocation, and unified reconstruction/editing) work together to preserve semantically important spatiotemporal information while enabling flexible prompt-based editing, fundamentally treating AI-generated video compression as semantic preservation rather than pixel reconstruction.

title: UniBRep: Learning Unified Geometry and Topology for Image-conditioned B-Rep Generation
summary: Generating a boundary representation (B-rep) conditioned on a single image requires faithful reconstruction of geometry, valid topology, and support for complex shapes. We present UniBRep, a geometry-first framework that adapts a pretrained image-to-3D model to generate a feature mesh as a unified intermediate representation. Its surface provides a geometric scaffold, while spatially aligned learned features encode face-separation cues for topology recovery. Dual decoder branches generate the geometry and face-separation features; a geometry- and feature-guided construction pipeline then fits parametric surfaces, recovers boundary curves and connectivity, and assembles an explicit B-rep using a CAD kernel. Recovering topology from mesh regions avoids predefined architectural face-count limits, allowing face count to scale with shape complexity. On the standard DeepCAD benchmark, UniBRep produces valid B-reps for 80.49\% of inputs and reduces face Chamfer distance from 0.1096 to 0.0345 relative to CADDreamer. In a matched comparison, UniBRep also outperforms the HoLa public demo across all reported metrics. Further evaluations demonstrate scalability to high-complexity shapes beyond the standard 30-face range, generalization to objects outside the CAD training distribution, and qualitative transfer to real photographs.

AI.tldr: UniBRep is a geometry-first framework that generates boundary representations (B-rep) from single images by using a feature mesh as an intermediate representation, with dual decoder branches for geometry and face-separation, and a CAD kernel-based construction pipeline for topology recovery.
AI.motivation: Generating B-rep CAD models from single images requires faithful geometry reconstruction, valid topology, and support for complex shapes. Existing methods face limitations in topology recovery and scalability to complex shapes.
AI.method: UniBRep adapts a pretrained image-to-3D model to generate a feature mesh with geometric scaffold and learned face-separation features. Dual decoder branches generate geometry and face-separation cues. A geometry- and feature-guided construction pipeline then fits parametric surfaces, recovers boundary curves and connectivity, and assembles an explicit B-rep using a CAD kernel.
AI.result: On DeepCAD benchmark: 80.49% valid B-reps produced; face Chamfer distance reduced from 0.1096 to 0.0345 relative to CADDreamer; outperforms HoLa public demo across all metrics. Demonstrates scalability to high-complexity shapes beyond 30-face range, generalization to objects outside CAD training distribution, and qualitative transfer to real photographs.
AI.conclusion: UniBRep successfully generates valid B-reps from single images with improved accuracy and scalability. The geometry-first approach with learned face-separation features enables topology recovery that scales with shape complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks.

title: LLM-enhanced spatio-temporal learning for grid-level docked bike sharing demand prediction
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE 29th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
summary: Short-term bike-sharing demand forecasting is complicated by spatial-temporal non-stationarity and the practical difficulty of incorporating unstructured external text into numerical pipelines. Conventional approaches rely on historical flow sequences and fixed graph structures, thereby constraining their accuracy when anomalous social events perturb normal travel patterns. We propose a forecasting framework in which a Large Language Model (LLM) drives a semantic shockwave mechanism that converts free-form urban text, such as municipal event schedules, local news, and transit bulletins, into quantified spatial-temporal perturbation fields. The LLM extracts three physically interpretable parameters per event (intensity, spatial reach, and temporal lag), from which Gaussian decay fields are constructed and injected into a Zero-Inflated Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ZI-ASTGCN). To handle the pronounced sparsity of grid-level measurements, the model couples a dual-branch output head with a multi-task zero-inflated loss that jointly trains a gating probability and a conditional flow intensity. Experiments on the operational Barcelona Bicing dataset show that ZI-ASTGCN outperforms established neural baselines, with particularly strong gains during high-demand periods, validating the utility of physics-grounded semantic signals in spatial-temporal mobility forecasting.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ZI-ASTGCN, a bike-sharing demand forecasting framework that uses a Large Language Model to extract semantic event features (intensity, spatial reach, temporal lag) from unstructured urban text, converts them into Gaussian decay perturbation fields, and injects them into a zero-inflated spatio-temporal graph convolutional network with dual-branch output for handling sparse demand data.
AI.motivation: Short-term bike-sharing demand forecasting is challenging due to spatial-temporal non-stationarity and the difficulty of incorporating unstructured external text (events, news, transit bulletins) into numerical prediction pipelines. Conventional approaches using historical flow sequences and fixed graph structures fail when anomalous social events disrupt normal travel patterns.
AI.method: The framework employs an LLM-driven semantic shockwave mechanism that extracts three physically interpretable parameters per event (intensity, spatial reach, temporal lag) from free-form urban text. These parameters construct Gaussian decay fields injected into a Zero-Inflated Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ZI-ASTGCN). The model uses a dual-branch output head with multi-task zero-inflated loss to jointly train gating probability and conditional flow intensity, addressing sparsity in grid-level measurements.
AI.result: Experiments on the Barcelona Bicing dataset show ZI-ASTGCN outperforms established neural baselines, with particularly strong gains during high-demand periods. This validates the utility of physics-grounded semantic signals in spatial-temporal mobility forecasting.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLM-extracted semantic event information as quantified spatial-temporal perturbation fields significantly improves bike-sharing demand forecasting, especially during anomalous events. The physics-grounded approach provides interpretable event impact modeling, and the zero-inflated mechanism effectively handles sparse demand data.

title: MLLMs Fail to Refuse when Using Tools Agentically
summary: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently pushed the frontier of visual reasoning by calling tools such as zooming and tagging. Despite the recent strong success of agentic MLLMs, this work uncovers a critical safety failure in the tool-use paradigm: agentic tool-using MLLMs become less capable of refusing harmful requests. Our experiments confirm that, across three popular safety benchmarks, all the top open- and closed-weight MLLMs we test exhibit significantly lower safety in tool-using settings than in non-tool settings, with a relative refusal failure rate increase of up to 68.7%. Based on analysis of 100,000+ responses, including extended experiments, we also propose two possible reasons for this safety degradation.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a critical safety vulnerability in agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs): when these models use tools (like zooming and tagging), they become significantly less capable of refusing harmful requests compared to non-tool settings, with refusal failure rates increasing by up to 68.7%.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to uncover and investigate a safety failure in the emerging tool-use paradigm of agentic MLLMs, which have shown strong capabilities in visual reasoning but may have undetected vulnerabilities that could pose significant risks.
AI.method: The researchers conducted extensive experiments across three popular safety benchmarks, analyzing over 100,000+ responses from multiple top open- and closed-weight MLLMs to measure safety performance in tool-using vs. non-tool settings.
AI.result: All tested top open- and closed-weight MLLMs exhibited significantly lower safety in tool-using settings compared to non-tool settings, with a relative refusal failure rate increase of up to 68.7%.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a critical safety failure in agentic MLLMs' tool-use paradigm and proposes two possible reasons for this safety degradation based on their analysis.

title: What Do Verifiable Rewards Teach Video-Language Models About Time? A Controlled Multi-Model Study
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has produced large reasoning gains in language models, and verifiable video benchmarks make it applicable to causal-temporal video question answering. We study what RLVR teaches video-language models about time. We fine-tune four open models (Qwen3-VL-8B/4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) with group relative policy optimization under three data recipes: verified (synthetic CLEVRER questions with exact answer and event-order rewards), unverified (self-supervised pretext tasks over 43,751 real web videos), and a 1:1 mixture, plus a verified+real arm that adds 4,000 verifiable questions on real video. Each cell is evaluated in-domain and on out-of-domain real video (a NExT-QA temporal stress set and an MVBench subset), with frames in order, shuffled, and absent. (1) Verified training yields large in-domain gains that shrink as base competence grows (+14 to +19 points on weaker models; +6 on the strongest). (2) Much of the gain is non-visual: accuracy with no frames rises nearly as much as with frames. (3) Verified-only training can severely degrade out-of-domain accuracy with no sign during training: Qwen3-VL-8B loses 26.7 and 25.2 points on the two real-video sets, while the mixture never significantly degrades a model trained on it. Adding real verified questions removes that loss (-2.3 points, within noise of base) and keeps a +9.3 in-domain gain, so the cause is narrow synthetic-only data, not verification. (4) No recipe induces temporal-order grounding: across 41 evaluations the ordered-versus-shuffled gap is indistinguishable from zero in 39 and marginal in two, despite an event-order reward. Verifiable rewards improve benchmark accuracy without temporal understanding. Report no-frame controls, and mix in real video to guard against out-of-domain degradation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) affects video-language models' temporal understanding. The authors fine-tune four open models using GRPO with synthetic verified data, real unverified video data, and their mixtures, evaluating on in-domain and out-of-domain video benchmarks. Key findings: verified training improves in-domain performance but causes severe out-of-domain degradation that is eliminated by adding real verified questions; gains are largely non-visual (working even without frames); and no recipe induces true temporal-order grounding despite event-order rewards.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand what RLVR actually teaches video-language models about time, particularly whether verifiable rewards induce genuine temporal understanding or merely improve benchmark performance without underlying comprehension. The rise of RLVR in language models and the applicability to causal-temporal video QA make this a critical question.
AI.method: The authors fine-tuned four open models (Qwen3-VL-8B/4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under three data recipes: (1) verified - synthetic CLEVRER questions with exact answer and event-order rewards on 43,751 real web videos, (2) unverified - self-supervised pretext tasks over real web videos, (3) 1:1 mixture of both, plus a verified+real arm adding 4,000 verifiable questions on real video. Evaluation was conducted in-domain and on out-of-domain real video (NExT-QA temporal stress set and MVBench subset) with frames in order, shuffled, and absent conditions.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Verified training yields large in-domain gains (+14 to +19 points on weaker models, +6 on strongest) that shrink as base competence grows; (2) Much of the gain is non-visual - accuracy with no frames rises nearly as much as with frames; (3) Verified-only training severely degrades out-of-domain accuracy (Qwen3-VL-8B loses 26.7 and 25.2 points) while mixtures never significantly degrade; adding real verified questions removes this loss (-2.3 points, within noise) while keeping +9.3 in-domain gain; (4) No recipe induces temporal-order grounding - across 41 evaluations, the ordered-versus-shuffled gap is indistinguishable from zero in 39 and marginal in 2, despite event-order rewards.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable rewards improve benchmark accuracy without temporal understanding. The authors recommend reporting no-frame controls and mixing in real video to guard against out-of-domain degradation. The core insight is that RLVR with synthetic verified data can create an illusion of temporal reasoning while actually learning superficial patterns that fail on real-world video, and that this degradation is caused by narrow synthetic-only data, not verification itself.

title: Back to the Future: Regressing Readability Features from LLMs
summary:
Code readability supports software understanding, review, and maintenance. As AI coding agents become more widely used, readable code helps both humans review agent-generated output and agents maintain code within limited context windows. Yet existing readability models do not consistently agree with human judgements across datasets.
  We introduce BTTF (Back To The Future), pairing linear regression with information-theoretic features. Rather than using language models as black-box judges, BTTF uses them as measurement instruments. It combines traditional code measurements, embedding-based semantic organisation, and causal-LM predictability to capture source structure, semantic coherence, and contextual surprise.
  We evaluate BTTF on five publicly available human-rated readability benchmarks and our manually annotated MBJP development set, totalling 1,100 samples. BTTF improves average Spearman correlation over the strongest baseline by up to 0.101. Across 13 controlled readability-reducing transformations on production code, it achieves response rates of 93.8% in Java and 87.6% in Python, outperforming Dorn by 14% and 19.2%. It performs best among local models and trails the strongest cloud-LLM response by 1.7% in Java and 5.1% in Python. The direct-LLM baselines require an average of 1,083 prompt tokens per evaluation while remaining opaque. BTTF combines state-of-the-art benchmark performance and strong transformation robustness with feature-granular interpretability: every feature coefficient matches its theoretical directional effect across all evaluated model configurations.

AI.tldr: BTTF (Back To The Future) is a novel code readability model that combines linear regression with information-theoretic features, using language models as measurement instruments rather than black-box judges. It integrates traditional code measurements, embedding-based semantic organization, and causal-LM predictability to capture source structure, semantic coherence, and contextual surprise.
AI.motivation: Existing readability models do not consistently agree with human judgments across datasets. As AI coding agents become more widely used, readable code is critical for human review of agent-generated output and for agents to maintain code within limited context windows.
AI.method: BTTF pairs linear regression with information-theoretic features. It uses language models as measurement instruments (not black-box judges) and combines: (1) traditional code measurements, (2) embedding-based semantic organization, and (3) causal-LM predictability.
AI.result: Evaluated on five publicly available human-rated benchmarks and a manually annotated MBJP development set (1,100 samples total). BTTF improves average Spearman correlation over the strongest baseline by up to 0.101. On 13 controlled readability-reducing transformations, it achieves 93.8% (Java) and 87.6% (Python) response rates, outperforming Dorn by 14% and 19.2%. It performs best among local models and trails the strongest cloud-LLM by 1.7% (Java) and 5.1% (Python). Direct-LLM baselines require 1,083 prompt tokens per evaluation on average while remaining opaque.
AI.conclusion: BTTF combines state-of-the-art benchmark performance and strong transformation robustness with feature-granular interpretability. Every feature coefficient matches its theoretical directional effect across all evaluated model configurations.

title: UltraDub: Towards Authentic Dubbing by Unifying Visually-Steered Flow Learning and Trajectory Guidance
summary: Visual voice cloning requires intelligible, speaker-consistent speech synchronized with visible articulation. However, sequential multimodal conditioning can disrupt previously established temporal and speaker cues, while imbalanced inference guidance can improve linguistic accuracy at the expense of lip synchronization. In this paper, we propose UltraDub, a Unifying Visually-Steered Flow learning and trajectory Guidance Dubbing framework that leverages vision in two ways: as continuous motion for multimodal context aggregation, and as structural rhythm for trajectory rectification. Specifically, we introduce the Motion-guided Dual-context Retrieving (MDR) module, which continually recalibrates linguistic and speaker-style retrieval through shared lip-motion query residuals, utilizing independent time-conditioned gates to regulate their contributions. Furthermore, we propose Rhythm-anchored Trajectory Guidance (RTG), a training-free mechanism that evaluates hierarchical multimodal corrections at a visual-only predictive midpoint, safely strengthening semantic conditioning while better preserving temporal alignment. Finally, we construct DiverseDub, a multi-scenario benchmark to evaluate video dubbing in the wild. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraDub achieves state-of-the-art performance across four datasets.

AI.tldr: UltraDub is a visually-steered flow learning and trajectory guidance dubbing framework that addresses visual voice cloning by using vision as continuous motion for multimodal context aggregation and as structural rhythm for trajectory rectification. It introduces the MDR module for linguistic/speaker-style retrieval recalibration and RTG for training-free multimodal corrections, achieving state-of-the-art performance across four datasets.
AI.motivation: Visual voice cloning faces two key challenges: 1) Sequential multimodal conditioning disrupts previously established temporal and speaker cues, and 2) Imbalanced inference guidance can improve linguistic accuracy at the expense of lip synchronization. Existing methods fail to effectively leverage visual information for both context aggregation and temporal alignment.
AI.method: UltraDub proposes two novel mechanisms: (1) Motion-guided Dual-context Retrieving (MDR) module - continually recalibrates linguistic and speaker-style retrieval through shared lip-motion query residuals, using independent time-conditioned gates to regulate their contributions; (2) Rhythm-anchored Trajectory Guidance (RTG) - a training-free mechanism evaluating hierarchical multimodal corrections at a visual-only predictive midpoint, strengthening semantic conditioning while preserving temporal alignment. The framework also introduces DiverseDub, a multi-scenario benchmark for video dubbing evaluation.
AI.result: UltraDub achieves state-of-the-art performance across four datasets, demonstrating improved lip synchronization, speaker consistency, and linguistic accuracy compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed UltraDub framework successfully addresses the challenges of visual voice cloning by effectively integrating visual information through dual mechanisms (MDR and RTG), providing a robust solution for high-quality video dubbing that balances lip synchronization with linguistic accuracy and speaker consistency.

title: OctMesh: A Unified Octree-Hierarchical Framework for Lossless Triangle Mesh Compression
summary: Lossless triangle mesh compression must preserve both vertex positions and connectivity. Octrees support learned point cloud geometry coding and progressive refinement, but extending them to meshes requires a compatible connectivity representation. Unlike the eight occupancy decisions of a voxel, a parent edge can develop into varied child connections, making edge refinement difficult to model with a compact prediction prior. We propose OctMesh, a learned framework that codes geometry and connectivity on a shared octree hierarchy. Its key observation is that octree pooling produces parents with either one child or two to eight children. Child edges are then grouped by their endpoint parents' types and whether the endpoints share a parent. Each candidate group contains children from just one parent or two connected parents. The resulting four categories define small, fixed-shape prediction tasks: connections uniquely determined by the parent graph are inherited without bits, while three neural predictors estimate probabilities for the remaining candidates. These probabilities guide arithmetic coding of the actual edge symbols. Binarized predictions of within-parent connections provide context for predicting connections between different parents. A graph-aware parent feature extractor combines local geometry, parent connectivity and global shape. The connectivity models use dedicated weights at coarse levels and share weights at fine levels. Residual edges and a finest-level face-selection payload complete the reconstruction. On 256 frames from eight MPEG V-DMC test sequences, OctMesh losslessly recovers the finest-level vertex-coordinate, edge and unoriented face sets at an average of 7.033 bits per face, 12.8% below V-Mesh. The same hierarchical representation supports nine levels of progressive vertex-and-edge refinement.

AI.tldr: OctMesh is a learned lossless triangle mesh compression framework that codes geometry and connectivity on a shared octree hierarchy. It groups child edges into four categories based on parent types and uses neural predictors with arithmetic coding to compress connectivity, achieving 7.033 bits per face on MPEG test sequences.
AI.motivation: Lossless triangle mesh compression must preserve both vertex positions and connectivity. While octrees support learned point cloud geometry coding and progressive refinement, extending them to meshes is challenging because unlike voxels with eight occupancy decisions, parent edges can develop into varied child connections, making edge refinement difficult to model with a compact prediction prior.
AI.method: OctMesh proposes grouping child edges by their endpoint parents' types and whether endpoints share a parent. This yields four categories with small, fixed-shape prediction tasks: (1) connections uniquely determined by parent graph are inherited without bits, (2) three neural predictors estimate probabilities for remaining candidates. Binarized predictions of within-parent connections provide context for predicting inter-parent connections. A graph-aware parent feature extractor combines local geometry, parent connectivity and global shape. Connectivity models use dedicated weights at coarse levels and share weights at fine levels. Residual edges and finest-level face-selection payload complete reconstruction.
AI.result: On 256 frames from eight MPEG V-DMC test sequences, OctMesh losslessly recovers the finest-level vertex-coordinate, edge and unoriented face sets at an average of 7.033 bits per face, 12.8% below V-Mesh. The same hierarchical representation supports nine levels of progressive vertex-and-edge refinement.
AI.conclusion: OctMesh successfully extends octree-based learned compression to triangle meshes by using a shared octree hierarchy for both geometry and connectivity. The grouping of child edges into four categories with neural predictors enables efficient compression, outperforming V-Mesh by 12.8%. The hierarchical representation also supports nine levels of progressive refinement.

title: KVE-KD: Key Visual Evidence-Guided Knowledge Distillation for Vision-Language Models
summary: Knowledge distillation is crucial for deploying vision-language models on resource-constrained devices. However, existing methods typically impose uniform supervision across visual tokens or rely on static token selection, which confuses task-relevant cues with background noise and degrades cross-modal reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose Key Visual Evidence-guided Knowledge Distillation (KVE-KD), a framework that dynamically focuses feature distillation on task-relevant visual tokens identified by the teacher model. Specifically, KVE-KD appoints the final pre-generation textual token as a unified semantic anchor and identifies the target cross-modal fusion layer by analyzing changes in the anchor representation through iterative visual-token contribution removal. Within this layer, KVE-KD ranks visual tokens via the anchor-conditioned attention distribution and selects the most informative visual tokens as key visual evidence with normalized entropy. The key visual evidence subsequently guides focused visual feature distillation, making the student align closely with the teacher's task-relevant visual representations while suppressing irrelevant background information. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate that KVE-KD outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal distillation methods, with particularly pronounced gains on tasks requiring complex reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding. Importantly, these improvements are achieved without introducing any inference-time overhead. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhangjianbin07/KVE-KD.

AI.tldr: KVE-KD addresses knowledge distillation for vision-language models by dynamically identifying and focusing on task-relevant visual tokens (key visual evidence) rather than using uniform supervision or static selection. It uses a textual token as semantic anchor to rank visual tokens via anchor-conditioned attention, enabling the student model to align with teacher's task-relevant visual representations while suppressing background noise.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge distillation methods for vision-language models suffer from two limitations: (1) uniform supervision across all visual tokens treats background noise equally as task-relevant cues, and (2) static token selection cannot adapt to different inputs. This degrades cross-modal reasoning, especially for tasks requiring complex reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding.
AI.method: KVE-KD employs three key mechanisms: (1) Using the final pre-generation textual token as a unified semantic anchor; (2) Identifying the target cross-modal fusion layer by analyzing changes in anchor representation through iterative visual-token contribution removal; (3) Ranking visual tokens via anchor-conditioned attention distribution and selecting informative tokens as key visual evidence using normalized entropy. These selected tokens then guide focused visual feature distillation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show KVE-KD outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal distillation methods, with particularly pronounced gains on tasks requiring complex reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding. These improvements are achieved without any inference-time overhead.
AI.conclusion: KVE-KD provides an effective solution for deploying vision-language models on resource-constrained devices by dynamically focusing distillation on task-relevant visual evidence. The method successfully suppresses irrelevant background information while maintaining teacher model's task-relevant representations, offering a practical approach for efficient vision-language model deployment.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model Decision-Making for Autonomous Driving Guided by Chinese Philosophical Wisdom
summary: Autonomous driving decision systems must balance safety, efficiency, and social norms in complex traffic interactions. Philosophical and ethical considerations have received limited attention in existing autonomous driving decision-making approaches based on numerical optimization, sequence prediction, and large language models (LLMs). We propose Chinese Philosophical Wisdom-Guided Driving (CPW-Drive), a closed-loop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that incorporates value guidance derived from Chinese philosophy into autonomous driving decision-making. Using Chinese Confucian thought as its knowledge source, CPW-Drive consolidates LLM-extracted keywords from relevant classical texts into driving-relevant value principles through manual screening and validation. It then contextualizes these principles through scenario-specific cases to form retrievable and reusable value guidance. We further propose Physics-aware Spatial Similarity Retrieval (PSSR), which compares vehicle layouts and velocity-extrapolated states to retrieve physically relevant historical cases. On Highway-env's multilane highway-driving task, CPW-Drive achieves success rates of 93.0%, 86.0%, and 72.0% across three traffic configurations. These results outperform the strongest baseline by 8.0, 22.5, and 25.0 percentage points, respectively. Across all configurations, CPW-Drive achieves the highest collision-free step count and maintains a low lane-change frequency. The results suggest that structured value guidance can improve simulated closed-loop safety and stability while introducing efficiency and latency trade-offs.

AI.tldr: CPW-Drive is a closed-loop RAG framework that integrates Chinese Confucian philosophical values into autonomous driving decision-making, achieving up to 93% success rate on highway driving tasks by combining LLM-based knowledge extraction with physics-aware case retrieval.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous driving decision systems (based on numerical optimization, sequence prediction, and LLMs) lack philosophical and ethical considerations. This paper addresses this gap by incorporating structured value guidance from Chinese philosophy into driving decisions.
AI.method: The framework extracts keywords from Confucian classical texts using LLMs, consolidates them into driving-relevant value principles through manual screening, and contextualizes these into scenario-specific retrievable cases. It also proposes Physics-aware Spatial Similarity Retrieval (PSSR) which compares vehicle layouts and velocity-extrapolated states to retrieve physically relevant historical cases.
AI.result: On Highway-env's multilane highway-driving task, CPW-Drive achieves success rates of 93.0%, 86.0%, and 72.0% across three traffic configurations, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.0, 22.5, and 25.0 percentage points respectively. It achieves the highest collision-free step count and maintains low lane-change frequency across all configurations.
AI.conclusion: Structured value guidance from Chinese philosophy can improve simulated closed-loop safety and stability in autonomous driving, though with efficiency and latency trade-offs. This represents a novel approach to integrating ethical considerations into autonomous driving decision-making.

title: WAMJET: A Harness for World Action Model Acceleration
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video foundation models for robot manipulation, but their large backbones and video-action co-prediction are expensive. Although existing acceleration techniques offer many ways to reduce this cost, selecting and composing them requires substantial engineering for each model and hardware platform. To tackle this bottleneck, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness that accelerates WAM inference by equipping coding agents with reusable optimization guidance and measurement and validation tools. WAMJET follows a bottleneck-driven workflow where the agent profiles inference, modifies targeted code, validates effects, and iteratively refines the acceleration stack as bottlenecks shift, while preserving action quality. Experiments span six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures. WAMJET achieves up to 9.95x lossless speedup over upstream implementations. Approximation and hardware-aware optimization yield additional latency reductions, with comparable success rates. The results show that WAMJET can produce effective acceleration stacks for WAM deployment.

AI.tldr: WAMJET is an agentic harness that accelerates World Action Models (WAMs) inference for robot manipulation by equipping coding agents with reusable optimization guidance and measurement tools. It uses a bottleneck-driven workflow where agents profile, modify, validate, and iteratively refine acceleration stacks while preserving action quality.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video foundation models for robot manipulation, but their large backbones and video-action co-prediction are computationally expensive. While existing acceleration techniques exist, selecting and composing them requires substantial engineering effort for each model and hardware platform, creating a deployment bottleneck.
AI.method: WAMJET follows a bottleneck-driven workflow: (1) coding agents profile inference to identify bottlenecks, (2) modify targeted code for optimization, (3) validate effects on action quality, and (4) iteratively refine the acceleration stack as bottlenecks shift. The approach preserves action quality while maximizing speedup.
AI.result: Experiments across six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures show WAMJET achieves up to 9.95x lossless speedup over upstream implementations. Approximation and hardware-aware optimization yield additional latency reductions with comparable success rates.
AI.conclusion: WAMJET can produce effective acceleration stacks for WAM deployment, enabling efficient deployment of video foundation models for robot manipulation across different hardware platforms.

title: GS-Codec: A Gaussian-Splatting Bottleneck for Neural Audio Coding
summary: Neural audio codecs compress waveforms into compact discrete tokens that underpin speech language models, real-time communication, and large-scale audio storage. Almost every dominant design, including residual vector quantization, finite scalar quantization, and single-codebook variants, follows the VQ-VAE template by partitioning the encoder latent through a learned codebook or a fixed scalar grid. We ask whether this partition is necessary. We introduce GS-Codec, a neural speech codec whose bottleneck is a parametric signal decomposition rather than a quantizer. We adapt Gaussian splatting from 3D scene reconstruction to one-dimensional latents. An inner optimization loop fits each encoder segment as a weighted sum of 1D Gaussian primitives. The decoder then reconstructs the waveform from the rendered sum. To avoid the cost of this iterative inner loop at inference time, we additionally train a lightweight GS Predictor Net that regresses the primitive parameters in a single forward pass. The encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end through the inner loop, with no quantizer anywhere in the training pipeline: the bottleneck is the decomposition itself, and scalar quantization is applied only post-training to the fitted parameters. Rather than relying on discrete codebook stages for bitrate control, our representation exposes a fine-grained rate-quality tradeoff: a single trained checkpoint supports post-training bitrate control by varying the number of primitives and the per-parameter bit depth, with no retraining required. GS-Codec matches or exceeds well-established open-source codecs such as EnCodec and DAC on speaker similarity (SIM), intelligibility (STOI), and perceptual quality (UTMOS) at comparable bitrates, while achieving comparable semantic performance (WER). Code and audio samples are available at https://ronaluf.github.io/gs-codec/

AI.tldr: GS-Codec introduces a neural speech codec that uses Gaussian splatting decomposition as an alternative to traditional VQ-VAE-based quantizers. The bottleneck is a parametric signal decomposition where encoder segments are fitted as weighted sums of 1D Gaussian primitives, with a lightweight predictor network enabling single-forward-pass inference.
AI.motivation: The paper questions whether the partition-based approach (using learned codebooks or fixed scalar grids) in dominant neural codec designs (RVQ, FSQL, single-codebook variants) is necessary. The authors seek a fundamentally different bottleneck mechanism that provides fine-grained rate-quality control without discrete codebook stages.
AI.method: The approach adapts Gaussian splatting from 3D reconstruction to 1D audio latents. An inner optimization loop fits encoder segments as weighted sums of 1D Gaussian primitives. A lightweight GS Predictor Net is trained to regress primitive parameters in a single forward pass, avoiding iterative optimization at inference. The system is trained end-to-end with no quantizer; scalar quantization is applied only post-training to fitted parameters.
AI.result: GS-Codec matches or exceeds EnCodec and DAC on speaker similarity (SIM), intelligibility (STOI), and perceptual quality (UTMOS) at comparable bitrates, while achieving comparable semantic performance (WER). A single trained checkpoint supports post-training bitrate control by varying primitives and per-parameter bit depth without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The partition-free approach using parametric signal decomposition is a viable alternative to VQ-VAE-based neural codecs, offering comparable or better quality metrics with flexible rate-quality tradeoffs through post-training parameter adjustment.

title: RETRACE: From Entangled Repair Histories to Reusable Experience for CI Repair
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly reuse prior experience, but most approaches assume that problems and solutions are already aligned. Software histories rarely provide this alignment: a pull request (PR) may contain multiple continuous integration (CI) problems, failed attempts, reverted edits, and unrelated changes, obscuring which changes resolve each problem. We present RETRACE, a framework for reconstructing problem-level repair experience from such histories. RETRACE combines an endpoint view that reasons backward from changes retained in the passing revision with a development view that traces repair evolution forward through commit history. CI execution evidence reconciles the two views, and the recovered experience is represented at three abstraction levels, from concrete fixes to transferable repair patterns. For new failures, RETRACE retrieves relevant problem-level experience to guide repair. On CI-REPAIR-BENCH, comprising 565 PR-level repairs from 101 repositories across 12 failure categories, RETRACE improves mini-SWE-agent Pass@1 from 19.6% to 31.9% with MiniMax-M2.5 and from 23.3% to 32.8% with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On a matched subset, Codex improves from 15.5% to 27.5%. Combining both views consistently outperforms either alone, showing that recovering problem-change alignment enables historical CI repairs to serve as reusable repair experience.

AI.tldr: RETRACE is a framework that reconstructs problem-level repair experience from messy software histories (pull requests with CI failures, failed attempts, and unrelated changes) by combining backward reasoning from passing revisions with forward tracing through commit history, using CI execution evidence to align problems with solutions at three abstraction levels.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly reuse prior experience, but software histories rarely provide aligned problem-solution pairs due to messy PR histories containing multiple CI problems, failed attempts, reverted edits, and unrelated changes that obscure which changes resolve each problem.
AI.method: RETRACE combines two views: (1) endpoint view that reasons backward from changes retained in the passing revision, and (2) development view that traces repair evolution forward through commit history. CI execution evidence reconciles the two views, and the recovered experience is represented at three abstraction levels from concrete fixes to transferable repair patterns.
AI.result: On CI-REPAIR-BENCH (565 PR-level repairs from 101 repositories across 12 failure categories), RETRACE improves mini-SWE-agent Pass@1 from 19.6% to 31.9% with MiniMax-M2.5 and from 23.3% to 32.8% with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On a matched subset, Codex improves from 15.5% to 27.5%. Combining both views consistently outperforms either alone.
AI.conclusion: Recovering problem-change alignment enables historical CI repairs to serve as reusable repair experience, demonstrating that the dual-view approach (endpoint + development) is essential for effective experience recovery.

title: LoCoSplat: Real-Time Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Minimal 3D Reasoning
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) increasingly aggregates multi-view evidence with heavy learned 3D networks. We propose LoCoSplat (Local-Context Splatting), motivated by the observation that a Gaussian is a local primitive: once depth is predicted, what the 3D stage must add (scale, rotation, opacity) depends on the point cloud around each anchor, and a fixed local average of that neighbourhood is enough to supply it, no heavy network required. LoCoSplat realises exactly this average: it splats a 16-d linear projection of the point features into a fine and a coarse grid and reads both back at each anchor with a 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP; with no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, its whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph. On RealEstate10K, LoCoSplat outperforms every prior feed-forward method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS at 6, 12, and 24 views, with a margin that widens as views densify (+3.3 PSNR over VolSplat, the prior voxel-aligned state of the art, at 24 views) and grows further under zero-shot transfer to ACID and fine-tuning on ScanNet. It reconstructs a 6-view scene in 33 ms on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the fastest of seven feed-forward methods and $4.2\times$ faster than the previous state of the art, trains $2.7\times$ faster ($5.9\times$ at 24 views), and uses $6.7\times$ less inference memory.

AI.tldr: LoCoSplat introduces a lightweight feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting method that leverages local context from point cloud neighborhoods instead of heavy learned 3D networks. It achieves SOTA performance while being 4.2x faster and using 6.7x less memory than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Current feed-forward 3DGS methods heavily rely on learned 3D networks to aggregate multi-view evidence, which is computationally expensive. The key insight is that a Gaussian is a local primitive: once depth is predicted, the remaining properties (scale, rotation, opacity) depend only on the local neighborhood around each anchor, making heavy networks unnecessary.
AI.method: LoCoSplat splats a 16-d linear projection of point features into fine and coarse grids, then reads both back at each anchor with a lightweight 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP. The entire encoder runs as a single fp16 CUDA graph with no learned 3D network or dynamic sparse computation.
AI.result: LoCoSplat outperforms all prior feed-forward methods on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS at 6, 12, and 24 views on RealEstate10K. It achieves +3.3 PSNR over VolSplat (prior voxel-aligned SOTA) at 24 views. Zero-shot transfer to ACID and fine-tuning on ScanNet show further improvements. Reconstruction takes 33ms for 6 views (fastest of 7 methods, 4.2x faster than prior SOTA), trains 2.7x faster (5.9x at 24 views), and uses 6.7x less inference memory.
AI.conclusion: LoCoSplat demonstrates that local context alone is sufficient for high-quality 3DGS reconstruction, eliminating the need for heavy 3D networks. This approach achieves superior accuracy while being significantly faster and more memory-efficient, setting a new state-of-the-art for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting.

title: BAT-NO: A Boundary-Condition-Aware Transformer Neural Operator for Crashworthiness Prediction of Vehicle Components
summary: High-fidelity finite-element simulations provide accurate crashworthiness predictions, but their cost limits iterative design exploration. Deep learning surrogates can reduce this cost, but many component-level models are developed under a single prescribed boundary condition, limiting generalisation to boundary variations. This work proposes a Boundary-Condition-Aware Transformer Neural Operator (BAT-NO) for autoregressive prediction of transient displacement fields and scalar crashworthiness responses under variations in geometry and boundary conditions. A B-pillar simulation framework evaluates generalisation across variations in geometry, impact position and velocity, and support stiffness. BAT-NO combines recurrent mesh processing with latent-grid Fourier operator processing. Boundary-condition information is transferred to the latent grid through a hybrid local--global mechanism. Slice-based attention models interactions among physically related regions, while direct boundary-to-grid projection preserves local spatial structure. Across the validation sets for the shape-only, shape-and-loading, and shape-loading-boundary cases, BAT-NO achieves the lowest mean final-step mean nodal Euclidean displacement error among the evaluated baselines. In the most challenging case, it reduces the mean error by 32.6% relative to the second-best model. Hyperparameter tuning reduces the validation error from 0.451 to 0.269 mm, with a comparable error of 0.267 mm on 300 unseen test simulations sampled within the investigated design space. An attention-based scalar decoder jointly predicts six response trajectories with a mean relative error of 2.46%. Most derived crashworthiness indicators have median errors below 3%. These results show that explicit local and global boundary-condition representations improve crashworthiness prediction over expanded component-level design spaces.

AI.tldr: BAT-NO is a transformer neural operator that predicts transient displacement fields and crashworthiness responses under varying geometry and boundary conditions, achieving 32.6% error reduction over baselines and 2.46% mean relative error for response trajectories.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity finite-element crash simulations are computationally expensive, limiting design exploration. Existing deep learning surrogates are limited to single boundary conditions, lacking generalisation to boundary variations in geometry, impact conditions, and support stiffness.
AI.method: BAT-NO combines recurrent mesh processing with latent-grid Fourier operator processing. It uses a hybrid local-global mechanism to transfer boundary-condition information to the latent grid, slice-based attention for physically related region interactions, and direct boundary-to-grid projection for local spatial structure. An attention-based scalar decoder jointly predicts six response trajectories.
AI.result: BAT-NO achieves lowest mean final-step displacement error across validation sets. In the most challenging case, it reduces error by 32.6% relative to the second-best model. Hyperparameter tuning reduces validation error from 0.451 to 0.269 mm, with test error of 0.267 mm on 300 unseen simulations. Mean relative error for six response trajectories is 2.46%, with most crashworthiness indicators having median errors below 3%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit modeling of both local and global boundary-condition representations significantly improves crashworthiness prediction accuracy over expanded component-level design spaces, enabling reliable predictions under varied loading and boundary conditions.

title: LatentQuant: Preserving the Policy-Facing Latent Contract under NVFP4 VAE Quantization
summary: Recent world action models (WAMs) reuse pretrained video VAEs whose encoder latents directly condition downstream action policies. Quantization must therefore preserve not only reconstruction fidelity but also the policy-facing latent contract expected by the frozen policy. Direct NVFP4 leaves W4A4 quantization error uncompensated, whereas joint quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover reconstruction by moving this representation. On Wan2.1, joint QAT nearly matches FP32 VBench-7 (0.7403 versus 0.7409), yet LIBERO success collapses from 95.5% to 10.5%. Controlled decoder-only experiments show that activation quantize-dequantize operations alter the reconstruction signal and decoder Jacobian, redirecting the gradient returned to the encoder and inducing persistent latent drift. Based on this mechanism, we introduce LatentQuant, a two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework that first aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision counterpart, then freezes it while adapting the decoder. Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, LatentQuant preserves near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality, achieving 95.75% success on LIBERO and 68.8% on RoboTwin. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17x-1.26x end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses quantization challenges in World Action Models (WAMs) where pretrained video VAE encoders condition downstream policies. Direct NVFP4 quantization preserves reconstruction but harms policy performance, while joint QAT recovers reconstruction but causes latent drift that collapses task success (95.5% → 10.5% on LIBERO). The proposed LatentQuant framework uses a two-stage approach: first align quantized encoder with high-precision counterpart, then freeze encoder while adapting decoder.
AI.motivation: World Action Models reuse pretrained video VAEs whose encoder latents directly condition downstream action policies. Quantization must preserve both reconstruction fidelity and the policy-facing latent contract. Direct NVFP4 quantization leaves quantization error uncompensated, while joint QAT causes latent drift that severely degrades policy performance.
AI.method: The authors first investigate the mechanism of performance collapse through controlled decoder-only experiments, discovering that activation quantize-dequantize operations alter reconstruction signal and decoder Jacobian, redirecting gradients to encoder and causing persistent latent drift. Based on this mechanism, they propose LatentQuant, a two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework: (1) align the quantized encoder with its high-precision counterpart, then (2) freeze the encoder while adapting the decoder.
AI.result: On Wan2.1, LatentQuant nearly matches FP32 VBench-7 (0.7403 vs 0.7409) while preserving 95.75% LIBERO success (vs 10.5% with joint QAT). Similar results on Wan2.2. Achieves 68.8% on RoboTwin. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17x-1.26x end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN.
AI.conclusion: LatentQuant successfully balances reconstruction quality and policy performance in quantized WAMs by addressing the latent drift problem through its two-stage approach. The method achieves near-baseline performance while delivering significant computational speedups on modern GPUs.

title: StepCAD: Mesh-to-CAD Code Generation via LLM Policy and Geometry-Guided Search
summary: Recovering executable CAD programs from 3D meshes is challenging due to the compositional nature of CAD construction and the interaction between discrete modeling choices and continuous parameters. Many learning-based methods predict complete programs in a single pass and rely predominantly on sketch-extrude representations, limiting operation diversity and opportunities to correct geometric errors during reconstruction.
