We introduce StepCAD, a generative optimization approach that combines a state-conditioned CAD policy with geometry-guided search. Given an input mesh, the policy predicts construction actions conditioned on both target and intermediate geometry, and an IoU-guided tree search refines the resulting program through local edits. We also introduce ARCADE-1.5M, a large-scale dataset of 1.5M executable CAD programs spanning diverse operations, sequences with a maximum length of 150+ counted operations, and 12.5M intermediate state-action transitions. Experiments across multiple CAD reconstruction benchmarks show that StepCAD achieves state-of-the-art geometric reconstruction accuracy with consistently high validity, yielding up to 87.2% relative IoU improvement over the strongest evaluated baseline, with particularly large gains on complex shapes. Project page: https://ghadinehme.com/stepcad.github.io/

AI.tldr: StepCAD is a generative optimization approach for recovering executable CAD programs from 3D meshes, combining a state-conditioned CAD policy with IoU-guided tree search. It addresses limitations of prior single-pass methods by using iterative refinement and handling diverse CAD operations beyond sketch-extrude representations.
AI.motivation: Recovering CAD programs from 3D meshes is challenging due to the compositional nature of CAD construction and the interaction between discrete modeling choices and continuous parameters. Existing learning-based methods predict complete programs in a single pass and rely predominantly on sketch-extrude representations, limiting operation diversity and opportunities to correct geometric errors during reconstruction.
AI.method: StepCAD combines: (1) A state-conditioned CAD policy that predicts construction actions conditioned on both target and intermediate geometry; (2) An IoU-guided tree search that refines the resulting program through local edits. The approach also introduces ARCADE-1.5M, a large-scale dataset with 1.5M executable CAD programs spanning diverse operations, sequences up to 150+ operations, and 12.5M state-action transitions.
AI.result: StepCAD achieves state-of-the-art geometric reconstruction accuracy with consistently high validity. It yields up to 87.2% relative IoU improvement over the strongest evaluated baseline, with particularly large gains on complex shapes.
AI.conclusion: The combination of a state-conditioned policy with geometry-guided search enables effective CAD program reconstruction from 3D meshes, outperforming single-pass approaches particularly on complex geometries. The large-scale diverse dataset enables learning of varied CAD operations beyond traditional sketch-extrude limitations.

title: Towards Automatically Pruning Logging Code with Coding Agents: How Far Are We?
summary: Logging code supports debugging, monitoring, and software maintenance, but excessive logging can add noise, impose runtime overhead, and obscure diagnostic information. While prior research has extensively studied logging code generation and modification, logging removal remains comparatively underexplored. In this paper, we study developer logging removal practices and explore the use of coding agents for this task. We extract and manually validate logging removal cases from Python and Java repositories and derive 10 removal patterns and 11 removal reasons that characterize how and why logging code was removed in real-world software changes. We further construct LogRem, a dataset of 387 real-world cases covering direct logging statement removal, logging infrastructure removal, and logging replacement. We evaluate four coding agents with multiple model settings and compare their outputs with accepted real-world changes. Although 95.6% to 100.0% of outputs pass validity checks, only 11.1% to 19.6% remove the same logging code as the corresponding real-world change while preserving unrelated code. Agents differ through missed removals, extra removals, and unrelated code edits, with substantial variation across logging removal categories and trajectories. Execution cost varies widely, but higher cost does not consistently yield closer alignment. Commit messages and developer discussions provide the largest alignment gains, while taxonomy guidance consistently reduces runtime. Overall, our study establishes logging removal as a distinct software maintenance task and shows that reliable automation depends on accurately determining removal scope while preserving necessary code. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine logging code removal from this perspective.

AI.tldr: First study examining developer logging code removal practices and evaluating coding agents for this task. Identifies 10 removal patterns and 11 removal reasons from Python/Java repositories, constructs a dataset of 387 cases, and evaluates four coding agents finding only 11.1%-19.6% alignment with real-world changes despite high validity rates.
AI.motivation: While logging code generation and modification have been extensively studied, logging removal remains underexplored. Excessive logging adds noise, imposes runtime overhead, and obscures diagnostic information, making removal important but poorly understood.
AI.method: Extracted and manually validated logging removal cases from Python and Java repositories, deriving 10 removal patterns and 11 removal reasons. Constructed LogRem dataset with 387 real-world cases covering direct statement removal, infrastructure removal, and replacement. Evaluated four coding agents with multiple model settings, comparing outputs with accepted real-world changes.
AI.result: 95.6% to 100% of agent outputs pass validity checks, but only 11.1% to 19.6% remove the same logging code as real-world changes while preserving unrelated code. Agents differ through missed removals, extra removals, and unrelated code edits. Commit messages and developer discussions provide largest alignment gains; taxonomy guidance consistently reduces runtime. Higher cost does not consistently yield better alignment.
AI.conclusion: Logging removal is a distinct software maintenance task. Reliable automation depends on accurately determining removal scope while preserving necessary code. This is the first study to examine logging code removal from this perspective.

title: CreativeFlow: A One-to-Many Analogical Relation Transfer Method for 3D Asset Generation
comment: 3 pages. To appear in SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Posters (SA Posters '26), Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, December 2026
summary: Inspired by cognitive science, we present CREATIVEFLOW, an analogical generation framework that explicitly models analogical divergent thinking to mitigate creative homogenization in text-to-3D pipelines. Our method derives a series of meaningful yet relationally similar source-target asset pairs, each featuring distinct geometric configurations. Expert evaluations demonstrate that our framework substantially enhances creative novelty and visual fascination. This workflow and its resulting assets establish a foundational dataset and benchmark for future relation-aware 3D model training.

AI.tldr: CREATIVEFLOW is a text-to-3D generation framework that uses analogical divergent thinking (inspired by cognitive science) to address creative homogenization. It creates meaningful source-target asset pairs with distinct geometric configurations, enhancing creative novelty and visual fascination while establishing a benchmark for relation-aware 3D model training.
AI.motivation: Mitigate creative homogenization in text-to-3D pipelines by drawing inspiration from cognitive science, specifically analogical thinking processes.
AI.method: Explicitly models analogical divergent thinking to derive a series of meaningful yet relationally similar source-target asset pairs, each featuring distinct geometric configurations.
AI.result: Substantially enhances creative novelty and visual fascination as demonstrated by expert evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The workflow and resulting assets establish a foundational dataset and benchmark for future relation-aware 3D model training.

title: Retrieval-Centric Deep Learning in Growing Nonparametric Neural Networks
summary: We investigate a general-purpose layer for deep learning that, instead of compressing arbitrary-size training data into fixed-size weight matrices, stores a new pair of key-value representations for every data point during training, and retrieves and recombines these representations through an attention mechanism at inference time - resulting in a growing neural net (NN). While Irie et al. (arXiv:2202.05798) have put forward this perspective from the classic duality expressing any linear layer in a deep NN trained by gradient descent as linear attention (LA) over the training data points, replacing LA by more powerful attention functions, as they suggest, turns out to be non-trivial: we show that naively applying learning rules from the LA case to advanced kernels does not lead to principled optimization. Here we fill this gap and develop functional gradient-based learning rules for kernelized attention layers, based on radial basis function (RBF) and softmax-like kernels - establishing the principled "retrieval-centric deep learning" (RCDL) paradigm. Empirically, we demonstrate the promising performance and learning-efficiency of RCDL on image classification and synthetic teacher-student learning tasks. Moreover, we show that replacing LA in the dual form of NNs by advanced LA variants, namely MesaNet/DeltaNet, yields a formal connection to recently proposed optimizers for conventional fixed-size NNs, offering a novel perspective on deep learning optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a "retrieval-centric deep learning" (RCDL) paradigm where neural network layers store key-value representations for each data point instead of fixed-weight matrices, using kernelized attention (RBF, softmax) for inference instead of traditional linear attention.
AI.motivation: The authors address the challenge of extending linear attention (LA) based neural networks to more powerful kernelized attention functions. While prior work (Irie et al., 2022) showed that linear layers can be expressed as linear attention over training data, applying similar learning rules to advanced kernels was found to be non-trivial and lacked principled optimization.
AI.method: The paper develops functional gradient-based learning rules for kernelized attention layers using radial basis function (RBF) and softmax-like kernels, establishing the RCDL paradigm. The approach treats the layer as a growing neural network that retrieves and recombines key-value representations through attention at inference time.
AI.result: Empirically demonstrates promising performance and learning efficiency on image classification and synthetic teacher-student learning tasks. Additionally, shows that replacing LA with advanced variants (MesaNet/DeltaNet) in the dual form of NNs yields formal connections to recently proposed optimizers for conventional fixed-size NNs.
AI.conclusion: The RCDL paradigm offers a principled approach to kernelized attention layers in deep learning, with empirical validation on classification tasks and theoretical connections to optimizer research, providing a novel perspective on deep learning optimization.

title: ROAR: Unifying Runs across Heterogeneous AI-Driven Research Systems
summary: Each run of an AI-driven research system (ADRS) is an expensive search over a vast solution space, and dependable evaluation requires many runs, making run data both costly to produce and valuable to retain for large-scale analysis. Yet this data remains fragmented: teams operate in isolation, ADRS frameworks emit results in different formats, and no shared infrastructure exists to aggregate or compare runs across problems and systems. We present ROAR, a solution for systematically unifying and analyzing heterogeneous ADRS outputs. ROAR addresses two challenges: reconciling heterogeneous ADRS outputs and enabling analytics across runs with different objectives and scoring functions. We achieve this through a relational schema and parsing layer that normalize heterogeneous ADRS outputs while preserving data lineage and temporal structure, and accommodating new systems without requiring schema modifications. From building a corpus of more than 900 runs from multiple ADRS, we show how pooled data can reveal properties of problem landscapes that are difficult to observe. Consistent with prior work, runs with identical configurations may converge to different scores. We find that many runs realize most gains early, and that the effectiveness of different strategies for incorporating prior solutions into the search process varies across problems. We further show that the pooled corpus is actionable and not merely analytical by using ROAR to configure ADRS runs. Together, these results illustrate how pooled ADRS data can expose problem-dependent structure in search behavior that is difficult to detect from any single system, team, or benchmark. Such cross-cutting insights are difficult to obtain while runs remain siloed; ROAR is the first infrastructure designed to unify them.

AI.tldr: ROAR is a system for unifying and analyzing heterogeneous AI-driven research system (ADRS) outputs across different teams and frameworks. It uses a relational schema and parsing layer to normalize data while preserving lineage and temporal structure, enabling cross-run analytics despite different objectives and scoring functions.
AI.motivation: AI-driven research system (ADRS) runs are expensive to produce but valuable for analysis. However, run data remains fragmented across teams, with different ADRS frameworks emitting results in incompatible formats, making it impossible to aggregate or compare runs across problems and systems.
AI.method: ROAR addresses heterogeneous outputs through a relational schema and parsing layer that normalizes data while preserving data lineage and temporal structure, accommodating new systems without requiring schema modifications. The researchers built a corpus of over 900 runs from multiple ADRS to demonstrate the system's capabilities.
AI.result: The pooled data revealed: (1) runs with identical configurations may converge to different scores, (2) many runs realize most gains early, (3) effectiveness of different strategies for incorporating prior solutions varies across problems. The corpus proved actionable by using ROAR to configure ADRS runs.
AI.conclusion: Pooled ADRS data can expose problem-dependent structure in search behavior that is difficult to detect from any single system, team, or benchmark. ROAR is the first infrastructure designed to unify fragmented ADRS data, enabling cross-cutting insights that would otherwise remain siloed.

title: Beyond Token Accuracy: Prioritizing What Matters for Visual Reconstruction
summary: Tokens have become a unified interface for multimodal foundation models, making visual-token communication a natural paradigm for efficient image delivery. However, existing methods typically rely on static policies that cannot jointly adapt to image content and channel conditions. Moreover, their token-level utility objectives do not necessarily translate into improved image reconstruction quality. In this paper, we propose AdapToC, an adaptive, reconstruction-oriented visual-token communication framework. At the transmitter, an adaptive selector jointly models image content, channel state, and communication budget to perform instance-wise resource allocation. Rather than using a fixed token rate and protection policy, it dynamically determines how many tokens should be transmitted and assigns different protection levels according to token importance and current channel conditions. At the receiver, an adaptive MaskGIT receiver incorporates channel reliability into contextual token modeling. It distinguishes tokens with different reliability levels, preserves high-confidence observations, corrects potentially corrupted tokens, and iteratively reconstructs missing content from the received evidence and global visual context. By co-designing token quantity, unequal protection, and reliability-aware recovery for image-level reconstruction quality, AdapToC achieves a peak mean PSNR gain of 4.20 dB over the strongest static baseline under matched communication costs and state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated visual-token communication methods.

AI.tldr: AdapToC is an adaptive visual-token communication framework that jointly optimizes token quantity, unequal error protection, and reliability-aware recovery for image reconstruction. It features an adaptive selector at the transmitter that allocates resources based on image content, channel state, and communication budget, and an adaptive MaskGIT receiver that corrects corrupted tokens and iteratively reconstructs missing content.
AI.motivation: Existing visual-token communication methods rely on static policies that cannot adapt to image content and channel conditions, and their token-level utility objectives do not translate into improved image reconstruction quality. There is a need for a framework that jointly optimizes token transmission and reconstruction for image-level quality.
AI.method: The framework uses two key components: (1) An adaptive selector at the transmitter that jointly models image content, channel state, and communication budget to perform instance-wise resource allocation, dynamically determining token count and protection levels based on token importance and channel conditions; (2) An adaptive MaskGIT receiver that incorporates channel reliability into contextual token modeling, distinguishing tokens with different reliability levels, preserving high-confidence observations, correcting potentially corrupted tokens, and iteratively reconstructing missing content from received evidence and global visual context.
AI.result: AdapToC achieves a peak mean PSNR gain of 4.20 dB over the strongest static baseline under matched communication costs and state-of-the-art performance among evaluated visual-token communication methods.
AI.conclusion: By co-designing token quantity, unequal protection, and reliability-aware recovery for image-level reconstruction quality, AdapToC demonstrates that adaptive, reconstruction-oriented visual-token communication can significantly improve image delivery quality in varying channel conditions.

title: Asymmetric Repository Lineage Modeling and Verifier-Guided Coordination in Concurrent AI Coding Agents
summary: Concurrent AI coding agents create a coordination problem in which cheap signals may prioritize work, but only an executable checker can establish the property being claimed. We study this separation through a property-scoped verification contract and MERGEGYM, a three-track benchmark for open-time scope forecasting, replay- conditioned conflict resolution, and scheduling. On a stratified 715-pair lineage set (167 textual conflicts), 79 conflicts (47.3%) occur despite disjoint authored file sets. This is an operationally important proxy mismatch expected from three-way merge: authored PR diffs are measured against PR-specific bases, whereas the checker compares both heads to their common merge base. A standalone lineage-union rule reaches held-out AUROC 0.877; a 12-feature logistic model reaches 0.882 [0.845, 0.917] with PR-AUC 0.661, and an untuned random forest on the same decision-time features reaches 0.902 [0.875, 0.928] with PR-AUC 0.701. At a 33.3% held-out replay budget, the logistic and random-forest models recover 81.2% and 82.9% of conflicts, respectively. Patch reconstruction succeeds for 48/79 zero- overlap conflicts and all 48 become clean; the other 31 cases are inconclusive, so this check validates the expected three-way-merge explanation rather than claiming a new Git mechanism. In T1, a zero-shot LLM reaches AUC 0.704 and LLM-plus- metadata fusion 0.740. In T3, a decision-time gate de-overlaps a median 91.7% of labeled scope collisions at 65.0% makespan inflation under frozen-label replay. Because local git merge-tree replay is already cheap in our logs (median 0.02 s), we do not claim that lineage triage saves this checker alone: when exact replay is cheap, verify everything. All empirical guarantees in this paper remain limited to textual mergeability or the explicitly stated frozen-label scheduling target.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the coordination problem in concurrent AI coding agents, focusing on property-scoped verification contracts. The authors find that 47.3% of merge conflicts occur despite disjoint authored file sets due to a proxy mismatch in three-way merge semantics. They develop MERGEGYM benchmark and show that machine learning models can effectively triage conflicts, though they note that when replay is cheap, verification of everything is preferable.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the coordination problem in concurrent AI coding agents where cheap signals may prioritize work but only executable checkers can establish the actual property being claimed. The key insight is that authored PR diffs are measured against PR-specific bases, while conflict checkers compare both heads to their common merge base, creating a proxy mismatch.
AI.method: The authors introduce MERGEGYM, a three-track benchmark for open-time scope forecasting, replay-conditioned conflict resolution, and scheduling. They analyze a stratified 715-pair lineage set with 167 textual conflicts. They evaluate multiple approaches: a lineage-union rule, logistic regression with 12 features, and a random forest model. They also test zero-shot LLM approaches and decision-time gating for scheduling.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) 79 conflicts (47.3%) occur despite disjoint authored file sets; (2) Lineage-union rule achieves AUROC 0.877; (3) Logistic model achieves AUROC 0.882 with PR-AUC 0.661; (4) Random forest achieves AUROC 0.902 with PR-AUC 0.701; (5) At 33.3% replay budget, logistic and random forest recover 81.2% and 82.9% of conflicts; (6) Patch reconstruction succeeds for 48/79 zero-overlap conflicts; (7) Zero-shot LLM achieves AUC 0.704, LLM-plus-metadata achieves 0.740; (8) Decision-time gate achieves 91.7% scope collision de-overlap at 65.0% makespan inflation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the proxy mismatch is an expected three-way-merge explanation rather than a new Git mechanism. Since local git merge-tree replay is cheap (median 0.02s), lineage triage does not save the checker alone - when exact replay is cheap, verify everything. All empirical guarantees remain limited to textual mergeability or the explicitly stated frozen-label scheduling target.

title: SteadySplats: Resampling of Low-Variance Gaussians for High-Fidelity Stochastic Rendering
summary: Stochastic order-independent transparency enables efficient and elegant rendering of primitive-based radiance fields like 3D Gaussian Splatting models, but remains impractical due to the inherent visible noise in the output. We propose a principled approach to minimize high-frequency noise, addressing its sources at the representation and image synthesis level. During stochastic rendering, our history-based spatial resampling scheme drastically accelerates image convergence, while temporal importance resampling ensures coherence under camera movement. During training, a color regularizer implicitly reduces the variance along view rays in the 3DGS models. With these properties, our optimized, Vulkan-based renderer effectively mitigates output noise at low and high sample counts, achieving a substantial 13~dB PSNR increase in quality over previous stochastic methods at 1 sample per pixel and quickly converging to sorted 3DGS with an average L1 error of less than $10^{-4}$.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the noise problem in stochastic order-independent transparency rendering for primitive-based radiance fields like 3D Gaussian Splatting. The authors propose a dual approach: during rendering, they use history-based spatial resampling and temporal importance resampling; during training, they apply a color regularizer to reduce variance. Their Vulkan-based renderer achieves 13 dB PSNR improvement at 1 sample/pixel and converges to sorted 3DGS with L1 error < 10^-4.
AI.motivation: Stochastic order-independent transparency enables efficient rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting models but suffers from inherent visible noise in the output, limiting its practical applicability.
AI.method: The proposed approach combines: (1) History-based spatial resampling to accelerate image convergence during stochastic rendering; (2) Temporal importance resampling to ensure coherence under camera movement; (3) A color regularizer during training to implicitly reduce variance along view rays in 3DGS models. Implementation uses an optimized Vulkan-based renderer.
AI.result: The method achieves a 13 dB PSNR increase over previous stochastic methods at 1 sample per pixel and converges to sorted 3DGS with an average L1 error of less than 10^-4, effectively mitigating output noise at both low and high sample counts.
AI.conclusion: The principled approach successfully addresses high-frequency noise sources at both representation and image synthesis levels, making stochastic order-independent transparency practical for rendering primitive-based radiance fields while maintaining efficiency and quality.

title: Reinforcement Learning on the Discrete Composition Channel of a Crystal Generator: Validated Gains and Reward Hacking
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code: https://github.com/paprakash/OMatGRPO. Models and structures: https://huggingface.co/paprakash/OMatGRPO
summary: Inverse materials design is a long-standing goal of computational materials discovery. Generative models for crystalline materials are typically trained to match the distribution of a structure database, while nothing in their training objective points them at specific design goals such as targeted properties. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to align a generative model based on stochastic interpolants and discrete flow matching with general black-box reward functions through reinforcement learning. Atom types are generated by a discrete flow and the policy gradient of our generalization of GRPO directly acts on the likelihoods of the atom-type transitions, which differentiates our work from previous reinforcement-learning approaches for diffusion and flow-based generative models of crystalline materials. We introduce a reward function that raises the yield of metastable, unique and novel structures (mSUN) from 13.4% for the pretrained model to 45.5% for the reinforced model, as evaluated by a community benchmark. Our reward also improves the performance of a reinforcement learning framework for crystalline materials based on latent denoising diffusion models. At the same time, we find that directly reinforcing atom-type transition likelihoods enables reward exploitation that has to be prevented with explicit guards. The same analysis also exposes a gap in the community metric. Single-element structures in distinct packings are counted as metastable, unique and novel materials and inflate mSUN without yielding any new compounds. A stability claim is only as good as its reference hull. We report every result split by the number of reference phases behind it and argue that benchmarks should do the same.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reinforcement learning approach using Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to align crystalline materials generative models with arbitrary black-box reward functions. The method directly optimizes atom-type transition likelihoods in discrete flow matching models, achieving a 3.4× improvement in generating metastable, unique, and novel structures (from 13.4% to 45.5%). The work also identifies critical issues in current benchmarking practices, notably that single-element structures in different packings are incorrectly counted as novel materials.
AI.motivation: Inverse materials design aims to discover materials with targeted properties, but existing generative models for crystalline materials are trained only to match structure databases without optimization toward specific design goals. This work addresses the need to guide generative models toward desired properties through reinforcement learning.
AI.method: The authors use GRPO to align a generative model based on stochastic interpolants and discrete flow matching with black-box reward functions. Unlike previous RL approaches for diffusion models, their policy gradient directly acts on the likelihoods of atom-type transitions. They introduce a reward function called mSUN (metastable, unique, novel) and evaluate on a community benchmark.
AI.result: The mSUN yield increased from 13.4% (pretrained model) to 45.5% (reinforced model). The reward also improves performance of latent denoising diffusion models. However, the authors identify two key issues: (1) direct reinforcement of atom-type likelihoods leads to reward exploitation requiring guards, and (2) the community metric incorrectly counts single-element structures in different packings as novel materials, inflating mSUN scores.
AI.conclusion: RL-based alignment of generative models with arbitrary reward functions is effective for targeted materials discovery. However, current benchmarks have significant flaws—single-element structures in distinct packings are falsely counted as novel compounds. The authors recommend that benchmarks report results split by number of reference phases and that stability claims should be evaluated against the reference hull.

title: Teaching Agents to Code Reliably
summary: Autonomous coding agents solve repository issues by reading code, running commands, editing files, and submitting patches. Extra inference-time compute yields gains only when it produces a useful repair and supplies reliable evidence for choosing one. Three behaviors decide both, and we argue they are teachable rather than byproducts of scale, so a policy can carry them instead of a scaffold. Location diversity remains narrow, since attempts return to the same site and extra samples add no coverage. Edit diversity is left unexploited, since methodologies that differ resolve complementary issues no single run reaches. Verification misleads, since a test the agent writes for its own patch accepts many incorrect ones. Directing search by execution feedback and scoring each patch against its own reverted tree resolves 52.8% of SWE-bench Verified using 48.1% of the agent-steps an eight-sample baseline spends. Training moves these behaviors into the policy. On the 270 issues held out from SFT and RL training, weighted supervised fine-tuning raises pass@1 from 31.9% to 35.2% and pass@8 from 46.7% to 51.1%. A reinforcement objective then trains the verifier against gold-labeled repairs and incorrect variants, crediting the assertions that detect them. It raises pass@1 to 43.0% and pass@8 to 60.7%, lifts verifier precision from 26.8% to 41.7%, and more than halves false acceptance. Resolution improves on two of three out-of-distribution suites and verifier precision on all three, and the gains hold at 7B, 14B, and 30B against published coder baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents methods to improve autonomous coding agents that solve repository issues. The authors identify three critical behaviors (location diversity, edit diversity, and verification) that determine success, and propose training a policy to carry these behaviors rather than relying on scaffolds. They introduce execution feedback for search direction and patch scoring against reverted trees. Their approach achieves 52.8% resolution on SWE-bench Verified using less than half the agent-steps of baseline, with training further improving pass@1 to 43.0% and pass@8 to 60.7%.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents face limitations in solving repository issues: location diversity is narrow (agents return to same site), edit diversity is unexploited (different methodologies resolve complementary issues), and verification misleads (agent-written tests accept incorrect patches). The authors argue these behaviors are teachable rather than byproducts of scale, enabling a policy to carry them.
AI.method: The authors propose two key methods: (1) Directing search by execution feedback and scoring each patch against its own reverted tree to resolve issues. (2) Training pipeline: weighted supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) that trains the verifier against gold-labeled repairs and incorrect variants, crediting assertions that detect them.
AI.result: Directing search resolves 52.8% of SWE-bench Verified using 48.1% of agent-steps vs eight-sample baseline. SFT raises pass@1 from 31.9% to 35.2% and pass@8 from 46.7% to 51.1% on 270 held-out issues. RL training raises pass@1 to 43.0%, pass@8 to 60.7%, verifier precision from 26.8% to 41.7%, and halves false acceptance. Resolution improves on 2/3 out-of-distribution suites, with gains holding at 7B, 14B, and 30B model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Three teachable behaviors (location diversity, edit diversity, reliable verification) are key to autonomous coding agents. Training these into the policy through SFT and RL significantly outperforms scaffold-based approaches. The method generalizes across model sizes and shows improvements on out-of-distribution test suites, demonstrating the approach's effectiveness for improving code repair capabilities.

title: Are We Measuring Anticipation? Auditing Privileged Information in Procedural Video Evaluation
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?
summary:
Benchmark scores license claims about the capabilities being evaluated. We audit the inference licensed by an evaluation protocol, rather than the predictive model alone. Using procedural action anticipation as a controlled case study, we study a broader evaluation-validity failure mode: a protocol can remain temporally causal and free of classical target leakage while still supplying a privileged intermediate representation. The failure is not merely optimistic accuracy, but a mismatch between the capability claimed and the construct actually measured.
  On Breakfast, matched recognizer-history and GT-history regimes score 30.3% and 62.3% (Delta_PH(R_BA) = +32.0, 95% Student-t interval [+24.1, +39.8]). A fixed-checkpoint 2 x 2 intervention isolates a +14.6-point test-time oracle contrast; a matched no-video provenance probe yields a +26.8-point gap; and a boundary-independent query/history control retains a +19.4-point gap. We refer to this discrepancy as a privileged-information gap, defined relative to a specified non-oracle recovery pipeline, and propose a reusable four-condition audit. Across five evaluation settings the gap is heterogeneous; a standard 50 Salads long-term-anticipation re-implementation provides cautious support beyond the audit-specific next-action construction.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a novel evaluation-validity failure mode in benchmark testing called "privileged-information gap." Even when evaluation protocols are temporally causal and free of classical target leakage, they can still supply privileged intermediate representations that inflate performance claims. Using procedural action anticipation as a case study, the authors demonstrate substantial score discrepancies between using ground-truth history (62.3%) versus recognized history (30.3%) on the Breakfast dataset, a +32.0 point gap.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to audit the inference licensed by an evaluation protocol itself, rather than just the predictive model. The authors argue that benchmark scores license claims about capabilities being evaluated, but there's a mismatch between the claimed capability and the construct actually measured. This represents a broader evaluation-validity failure mode beyond classical target leakage.
AI.method: The authors propose a reusable four-condition audit to detect privileged-information gaps. They conduct multiple interventions: (1) a fixed-checkpoint 2×2 intervention isolating a +14.6-point test-time oracle contrast, (2) a matched no-video provenance probe yielding a +26.8-point gap, and (3) a boundary-independent query/history control retaining a +19.4-point gap. They test across five evaluation settings and re-implement the 50 Salads long-term-anticipation benchmark.
AI.result: On the Breakfast dataset, matched recognizer-history and GT-history regimes score 30.3% and 62.3% respectively (Delta_PH(R_BA) = +32.0, 95% CI [+24.1, +39.8]). The privileged-information gap is heterogeneous across five evaluation settings. The 50 Salads re-implementation provides cautious support beyond the audit-specific next-action construction.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that evaluation protocols can remain temporally causal and free of classical target leakage while still supplying privileged intermediate representations, leading to a mismatch between claimed and measured capabilities. Their four-condition audit provides a reusable method to detect such privileged-information gaps in benchmark evaluations.

title: A Multidimensional Model for Quantifying Tonal Strength: A Continuous Framework of Analyzing Tonal Evolution Beyond Tonal-Atonal Binary Classification
summary: Tonality is a fundamental organizing principle of Western music. However, the gradual transition from common-practice tonality to atonality around the turn of the twentieth century cannot be captured by binary labels. To characterize intermediate tonal states and trace this evolution, we propose a multidimensional framework for quantifying tonal strength, grounded in tonal theory and mechanisms underlying tonal dissolution. This framework operationalizes the global statistical regularity, temporal coherence, and local perceptual alignment of tonal organization through three complementary features: pitch-class distribution uniformity, temporal stability of tonal centers, and local tonal clarity, respectively. To validate the model, we introduce two new datasets: a binary dataset comprising 196 tonal and atonal pieces, and a historical MIDI corpus of 1,561 compositions by 21 composers spanning the Baroque era to the early twentieth century. The proposed model achieves high discriminative performance on the binary classification task (F_1=0.985), and quantitatively reveals a continuous historical trajectory from established tonality through progressive weakening to eventual dissolution. Computational analysis of representative composers further confirms significant declines in tonal strength throughout the careers of late-Romantic and modernist figures. Additionally, analysis of EMOPIA dataset reveals a weak but statistically significant positive correlation between higher tonal strength values and positive emotional valence. This work establishes a unified quantitative model for analyzing tonal evolution and provides a continuous measure for future behavioral and neurophysiological investigations of the relationships among tonal organization, musical emotion, and cognition.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multidimensional framework to quantify tonal strength in Western music, addressing the gap between binary tonality/atonal labels. The model uses three features (pitch-class distribution uniformity, temporal stability of tonal centers, and local tonal clarity) to capture the gradual transition from common-practice tonality to atonality. Validated on two datasets (196 pieces binary classification, 1,561 compositions from 21 composers), the model achieves F_1=0.985 and reveals continuous historical tonal evolution, with late-Romantic and modernist composers showing significant tonal decline. A weak positive correlation between tonal strength and emotional valence was also found.
AI.motivation: The binary classification of music as tonal or atonal fails to capture the gradual transition from common-practice tonality to atonality around the turn of the twentieth century. There was a need for a quantitative framework to characterize intermediate tonal states and trace this evolutionary process.
AI.method: The framework operationalizes three dimensions of tonal organization: (1) pitch-class distribution uniformity to measure global statistical regularity, (2) temporal stability of tonal centers for temporal coherence, and (3) local tonal clarity for local perceptual alignment. The model was validated using two new datasets: a binary dataset of 196 tonal/atonal pieces and a historical MIDI corpus of 1,561 compositions by 21 composers spanning Baroque to early twentieth century.
AI.result: The model achieves high discriminative performance (F_1=0.985) on binary classification. It quantitatively reveals a continuous historical trajectory from established tonality through progressive weakening to eventual dissolution. Significant declines in tonal strength were found throughout the careers of late-Romantic and modernist figures. Analysis of EMOPIA dataset shows a weak but statistically significant positive correlation between higher tonal strength values and positive emotional valence.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a unified quantitative model for analyzing tonal evolution and provides a continuous measure for future behavioral and neurophysiological investigations into the relationships among tonal organization, musical emotion, and cognition.

title: Agent Skill Evolution: How Revisions Affect Coding Agents
summary: Agent Skills, the SKILL.md files that tell an LLM coding agent how a project works, are revised like code, yet what a revision does to the agent is unknown. From 2,608 first/last revision pairs of 3,159 Skills, we characterize how Skills evolve and how they change together with the configuration of the agent's harness. We then focus on rule changes, revisions that add or remove a rule we can check automatically, such as "run allium check". We measure their effect on 21 models in single answers and on four agents in a sandbox, and their cost on 20 of these models and the four agents. Most revisions (55%) change a rule or procedure, and commits that revise a Skill change harness files such as CLAUDE.md more often than other commits of the same size. Across 16 open-weight models, an added rule raises compliance in a single answer by +0.41 on average. Across the four agents, the rate at which the agent takes the required action rises by +0.23 on average (+0.16 to +0.36), and for the three agents that blind judges assessed, final correctness rises by +0.10 on average (+0.06 to +0.14). The gain comes mainly from rules that name a command or path the old Skill did not mention. Real tools load a Skill's body only when the agent decides it needs it. In that setting the four agents keep about half of the action gain on average (51%), and the three open models about 38%. A revision adds 18-19% input tokens to a single answer and no detectable cost to an agent episode, while loading a Skill's body raises the tokens of an episode by 50% on average.

AI.tldr: This paper studies SKILL.md files (Agent Skills) that configure LLM coding agents. Through analyzing 2,608 revision pairs from 3,159 Skills, the authors find that 55% of revisions change rules/procedures, and Skills revisions often co-occur with harness file changes. Adding new rules increases agent compliance by +0.41 in single answers and +0.23 in sandbox agents, with final correctness improving by +0.10. The gains come mainly from rules naming specific commands/paths. When tools lazily load Skills only when needed, agents retain ~51% of the action gain. Revision costs include 18-19% more input tokens for single answers, with lazy loading adding 50% token overhead per episode.
AI.motivation: Agent Skills (SKILL.md files) are revised like code but the effect of these revisions on agent behavior is unknown. Understanding how Skill changes affect agent performance and cost is crucial for optimizing LLM coding agent configurations.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of 2,608 first/last revision pairs from 3,159 Skills, measuring rule changes (additions/removals), their effects on 21 models in single-answer settings and 4 agents in sandbox environments, and token costs across 20 models and 4 agents.
AI.result: 55% of revisions change rules/procedures. Added rules raise compliance by +0.41 (single answers) and +0.23 (sandbox agents), with correctness gains of +0.10. Gains primarily come from rules naming new commands/paths. Lazy loading retains 51% of action gains. Revisions add 18-19% input tokens; lazy loading adds 50% token overhead.
AI.conclusion: Rule changes in Agent Skills significantly improve agent compliance and correctness, with most gains from rules mentioning specific commands/paths. The performance improvements come with moderate token costs, though lazy loading mitigates overhead while retaining substantial benefits.

title: UniSlider: Perceptually Uniform Sliders for Continuous Image Editing
summary: Sliders provide an intuitive interface for continuous image editing. In current generative approaches, however, the slider is simply a rescaling of the method's strength parameter, such as an adapter coefficient, a prompt weight, or an interpolation factor. This strength relates poorly to perceptual change. The image can partially revert as the slider moves, long stretches of the range produce no visible difference, and short intervals transform the image abruptly. Remapping the strength could fix this uneven pace, but only if the trajectory is monotone, which current methods do not enforce. We therefore distinguish the slider from the strength, and require perceptual distance from the input to grow linearly with the slider value. We introduce UniSlider, a lightweight LoRA trained on a few-step editing backbone so that its strength approximates this ideal slider. Few-step sampling lets us impose this objective in pixel space without intermediate ground truth, and the backbone's output is preserved at full strength. However, a low-rank adapter cannot make the strength fully uniform. Our slider is thus an inference-time remapping of the strength, obtained by adaptive sampling. Since training optmizes to make the trajectory monotone, this remapping closes the remaining gap without extra training or parameters. On a new benchmark of 300 continuous edits evaluating uniformity, monotonicity, edit fidelity, and identity preservation, UniSlider outperforms all prior methods and is preferred in a user study.

AI.tldr: UniSlider introduces a method to make continuous image editing sliders more perceptually uniform by decoupling the slider from the strength parameter, using a lightweight LoRA trained on few-step editing backbone with inference-time remapping to achieve linear perceptual distance growth.
AI.motivation: Current generative image editing methods use sliders that simply rescale strength parameters (adapter coefficients, prompt weights, interpolation factors). This approach has fundamental issues: images can partially revert as the slider moves, long ranges produce no visible difference, short intervals cause abrupt changes, and the trajectory is not monotone. The authors sought to create a slider where perceptual distance from the input grows linearly with slider value.
AI.method: The authors propose UniSlider, a lightweight LoRA trained on a few-step editing backbone. Key aspects include: (1) Distinguishing the slider from the strength parameter; (2) Using few-step sampling to impose the linear perceptual distance objective in pixel space without intermediate ground truth; (3) Preserving backbone output at full strength; (4) Using inference-time remapping (adaptive sampling) to address the limitation that low-rank adapters cannot make strength fully uniform; (5) Training to make the trajectory monotone so remapping closes the remaining gap without extra parameters.
AI.result: UniSlider was evaluated on a new benchmark of 300 continuous edits measuring uniformity, monotonicity, edit fidelity, and identity preservation. It outperforms all prior methods and is preferred in user studies.
AI.conclusion: By separating the slider from the strength and using training with few-step backbone plus inference-time remapping, UniSlider achieves more perceptually uniform image editing trajectories. This addresses the fundamental limitation of previous approaches where slider movement did not correspond to linear perceptual change, providing a more intuitive and predictable editing experience.

title: AdaEva: Accelerating LLM-Driven Algorithm Design with Adaptive Partial Evaluation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for automated algorithm design. However the computational cost of evaluating the generated algorithms can be excessive. We consider the common LLM-driven automated algorithm design (LLM4AD) setting in which a candidate algorithm is evaluated by aggregating its performance over a shared set of training instances. This instance-wise structure raises a natural question: must every candidate be evaluated on the entire instance set before deciding whether it remains competitive? Taking inspiration from algorithm configuration, we introduce AdaEva, a drop-in adaptive partial-evaluation framework that progressively evaluates candidates on larger subsets of the same instance pool and eliminates unpromising candidates as evidence accumulates. Importantly, AdaEva leaves the underlying LLM4AD procedure and per-instance evaluator unchanged and requires no prior knowledge about instance difficulty. We instantiate this idea using successive halving (AdaEva-S) and statistical racing (AdaEva-R), and evaluate both mechanisms across three representative LLM4AD frameworks, multiple LLM backbones, and optimization domains spanning combinatorial and continuous black-box optimization. Under matched evaluation budgets, AdaEva more reliably balances evaluation effort across candidates than fixed partial-evaluation strategies, yielding strong search efficiency and anytime performance together with improved held-out generalization across the evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: AdaEva is an adaptive partial-evaluation framework for LLM-driven automated algorithm design (LLM4AD) that progressively evaluates candidates on larger instance subsets and eliminates unpromising candidates early, without requiring prior knowledge about instance difficulty.
AI.motivation: Evaluating candidate algorithms generated by LLMs is computationally expensive when using the full training instance set. The authors address the inefficiency of evaluating every candidate on the entire instance set by introducing adaptive early elimination.
AI.method: AdaEva uses two instantiations: (1) AdaEva-S based on successive halving, and (2) AdaEva-R based on statistical racing. Both progressively evaluate candidates on larger subsets of the shared instance pool and eliminate unpromising candidates as evidence accumulates. The framework is drop-in compatible, leaving the underlying LLM4AD procedure and per-instance evaluator unchanged.
AI.result: Under matched evaluation budgets, AdaEva more reliably balances evaluation effort across candidates than fixed partial-evaluation strategies, yielding strong search efficiency and anytime performance together with improved held-out generalization across three LLM4AD frameworks, multiple LLM backboards, and optimization domains spanning combinatorial and continuous black-box optimization.
AI.conclusion: AdaEva provides an effective solution for reducing computational cost in LLM4AD while maintaining or improving algorithm quality, offering practical benefits for automated algorithm design tasks.

title: Behavioral History Outperforms Descriptions of the Person for LLM Synthetic Personas
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic personas representing survey respondents. Their validity as substitutes for particular respondents depends on whether they reproduce individuals' decisions. We examine what information helps synthetic respondents predict each individual's later choices, using five conditions that add progressively richer information: no personal information, demographics, personality traits, cognitive scores, and finally the respondent's earlier survey choices as behavioral history. We use a two-wave panel of 845 US adults who completed measures of 14 behavioral biases (spanning risk, time preferences, overconfidence, and reasoning), so each respondent's earlier answers provide a human test-retest benchmark; in the behavioral-history condition, all items that score the target bias are withheld. At the population level, the average number of biases per respondent in every condition is close to the human average (7.1-8.1 biases, against 7.1 for humans). This aggregate similarity masks differences in variance: persona descriptions recover only 53-67% of human between-person variation, whereas adding behavioral history restores it to approximately the human level. At the individual level, description-based personas achieve only 7-12% of the informedness observed in human test-retest responses, while adding behavioral history raises this to 28%. The condition including behavioral history has the highest estimated informedness in all 17 demographic groups, whereas description-based conditions provide little or no information for some groups. Synthetic responses also exhibit stronger education- and income-related differences than human responses. For LLM synthetic personas, a respondent's past answers add more to individual-level prediction than a description of who they are.

AI.tldr: This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as valid synthetic respondents for survey research by replicating individual human decision-making. Using a two-wave panel of 845 US adults measuring 14 behavioral biases, the study tests five conditions with progressively richer information (no info, demographics, personality, cognitive scores, behavioral history). While LLMs match human population averages, they only capture 53-67% of between-person variance with description-based personas, and achieve 7-12% individual-level informedness. Adding behavioral history substantially improves performance (28% informedness, near-human variance), suggesting that past behavior predicts future choices better than demographic or personality descriptions.
AI.motivation: The researchers aim to validate LLM-based synthetic personas as substitutes for human respondents in survey research. They investigate what information helps synthetic respondents predict individual choices, addressing the fundamental question of whether LLMs can accurately replicate human decision-making patterns.
AI.method: Two-wave panel study with 845 US adults. Participants completed measures of 14 behavioral biases (risk preferences, time preferences, overconfidence, and reasoning). Five conditions were tested progressively adding: no personal information, demographics, personality traits, cognitive scores, and behavioral history (withheld target bias items). Human test-retest reliability provided the benchmark. Analysis included population-level bias counts, between-person variance, and individual-level informedness (rank-order correlation).
AI.result: At population level, all conditions showed similar average biases (7.1-8.1 vs 7.1 humans). However, variance differed significantly: description-based personas captured only 53-67% of human between-person variation, while behavioral history restored it to near-human levels. At individual level, description-based personas achieved only 7-12% of human informedness; adding behavioral history raised this to 28%. The behavioral history condition outperformed all others across all 17 demographic groups. Synthetic responses showed stronger education- and income-related disparities than actual human responses.
AI.conclusion: For LLM synthetic personas, a respondent's past answers provide substantially more predictive power for future choices than demographic or personality descriptions. While LLMs can match population-level averages, they fail to capture individual-level variation without behavioral history. This suggests that behavioral history is essential for valid synthetic respondent applications, though even with this information, LLMs achieve only modest individual-level prediction (28% of human test-retest informedness).

title: Streaming Multi-Track Timeline Control for 3D Human Motion Generation
summary: Text-driven human motion generation has advanced substantially, yet most methods assume instructions are available before synthesis. Interactive applications require responding to new instructions while continuing ongoing actions, such as answering a phone while walking. Existing approaches address streaming generation or simultaneous composition without explicitly combining streaming instruction arrival with independently timed, overlapping actions. We introduce streaming multi-track timeline control and propose TimelineControl to incorporate new instructions alongside ongoing actions. Interval-aware conditioning preserves instruction timing, while causal part-structured representations and part-aware denoising coordinate concurrent actions across body regions. We also construct TimelineMotion, a dataset with overlapping instruction intervals and body-part annotations. Experiments on TimelineMotion and MTT demonstrate improved semantic alignment and temporal adherence over evaluated streaming baselines, including models retrained on the same data. Ablations and human evaluations validate our design, complemented by spatial conditioning and humanoid execution demonstrations. Our code, data and models will become publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TimelineControl, a framework for text-driven human motion generation that handles streaming instructions while maintaining ongoing actions. It addresses the gap between batch synthesis methods and interactive applications requiring real-time response to new instructions alongside concurrent actions.
AI.motivation: Existing text-driven motion generation methods assume all instructions are available before synthesis begins. However, interactive applications require responding to new instructions while continuing ongoing actions (e.g., answering a phone while walking). Prior work addresses either streaming generation or simultaneous composition, but not both combined.
AI.method: The proposed TimelineControl framework incorporates three key components: (1) Streaming multi-track timeline control for handling new instructions alongside ongoing actions; (2) Interval-aware conditioning to preserve instruction timing; (3) Causal part-structured representations with part-aware denoising to coordinate concurrent actions across body regions. The method is evaluated on a new dataset called TimelineMotion with overlapping instruction intervals and body-part annotations.
AI.result: Experiments on TimelineMotion and MTT datasets demonstrate improved semantic alignment and temporal adherence over evaluated streaming baselines, including models retrained on the same data. Ablations validate the design choices, and human evaluations confirm the improvements.
AI.conclusion: TimelineControl successfully enables text-driven human motion generation that responds to streaming instructions while maintaining ongoing actions. The framework achieves superior semantic alignment and temporal adherence compared to baseline methods, with validated design through ablations and human evaluations. The approach is demonstrated through spatial conditioning and humanoid execution.

title: CARET: Training-Free Test-Time Scaling for Repository-Level Code Completion
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) dominates repository-level code completion: it retrieves cross-file context (R), then decodes one greedy completion (G). Existing work mainly focuses on retrieval and stops there. We argue both stages can be improved together, with generation in particular gaining from test-time scaling. We present CARET, a training-free method. For R, CARET routes among retrieval contexts using the agreement among its own samples, cascading to an alternative context when the samples scatter. For G, it samples candidates over a cached prompt prefix, so the long retrieved context is encoded once rather than once per sample. It then selects the final completion by reverse-context likelihood: a correct completion makes the code after the cursor more probable, so the same model grades its own candidates by reading ahead. Across CrossCodeEval, RepoEval-Line, and RepoEval-API with six code models (1.1B to 7B, four families), CARET improves exact match in all 18 combinations by 10.8 points on average over greedy decoding and 5.3 over self-consistency@10. Token-level compute stays near 1.45 times one generation (measured wall-clock 1.3-2.9 times, growing with generator size). Improving retrieval and generation together yields more accurate code than improving retrieval alone, at a budget that stays close to a single pass.

AI.tldr: CARET is a training-free method that improves repository-level code completion by jointly optimizing retrieval and generation. It uses agreement among samples to route between retrieval contexts, caches encoded context for efficient sampling, and selects final completions using reverse-context likelihood (grading candidates by reading ahead in the code). It achieves 10.8 point improvement over greedy decoding and 5.3 over self-consistency@10 across 18 model/dataset combinations.
AI.motivation: Current RAG-based code completion systems retrieve cross-file context and decode greedy completions, but existing work focuses only on retrieval improvement. The authors argue that both retrieval and generation stages can be improved together, with generation particularly benefiting from test-time scaling.
AI.method: CARET has three key components: 1) Retrieval routing - uses agreement among self-samples to select between retrieval contexts, cascading to alternatives when samples scatter; 2) Efficient sampling - caches encoded prompt prefix so long retrieved context is encoded once rather than per sample; 3) Selection via reverse-context likelihood - grades candidates by reading ahead to see if completion makes subsequent code more probable.
AI.result: Across CrossCodeEval, RepoEval-Line, and RepoEval-API with six code models (1.1B to 7B, four families), CARET improves exact match in all 18 combinations by 10.8 points on average over greedy decoding and 5.3 over self-consistency@10. Token-level compute stays near 1.45x single generation (wall-clock 1.3-2.9x).
AI.conclusion: Improving retrieval and generation together yields more accurate code than improving retrieval alone, at a budget that stays close to a single pass. The method demonstrates that joint optimization of both RAG stages can achieve significant gains with minimal computational overhead.

title: Learning to Read the Contextual Tokens in Diffusion Transformers
summary: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) jointly process visual and textual representations throughout generation. These models repeatedly update the text tokens through multimodal attention, forming dynamic contextual tokens whose function is not well understood. In this work, we introduce a framework for reading this contextual space through natural-language interrogation. We train a lightweight bottleneck network that maps intermediate contextual tokens into the input space of a frozen Large Language Model (LLM), allowing the LLM to answer questions about the emerging image directly from these hidden representations. Our reader reveals that contextual tokens encode a rich, global representation of the emerging scene: generation-specific semantics, including attributes left underspecified by the prompt, are accessible surprisingly early in denoising, while increasingly fine-grained details become readable over time. Remarkably, this information remains decodable even when the MM-DiT receives an empty prompt, showing that contextual tokens accumulate substantial image-specific information from the evolving visual representation itself. We further find that generations with more readable contextual representations tend to receive higher human-preference scores. Building on these observations, we introduce Contextual Alignment, a training technique that explicitly reinforces the visual-semantic information encoded in the contextual tokens, improving generation quality and distributional coverage. Together, our results establish contextual tokens as both an interpretable view into the internal dynamics of MM-DiTs and an effective target for improving generative models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework to interpret Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) by training a bottleneck network that maps intermediate contextual tokens to a frozen LLM, enabling natural-language interrogation of the model's internal representations. The method reveals that contextual tokens encode rich, generation-specific semantic information that becomes increasingly detailed over the denoising process, and that this readability correlates with human preference scores. The authors further propose "Contextual Alignment" to improve generation quality by reinforcing visual-semantic information in these tokens.
AI.motivation: MM-DiTs jointly process visual and textual representations during generation, but the function of dynamically updated contextual tokens is not well understood. The authors seek to "read" this internal representational space to understand what information the model accumulates during generation.
AI.method: The authors train a lightweight bottleneck network that maps intermediate contextual tokens from the MM-DiT into the input space of a frozen Large Language Model (LLM). This allows the LLM to answer questions about the emerging image directly from the hidden representations, effectively creating an "interpreter" for the model's internal states.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Contextual tokens encode rich, global representations of the emerging scene including generation-specific semantics and attributes not specified in the prompt; (2) coarse semantic information is accessible early in denoising, with fine-grained details emerging over time; (3) information remains decodable even with empty prompts, showing tokens accumulate image-specific information from visual representations alone; (4) generations with more readable contextual representations receive higher human-preference scores.
AI.conclusion: Contextual tokens serve as both an interpretable window into MM-DiT dynamics and an effective target for improvement. The authors introduce "Contextual Alignment," a training technique that reinforces visual-semantic information in contextual tokens, improving generation quality and distributional coverage. This work establishes a new paradigm for understanding and improving multimodal diffusion models.

title: COVER: Learning to Accept More in Selective Sleep Staging
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures; code and frozen-result reproduction: https://github.com/Kevin11Kaikai/COVER-Selective-Sleep-Staging
summary: Traditional sleep-staging methods apply the same model to every EEG epoch. Such uniform deployment expends computation on epochs that a smaller model could handle reliably, motivating cascades in which a primary classifier accepts its reliable predictions and defers the remainder to a more capable model. In this paper, we study the first stage of such a cascade: maximizing the coverage of fixed primary predictions subject to a prescribed accepted-risk target. We propose COVER (COVerage-oriented Error Ranking), which integrates two key innovations: (i) auxiliary-informed primary-error learning, which replaces maximum softmax probability (MSP) with a learned error score while preserving the primary labels, and (ii) fixed-scale scorer refinement, which builds on this score to directly maximize coverage under an empirical accepted-risk constraint rather than error-prediction accuracy over all epochs. We evaluate COVER on Sleep-EDF-20 at a 5% accepted-risk target, with subjects held out from all fitting and selection. Auxiliary-informed error learning raises mean subject coverage from 31.5% for MSP to 48.8% at similar subject-equal risk. At equal acceptance volume, with MSP accepting the same number of epochs as the learned scorer in each subject (20,639 in total), errors fall from 1,467 to 867. Fixed-scale refinement then adds 1.7 percentage points of coverage over its initialization in nested development, and COVER attains the highest mean coverage among eight evaluated scorers, 50.4% at 4.5% subject-equal risk, above the selective-ranking baseline SELE (49.3%) and the probability-fusion comparator DuoF (43.6%). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to combine auxiliary-informed primary-error learning with fixed-scale coverage refinement for selective sleep staging, offering a basis for reliability-aware allocation of computation in cascaded sleep staging.
