title: SkillScriptBench: Benchmarking Self-Evolution of Executable Agent Skill Packages Beyond Markdown
summary: Executable Agent Skills combine natural-language instructions and scripts into reusable packages for LLM agents, and revising them requires fixing errors without breaking correct behavior. Existing benchmarks do not systematically distinguish documentation repair, script repair, and preservation when evaluating skill self-evolution. We introduce SkillScriptBench, a 350-task benchmark designed to evaluate these capabilities separately. From a survey of over 35,000 GitHub-hosted Skill roots, we select 100 packages and construct 150 repair tasks. Each task pairs a package containing injected script faults with a maintenance request and executable checks of the required behavior. A complementary controlled track contains 200 tasks from 50 packages, each evaluated under the same maintenance request in four states: clean, documentation faults, script faults, and faults in both. Across four LLMs, methods that edit both documentation and scripts can repair script faults but do not consistently outperform Markdown-only revision on documentation repair or preservation. We therefore introduce AST-Guided Skill Revision, which uses abstract syntax trees and calling relationships to link maintenance requirements to relevant code locations. It restricts script edits to these locations and updates the documentation to match the revised scripts. Averaged across models, this revision stage yields absolute gains in repair success of 21.9% for Raw Package and 27.7% for CoEvoSkills on faulty packages. Absolute gains in the proportion of tasks solved in all three runs reach 20.8% and 31.5%, respectively, indicating more consistent repair success across repeated runs.

AI.tldr: SkillScriptBench is a 350-task benchmark evaluating LLM agents' ability to repair executable agent skills (combining natural-language instructions and scripts). It distinguishes between documentation repair, script repair, and preservation capabilities. A new method called AST-Guided Skill Revision uses abstract syntax trees to link maintenance requirements to code locations, achieving 21.9-27.7% absolute gains in repair success.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks do not systematically distinguish documentation repair, script repair, and preservation when evaluating skill self-evolution for LLM agents. This gap prevents proper evaluation of agent self-repair capabilities.
AI.method: SkillScriptBench contains 150 repair tasks from 100 packages (with injected script faults paired with maintenance requests and executable checks) plus a controlled track of 200 tasks evaluated under 4 states (clean, documentation faults, script faults, both faulty). The proposed AST-Guided Skill Revision uses abstract syntax trees and calling relationships to link maintenance requirements to relevant code locations, restricting script edits to these locations and updating documentation accordingly.
AI.result: Methods editing both documentation and scripts can repair script faults but do not consistently outperform Markdown-only revision on documentation repair or preservation. AST-Guided Skill Revision yields 21.9% absolute gain for Raw Package and 27.7% for CoEvoSkills on faulty packages. Gains in consistent repair success (all three runs) reach 20.8% and 31.5% respectively.
AI.conclusion: AST-Guided Skill Revision significantly improves repair success and consistency across repeated runs by using AST analysis to target relevant code locations and synchronize documentation with script changes.

title: Tracing a Sparse Emotion-Control Circuit in LLM-Based Text-to-Speech
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 15 pages, 4 figures
summary: LLM-based text-to-speech (TTS) models can generate emotionally expressive speech, but how reference emotion is routed through the model and realized in decoded speech remains unclear. We introduce two emotion-sensitive metrics for matched neutral and emotional syntheses---a codec trajectory score and a late residual direction score---and use them to score activation-patching interventions. Under controlled matched-reference conditions, this analysis identifies a sparse source-to-readout component-level circuit: 23--27 attention heads and MLPs per emotion, roughly 5% of the components considered, recover or suppress 74--88% of the late emotion-readout shift on held-out cases. The circuit combines a shared component backbone with emotion-specific components; cross-emotion activation swaps reduce the target readout in 47 of 48 cases. In decoded speech, the same intervention produces consistent changes in pitch, energy, and spectral brightness over 24 matched pairs per emotion. A readout-matched residual-direction baseline produces only 17--27% of the intervention's pitch effect, showing that internal readout movement alone does not explain the decoded acoustic changes. These results trace a compact causal route from reference-derived prefix information to emotion-relevant properties of generated speech.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how emotional expression is routed through LLM-based text-to-speech models, introducing two emotion-sensitive metrics (codec trajectory score and late residual direction score) to identify a sparse causal circuit of 23-27 attention heads and MLPs per emotion that can recover or suppress 74-88% of emotion-readout shift, demonstrating a compact route from reference-derived prefix information to decoded speech properties.
AI.motivation: Understand how reference emotion is routed through LLM-based TTS models and realized in decoded speech, which remains unclear despite these models' ability to generate emotionally expressive speech.
AI.method: Introduced two emotion-sensitive metrics (codec trajectory score and late residual direction score) for matched neutral and emotional syntheses; used activation-patching interventions under controlled matched-reference conditions; performed cross-emotion activation swaps; measured decoded acoustic changes in pitch, energy, and spectral brightness.
AI.result: Identified a sparse source-to-readout component-level circuit: 23-27 attention heads and MLPs per emotion (~5% of components) recover or suppress 74-88% of late emotion-readout shift on held-out cases; circuit combines shared component backbone with emotion-specific components; cross-emotion activation swaps reduce target readout in 47 of 48 cases; intervention produces consistent changes in pitch, energy, and spectral brightness over 24 matched pairs per emotion; readout-matched residual-direction baseline produces only 17-27% of intervention's pitch effect.
AI.conclusion: A compact causal route exists from reference-derived prefix information to emotion-relevant properties of generated speech, with internal readout movement alone not explaining decoded acoustic changes.

title: Complex Agents, Shallow Tests: Demystifying and Enhancing Test Adequacy of Agent Harness in the Wild
summary: LLM-based agentic systems are emerging as a new software paradigm. Modern agents are typically composed of backbone LLMs and a surrounding harness that serves as the operational software infrastructure for agent execution. As agent harnesses grow increasingly complex, agents suffer from diverse harness implementation bugs, raising substantial reliability concerns. In this work, we conduct the first empirical study to systematically investigate the test adequacy of harness in real-world agentic systems. Our analysis reveals that agent harness remains substantially undertested. In particular, LLM-dependent harness (LDH) code, despite its critical role in processing LLM outputs and governing agent behavior, receives limited testing attention, with less than half of its lines and branches covered by existing tests. Motivated by these findings, we further propose HarnessTester, the first harness-oriented test generation technique that incorporates explicit agent-harness contract support to construct contract-faithful test setups and extensively exercise LDH code. Our evaluation shows that HarnessTester substantially outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose test generation techniques in achieving 75.95%/84.76% larger line/branch coverage gains and 69.89% larger mutation-score gains. Furthermore, HarnessTester detects 122 real-world harness bugs in widely-used agentic systems (e.g., OpenClaw), among which, 88 bugs are previously-unknown bugs and 69 bugs have been confirmed by agent developers. These results highlight the practical effectiveness of HarnessTester in improving test adequacy and assuring the reliability of real-world agentic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first empirical study on test adequacy of agent harnesses in LLM-based agentic systems, revealing substantial undertesting, particularly in LLM-dependent harness (LDH) code. It proposes HarnessTester, a novel test generation technique that uses explicit agent-harness contract support to construct contract-faithful test setups and exercise LDH code. The approach achieves 75.95%/84.76% larger line/branch coverage gains and 69.89% larger mutation-score gains compared to state-of-the-art techniques, and detects 122 real-world harness bugs (88 previously-unknown, 69 confirmed by developers).
AI.motivation: LLM-based agentic systems are emerging as a new software paradigm, but as agent harnesses grow increasingly complex, agents suffer from diverse harness implementation bugs, raising substantial reliability concerns. The authors identify that agent harness remains substantially undertested, especially LLM-dependent harness (LDH) code which processes LLM outputs and governs agent behavior.
AI.method: The authors conducted the first empirical study to systematically investigate test adequacy of harness in real-world agentic systems. They proposed HarnessTester, the first harness-oriented test generation technique that incorporates explicit agent-harness contract support to construct contract-faithful test setups and extensively exercise LDH code.
AI.result: HarnessTester substantially outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose test generation techniques, achieving 75.95%/84.76% larger line/branch coverage gains and 69.89% larger mutation-score gains. It detected 122 real-world harness bugs in widely-used agentic systems (e.g., OpenClaw), among which 88 are previously-unknown bugs and 69 have been confirmed by agent developers.
AI.conclusion: HarnessTester demonstrates practical effectiveness in improving test adequacy and assuring the reliability of real-world agentic systems. The findings highlight the importance of dedicated testing techniques for agent harnesses, particularly for LLM-dependent code paths.

title: TreeWalker: Partial Evaluation for Grouped Tree-Ensemble Inference
comment: 23 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/Shopify/treewalker
summary:
Many inference workloads evaluate a trained tree ensemble on row groups that share feature values: discrete-time survival models expand each patient into $G$ time steps, click-through-rate models score every item in a search session, and scenario analyses vary a few inputs while holding the rest fixed. Standard inference treats each row independently and repeats the shared work $G$ times.
  We present TreeWalker, which applies partial evaluation to grouped inference: constant features are static, varying features dynamic. It walks each tree once per group, partitions a row bitmask at varying splits, and skips empty subtrees. Training is unchanged: TreeWalker reads standard LightGBM and XGBoost models.
  We prove a structural work decomposition: per-tree work splits into the constant-projected subtree size $|T_c|$, $G$ leaf writes, and a predicate-mask provisioning cost $Q$. For the trace evaluator, per-row work approaches a $(d_v+1)/(d+1)$ fraction of a row-independent walk as $G \to \infty$.
  On Intel, TreeWalker is 2.5-3.2$\times$ faster than a row-independent traversal at the reference configuration ($T=500$, $L=8$) and 6.8-7.8$\times$ faster at $G=128$ on the survival datasets, with larger gains on Arm. On a scenario-analysis benchmark it is faster in all 16 configurations on both architectures. For f64 models, outputs match treelite's GTIL up to summation order; for f32 models, f64 accumulation is closer to a Kahan-compensated reference than native f32 on 99.98% of rows and never farther.

AI.tldr: TreeWalker optimizes tree ensemble inference for grouped data (e.g., survival analysis, CTR prediction, scenario analysis) where rows share feature values. Instead of evaluating each row independently, it walks each tree once per group, partitions row bitmasks at varying splits, and skips empty subtrees. It reads standard LightGBM/XGBoost models without training changes. Achieves 2.5-7.8× speedup on Intel/Arm across various benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard inference treats each row independently, repeating shared work G times when rows share feature values (discrete-time survival models with G time steps, CTR models scoring items in a session, scenario analyses). This inefficiency motivates grouped inference optimization.
AI.method: TreeWalker applies partial evaluation to grouped inference: identifies constant features (static) vs varying features (dynamic). Walks each tree once per group, partitions a row bitmask at varying splits, and skips empty subtrees. Uses a trace evaluator with predicate-mask provisioning. Proven structural work decomposition: constant-projected subtree size |Tc|, G leaf writes, and predicate-mask provisioning cost Q.
AI.result: 2.5-3.2× faster than row-independent traversal at reference config (T=500, L=8), 6.8-7.8× faster at G=128 on survival datasets (larger gains on Arm). Faster in all 16 configurations on scenario-analysis benchmark. For f64 models, outputs match treelite's GTIL up to summation order; for f32 models, f64 accumulation is closer to Kahan-compensated reference than native f32 on 99.98% of rows.
AI.conclusion: TreeWalker enables efficient grouped inference for tree ensembles by exploiting shared feature values across row groups. It provides significant speedups across architectures (Intel, Arm) and configurations while maintaining numerical accuracy. The approach is practical as it accepts standard LightGBM/XGBoost models without retraining.

title: Exploration-Preserving Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning, while the allocation of learning signal shapes which solutions remain accessible under repeated sampling. Group-relative objectives assign equal advantages to equally rewarded responses, making aggregate credit proportional to sampled mode frequency. We introduce Exploration-Preserving Policy Optimization (ExPPO), a lightweight advantage-shaping rule that redistributes credit using prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate. ExPPO combines bounded shaping with shared normalization to preserve verifier polarity and approximately maintain each prompt group's total absolute sequence-advantage mass. Our analysis characterizes response-level credit allocation alongside sampled mode updates, deriving local conditions for gains in entropy and correct-mode discovery. Experiments show improved in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning coverage, higher aggregate response accuracy, and strong coverage at large sampling budgets. A controlled multi-answer evaluation further demonstrates increased correct-mode yield and gains in diversity among verified-correct responses. Code is available at https://github.com/jinhangzhan/ExPPO

AI.tldr: ExPPO introduces a lightweight advantage-shaping rule for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards that redistributes credit using prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate, preserving verifier polarity while maintaining each prompt group's total absolute sequence-advantage mass.
AI.motivation: Current reinforcement learning methods with verifiable rewards allocate equal advantages to equally rewarded responses, making aggregate credit proportional to sampled mode frequency. This limits exploration and accessibility of solutions under repeated sampling. The authors aim to address this credit allocation problem while preserving verifier signals and exploration capabilities.
AI.method: ExPPO combines bounded shaping with shared normalization. It uses prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate to redistribute credit. The approach preserves verifier polarity and approximately maintains each prompt group's total absolute sequence-advantage mass. The analysis characterizes response-level credit allocation alongside sampled mode updates, deriving local conditions for gains in entropy and correct-mode discovery.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning coverage, higher aggregate response accuracy, and strong coverage at large sampling budgets. A controlled multi-answer evaluation shows increased correct-mode yield and gains in diversity among verified-correct responses.
AI.conclusion: ExPPO provides an effective solution for improving reasoning in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards by preserving exploration capabilities while maintaining proper credit allocation. The method successfully improves both the quantity and diversity of correct responses across various sampling budgets.

title: Dynamic Time Step Prediction in Inverse Heat Dissipation for Blur-Like Image Restoration Tasks
summary: When using diffusion models to target image restoration problems, diffusion inversion is typically employed to retain relevant image information from the degraded images. Instead of inverting back to the initial time step (i.e., T), many methods invert to a pre-determined intermediate time step, in order to better preserve information from degraded source images. However, a pre-determined time step for inversion is not ideal for reconstruction, as a severely degraded image requires an earlier starting time step than a mildly degraded one. In addition, DDIM-based models corrupt the original signal by adding Gaussian noise, which can be mismatched to the nature of blur-like degradations, such as blur, haze, and low-light. To address these problems, we propose two solutions: (1) we adopt an alternative diffusion process, called the Inverse Heat Dissipation Model, that diffuses the input image by gradually blurring a data point (2) we propose to implement a time predictor to estimate the starting time step for the inversion, with the model learning to adapt to the degradation severity. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, with excellent generalization to many restoration tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses limitations in diffusion model-based image restoration by proposing two solutions: (1) replacing the standard Gaussian noise diffusion process with an Inverse Heat Dissipation Model that uses gradual blurring, and (2) introducing a time predictor to dynamically estimate the optimal starting time step based on degradation severity. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple restoration tasks.
AI.motivation: The key problems are: (1) pre-determined inversion time steps are suboptimal since severely degraded images need earlier starting points than mildly degraded ones, and (2) DDIM-based models use Gaussian noise which mismatches blur-like degradations (blur, haze, low-light).
AI.method: Two solutions: (1) Adopt Inverse Heat Dissipation Model - an alternative diffusion process that diffuses by gradually blurring data points instead of adding Gaussian noise; (2) Implement a time predictor network that estimates the starting time step for inversion, allowing the model to adapt to degradation severity.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, with excellent generalization to many restoration tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully addresses the limitations of fixed time step inversion and Gaussian noise-based diffusion for blur-like degradations, achieving superior performance across multiple image restoration tasks.

title: NeuMark-Native: Robust Text-to-Speech-Native Watermarking Through Full Utilization of Neural Audio Codec Latent Space
summary: Speech watermarking offers proactive traceability for synthetic speech, yet most existing models operate only after text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis by adding a watermark perturbation to the generated waveform. This post-hoc design leaves watermarking as an external step that can be omitted or bypassed and restricts the watermark to a shallow waveform representation. We propose NeuMark-Native, a TTS-native watermarking framework for neural codec-based synthesis. It embeds payload information into every generated codec-latent layer before waveform decoding, improving watermark persistence under downstream digital signal processing (DSP) and neural codec resynthesis. NeuMark-Native keeps the pretrained TTS model and the neural codec frozen, while optimizing only the watermark modules on generated codec tokens. Experiments on two corpora under 11 DSP attacks and 9 neural-codec attacks demonstrate robust watermark detection while preserving naturalness, intelligibility, and speech quality close to synthetic speech.

AI.tldr: NeuMark-Native is a TTS-native watermarking framework that embeds payload information into codec-latent layers before waveform decoding, improving watermark persistence under DSP and neural codec attacks while preserving speech quality.
AI.motivation: Current speech watermarking operates post-hoc (after TTS synthesis), leaving it as an external step that can be bypassed or omitted. Additionally, the watermark is restricted to shallow waveform representation, limiting its persistence and robustness.
AI.method: NeuMark-Native embeds payload information into every generated codec-latent layer before waveform decoding in neural codec-based synthesis. The pretrained TTS model and neural codec remain frozen while only the watermark modules are optimized on generated codec tokens.
AI.result: Experiments on two corpora under 11 DSP attacks and 9 neural-codec attacks demonstrate robust watermark detection while preserving naturalness, intelligibility, and speech quality close to synthetic speech.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully integrates watermarking natively into the TTS synthesis process, providing robust detection under various attacks while maintaining speech quality, enabling proactive traceability for synthetic speech.

title: Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems
summary:
Agentic machine learning engineering (MLE) is an emerging AI4SE application for complex ML tasks and a step toward recursive self-improvement of AI systems. Recent agentic MLE systems show the value of leveraging insights from related MLE tasks: some systems condition code generation on expert domain knowledge, which is implicitly curated from peer MLE tasks; some systems have a loop of solving an MLE task, gathering memory to benefit future tasks. However, insight collection and injection remain ad hoc, and existing evaluations often do not control insight sources, making data leakage a threat to validity.
  To close these gaps, we systematically study how insights from related MLE tasks affect agentic MLE systems, and how their impact depends on insight type and injection method. We introduce MLE-InsightBench, a benchmark of 160 Kaggle competitions across 12 domains. To prevent leakage, one competition per domain is held out as the target, while the remaining 148 serve as sources only when they cannot have been influenced by the target task, such as through later editions or reused solutions. We also develop MLE-InsightForge, an insight assembly agent that explores source competitions, top human solutions, and writeups to construct three insight types: 12 domain insights summarizing best practices, 148 competition insights describing winning solutions, and 16 improvement insights capturing generic debugging and optimization strategies. These insights are injected either as on-demand skills or as an upfront playbook. In our evaluation, the extracted insights improve the normalized private-test score by 123.9% over a no-insight baseline. Controlled experiments further show that the three insight types are complementary; the better injection mode (skill vs. playbook) varies by tasks, with skills more cost-effective overall; and the gains generalize across backend LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MLE-InsightBench, a benchmark of 160 Kaggle competitions to study how insights from related ML tasks affect agentic MLE systems, along with MLE-InsightForge, an agent that extracts three types of insights (domain, competition, improvement) and injects them via skills or playbook. The approach achieves 123.9% improvement over baseline.
AI.motivation: Current agentic MLE systems leverage insights from related tasks but do so ad hoc, with no systematic study of insight types and injection methods. Additionally, data leakage threatens validity in existing evaluations since insight sources are not controlled.
AI.method: The authors created MLE-InsightBench with 160 Kaggle competitions across 12 domains, holding out one competition per domain as target to prevent leakage. They developed MLE-InsightForge to extract three insight types: domain insights (12), competition insights (148), and improvement insights (16). These insights were injected via two methods: on-demand skills or upfront playbook. Evaluation measured normalized private-test score improvements across different LLMs.
AI.result: Extracted insights improve normalized private-test score by 123.9% over no-insight baseline. Three insight types are complementary. Skills injection is more cost-effective overall. Gains generalize across backend LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Systematic insight collection and injection can significantly improve agentic MLE systems. The three insight types provide complementary benefits, and the choice between skills vs. playbook injection depends on the task. The benchmark and findings provide a foundation for future research in AI-driven ML engineering.

title: DePICT: Decision-Preserving Interface for Constrained Downstream Tasks
summary: A constrained optimization problem may involve a parameter in its objective and active constraints, yet the final decision may remain insensitive to small changes in that parameter. This raises a fundamental question: which inputs does a decision making system truly depend on? Building on this question, we introduce DePICT, a procedure for constructing decision preserving interfaces by ranking context directions according to the optimizer's solution sensitivity and aggregating them across an operating regime. We study this problem in a high dimensional setting where primitive context parameterizes a constrained task and the downstream agent observes only a selected subset of context directions. For locally regular constrained programs, we derive a Karush Kuhn Tucker (KKT) based characterization of when a context direction is optimizer relevant. Our analysis shows that appearing in the active optimization problem does not necessarily imply that a variable affects the final decision. Some context directions can alter the KKT conditions while leaving the optimal solution unchanged because their effect is absorbed by the dual variables. DePICT is designed to remove exactly these directions. In a controlled diagnosis, it recovers the decision relevant interface exactly and reduces linear predictor regret to 0.009, compared with 0.475 for the strongest competing baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DePICT, a method to identify which context parameters actually affect decisions in constrained optimization problems. It addresses the fundamental question of which inputs a decision-making system truly depends on, distinguishing between variables that appear in the active optimization problem versus those that actually change the optimal solution.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand which inputs a decision-making system truly depends on. In constrained optimization, a parameter may appear in the objective and active constraints, yet the final decision may remain insensitive to small changes in that parameter. This raises a fundamental question about decision dependency in optimization systems.
AI.method: The paper proposes DePICT (Decision Preserving Interface Construction), which ranks context directions according to the optimizer's solution sensitivity and aggregates them across an operating regime. For locally regular constrained programs, they derive a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) based characterization to determine when a context direction is optimizer relevant. The key insight is that some context directions can alter KKT conditions while leaving the optimal solution unchanged because their effect is absorbed by the dual variables.
AI.result: In a controlled diagnosis, DePICT recovers the decision relevant interface exactly and reduces linear predictor regret to 0.009, compared with 0.475 for the strongest competing baseline. The analysis shows that appearing in the active optimization problem does not necessarily imply that a variable affects the final decision.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that DePICT can precisely identify which context directions truly affect decisions in constrained optimization problems, successfully removing directions that only alter KKT conditions but don't change the optimal solution. This provides a systematic way to construct decision-preserving interfaces that capture only the decision-relevant aspects of the context.

title: Beyond the Parameter Monolith: Reconstructive Memories, Executable Skills, and Residual Assembly for Language Models
summary: Language-model systems can separate contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution instead of updating all capabilities through one shared parameter system. We investigate FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired organization in which independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes. We evaluate this organization through controlled experiments and negative results rather than claiming a physical finite-element formulation of language. An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype learns causal language modeling but does not establish competitive general capability. A versioned store contains 52,809 reconstructive memory elements near a 1.7-billion-floating-value budget; reconstruction is incomplete, with approximately 75\% token accuracy. Support-aware lexical indices make these elements addressable under provenance-controlled query construction. For executable arithmetic, positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering relative to a repeated global result vector, and output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. A bounded attachment demonstration further measures the effect of making selected evidence available, without establishing the utility of loading an entire multi-billion-value store. The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination, while identifying unresolved limitations in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired architecture that separates contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution in language model systems. The prototype uses a versioned store with ~52,809 memory elements (1.7B floating values) achieving ~75% token accuracy, with experiments on arithmetic tasks and bounded attachment demonstrating the separation of concerns approach.
AI.motivation: Current language models rely on shared parameter systems that combine all capabilities. This work seeks to decouple contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution into separate components, enabling more modular and interpretable language model systems.
AI.method: FEM-ASM uses independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills that contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals at common interface nodes. The system includes: (1) an attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype for causal language modeling, (2) a versioned store with 52,809 reconstructive memory elements, (3) support-aware lexical indices for provenance-controlled query, and (4) positional result observations for executable arithmetic.
AI.result: The attention-free prototype does not establish competitive general capability. The versioned store achieves ~75% token accuracy with incomplete reconstruction. Positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering compared to repeated global result vectors. Output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. Bounded attachment demonstrates measurable effects of making selected evidence available, but loading the entire multi-billion-value store is not justified.
AI.conclusion: The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination in language model systems. However, significant limitations remain in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency. The approach identifies unresolved challenges rather than claiming a complete solution.

title: FADE: Frame-Aware Diffusion-Transformer-based Multi-Concept Erasure for Video Unlearning
summary: Text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models can reproduce copyrighted, violent, or explicit content, which motivates concept erasure: removing designated concepts from a pretrained model while preserving its behavior on everything else. Existing T2V erasure methods leave two problems open. Their frame-agnostic suppression can leave isolated frames in which an erased concept resurfaces, a frame-reactivation gap that clip-level averages obscure; and they are usually evaluated with one target concept or category at a time. We propose Frame-Aware Diffusion Erasure (FADE), a multi-concept video unlearning framework. FADE first applies a joint closed-form key/value edit that suppresses all target concepts, then trains per-concept frame-aware low-rank adapters whose strength is gated by the frame index and the denoising timestep to remove residual per-frame leakage. Each adapter is trained with the other targets' prompts as hard negatives, which keeps the concept-specific components of different adapters well separated, and a similarity-based soft router combines the adapters according to the prompt. With 16 concepts (objects, artistic styles, and nudity) erased from a single Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B backbone, FADE reduces the residual accuracy on the object benchmark to 4.9%, against 15.5% for the strongest of eight baselines, while keeping the VBench average within 0.9% of the unedited model. The ranking is unchanged under a VLM judge and a blinded human study, and the advantage over the strongest baseline carries over to prompts that combine several erased concepts, to 30 simultaneously erased celebrity identities, and to Wan2.1-T2V-14B, CogVideoX-2B, and HunyuanVideo-1.5.

AI.tldr: FADE (Frame-Aware Diffusion Erasure) is a multi-concept video unlearning framework that removes designated concepts from pretrained text-to-video diffusion models while preserving overall performance. It addresses two key limitations of prior work: frame-reactivation gaps where erased concepts resurface in isolated frames, and limited evaluation to single-concept erasure.
AI.motivation: Text-to-video diffusion models can generate copyrighted, violent, or explicit content, necessitating concept erasure techniques. Existing methods suffer from frame-agnostic suppression that allows concepts to reappear in isolated frames (frame-reactivation gap), and are typically evaluated on only one target concept at a time.
AI.method: FADE combines two techniques: (1) Joint closed-form key/value editing to suppress all target concepts simultaneously; (2) Per-concept frame-aware low-rank adapters with gating mechanisms controlled by frame index and denoising timestep to eliminate residual per-frame leakage. Training uses other targets' prompts as hard negatives to maintain separation between concept-specific components, and a similarity-based soft router combines adapters according to the prompt.
AI.result: On 16 erased concepts (objects, artistic styles, nudity) from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, FADE achieves 4.9% residual accuracy vs 15.5% for the strongest of 8 baselines, while maintaining VBench average within 0.9% of the unedited model. The advantage generalizes to: combined erased concepts, 30 simultaneous celebrity identity erasures, and transfers to larger models (Wan2.1-T2V-14B, CogVideoX-2B, HunyuanVideo-1.5). Ranking validated by VLM judge and blinded human study.
AI.conclusion: FADE demonstrates effective multi-concept video unlearning with state-of-the-art concept suppression while preserving generation quality. The frame-aware approach successfully addresses the frame-reactivation gap, and the method scales to multiple models and diverse concept types including celebrity identities.

title: Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation for Efficient Audio Deepfake Detection
summary: Advances in speech synthesis have made deepfake speeches increasingly convincing, posing growing threats to security. While self-supervised learning (SSL) based detectors achieve state-of-the-art performance, their computational demands (typically 300M+ parameters) prevent deployment on resource-constrained devices. Existing compression methods, designed mainly for content-centric tasks, struggle to maintain competitive performance when directly adapted to deepfake detection. We propose a Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation framework that combines cross-domain knowledge distillation with movement-guided structured pruning to transfer forgery-discriminative knowledge and preserve critical structures under aggressive compression. Our framework reduces the model to 31.9M parameters with 6.3$\times$ FLOPs reduction, with an average performance drop of only 1.30\% across multiple datasets compared to the uncompressed baseline, demonstrating strong potential for on-device deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation framework to compress large self-supervised learning-based speech deepfake detectors for on-device deployment, achieving 6.3× FLOPs reduction with only 1.30% performance drop.
AI.motivation: Speech synthesis deepfakes pose security threats, but state-of-the-art SSL-based detectors require 300M+ parameters, making them unsuitable for resource-constrained devices. Existing compression methods designed for content-centric tasks fail to maintain detection performance when applied to deepfake detection.
AI.method: The framework combines cross-domain knowledge distillation (to transfer forgery-discriminative knowledge) with movement-guided structured pruning (to preserve critical structures under aggressive compression). The approach is task-aware, specifically designed for deepfake detection rather than generic compression.
AI.result: The model was compressed to 31.9M parameters with 6.3× FLOPs reduction, maintaining competitive performance with only 1.30% average drop across multiple datasets compared to the uncompressed baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates strong potential for on-device deployment of speech deepfake detection, effectively balancing model efficiency and detection accuracy through task-aware compression techniques.

title: TeleGen: Improving LLM-Based Web Application Generation via Runtime Telemetry
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language models can generate runnable web applications from natural-language requirements, but many generated applications still fail interactive tasks. Existing generate-execute-repair pipelines execute the generated application and use task outcomes or error messages to guide code revision. However, this feedback often misses the runtime behavior between a browser action and the final task outcome, making interaction-level failures difficult to diagnose. Therefore, we propose TeleGen, an observability-enhanced framework for LLM-based web application generation. TeleGen instruments generated applications, collects runtime telemetry during task execution, and compresses raw telemetry logs into concise briefs for repair. We evaluate TeleGen on WebGen-Bench and Web-Bench. On WebGen-Bench, TeleGen improves task success from 67.7% with repair without telemetry to 76.2%, an increase of 8.5 percentage points. On Web-Bench, it improves cumulative Pass@2 from 21.7% to 29.8%. Ablation results show that runtime telemetry provides a useful diagnostic signal, while telemetry briefs make this signal more effective and less costly to use. Further analysis shows that telemetry is especially helpful for failures involving hidden execution paths, such as navigation, form workflows, and frontend-backend coordination.

title: Synthesizing Physics Formulae with Transformers
summary: Finding a compact formula that fits a set of input-output pairs and predicts outputs on unseen inputs is a fundamental problem in science. Symbolic regression automates the search for such formulae: search-based methods explore the space of possible formulae directly, while transformers pre-trained on synthetic data produce formulae of comparable quality substantially faster. Existing transformers, however, are prone to overfitting --- they find formulae that fit the training data well but do not extrapolate to input ranges unseen during training. We address this by shaping the set of formulae used to train a transformer, and show that the resulting formulae extrapolate substantially better. Fine-tuning the transformer on data with noise-corrupted target values further makes the synthesized formulae robust to noise in the observations. On SRBench and LLM-SRBench our transformer synthesizes a formula in about ten seconds and extrapolates better than all evaluated methods at a comparable budget. Search-based methods surpass our accuracy only when given one to three orders of magnitude more time.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses symbolic regression using transformers, focusing on improving extrapolation ability. The authors shape the training formula set and fine-tune with noise-corrupted data to make transformers more robust and better at generalizing to unseen input ranges.
AI.motivation: Existing transformer-based symbolic regression methods suffer from overfitting—they fit training data well but fail to extrapolate to input ranges not seen during training. This limits their practical utility in scientific discovery.
AI.method: Two key innovations: (1) shaping the set of formulae used to train the transformer to improve extrapolation capability, and (2) fine-tuning on data with noise-corrupted target values to enhance robustness to observational noise.
AI.result: The transformer synthesizes a formula in approximately ten seconds and extrapolates better than all evaluated methods at comparable budget on SRBench and LLM-SRBench. Search-based methods only outperform it when given 1-3 orders of magnitude more computation time.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based symbolic regression can achieve superior extrapolation performance and noise robustness while being significantly faster than search-based methods, making it practical for scientific discovery tasks.

title: A Quantitative Analysis of Graph Representation Strategies for Cyber Attack Detection
summary: Graph based cyber attack detection studies employ various graph construction and representation strategies across different cybersecurity application domains. This diversity motivates a quantitative examination of how representation strategies are distributed across these application domains. This study presents a quantitative analysis of 37 original studies published between 2019 and 2026. Each study was coded according to publication year, application domain, graph representation type, feature extraction strategy, learning paradigm, algorithm, and dataset. Frequency analysis, cross tabulation, and statistical association tests were applied. Automated representation learning was the most frequently employed strategy, accounting for 73.0% of the studies, while handcrafted representation strategies accounted for 27.0%. The Fisher Freeman Halton exact test revealed a statistically significant association between application domain and representation strategy (exact p = 0.008; Cramer's V = 0.540). The findings indicate that automated representation learning predominates within the analyzed corpus and that the distribution of representation strategies differs across cybersecurity application domains.

AI.tldr: This systematic review analyzes 37 graph-based cyber attack detection studies (2019-2026), examining how representation strategies are distributed across cybersecurity application domains. Automated representation learning (73%) significantly outweighs handcrafted approaches (27%), with a statistically significant association found between application domain and representation strategy (p=0.008).
AI.motivation: The diversity in graph construction and representation strategies across different cybersecurity application domains motivated a quantitative examination of how these strategies are distributed.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of 37 original studies coded by publication year, application domain, graph representation type, feature extraction strategy, learning paradigm, algorithm, and dataset. Applied frequency analysis, cross tabulation, and Fisher Freeman Halton exact test.
AI.result: Automated representation learning was most frequent (73.0%) vs handcrafted strategies (27.0%). Significant association found between application domain and representation strategy (exact p=0.008; Cramer's V=0.540).
AI.conclusion: Automated representation learning predominates in the analyzed corpus, and the distribution of representation strategies differs significantly across cybersecurity application domains.

title: Masked Privileged-Information Distillation for Multimodal Skin Lesion Classification Under Missing Clinical Metadata
summary: Multimodal skin lesion classification combines clinical images with patient metadata to improve diagnostic accuracy. However, complete metadata available during training may be only partially accessible at deployment, and resource-constrained settings additionally require computational efficiency. We address these challenges with a privileged-information distillation framework in which a multimodal teacher trained on complete metadata supervises a 9.2x smaller student trained with randomly masked clinical fields. Clinical fields are masked as whole groups at a per-sample rate drawn from U(0,1), so one training run covers the full metadata availability range. Fusion is residual, with metadata added as a gated correction to an unconditional image base. On the PAD-UFES-20 dataset, distillation under masked training improves balanced accuracy over cross-entropy training at every availability level, by an average of +4.7 points versus +1.8 points without masking. The masked student loses only 7.8 balanced-accuracy points as metadata decreases from complete to absent, compared with 36.6 points for the same student trained on complete metadata, highlighting the role of masked training in graceful degradation beyond distillation alone. Grad-CAM visualizations further show that the masked student's attention generally remains lesion-centered as metadata is withdrawn. The resulting compact model targets point-of-care settings, where clinical metadata is often incomplete.

AI.tldr: A privileged-information distillation framework for multimodal skin lesion classification that uses a multimodal teacher (trained on complete metadata) to supervise a 9.2x smaller student trained with randomly masked clinical fields. The method enables graceful degradation when metadata is incomplete at deployment, targeting point-of-care settings.
AI.motivation: Address challenges in multimodal skin lesion classification where: 1) complete metadata available during training may be only partially accessible at deployment, and 2) resource-constrained settings require computational efficiency. The goal is to maintain diagnostic accuracy even when clinical metadata is incomplete or absent.
AI.method: Privileged-information distillation with masked training: 1) Train a multimodal teacher on complete metadata, 2) Use this teacher to supervise a 9.2x smaller student, 3) Train the student with randomly masked clinical fields (masked as whole groups at per-sample rate from U(0,1)), 4) Use residual fusion with metadata added as gated correction to unconditional image base. One training run covers the full metadata availability range.
AI.result: Distillation under masked training improves balanced accuracy over cross-entropy training at every availability level (+4.7 points average vs +1.8 points without masking). The masked student loses only 7.8 balanced-accuracy points as metadata decreases from complete to absent (compared with 36.6 points for the same student trained on complete metadata). Grad-CAM visualizations show the masked student's attention remains lesion-centered as metadata is withdrawn.
AI.conclusion: Masked training during distillation enables graceful degradation when metadata is unavailable, significantly outperforming standard training. The resulting compact model is suitable for point-of-care settings where clinical metadata is often incomplete.

title: LLM-Based Test Generation: Information Sources, Generation Strategies, and Quality Evidence
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to generate test scenarios, executable test suites, assertions, interaction sequences, and fuzzing infrastructure. These artifacts serve different purposes and rely on different sources of information about correct behavior. A test that increases implementation coverage, a test that agrees with a reference program, and a test that detects a requirements violation therefore provide distinct kinds of evidence. We present a structured narrative survey that connects the generation process to the evidence used to justify test quality. Drawing on 95 curated source records through 29 September 2026, we organize the field along four dimensions: testing objectives and artifacts, information available during training and generation, generation and learning mechanisms, and evaluation evidence. We synthesize work on unit and requirements-based testing, test oracles, API and GUI testing, fuzzing, and learned test generators. The resulting framework explains how execution feedback can improve executability while also affecting the independence of an oracle, why specification provenance and training-time reference supervision matter for comparisons, and how downstream code-selection gains differ from test correctness. We use these distinctions to organize benchmarks and derive a research agenda for independent oracle assessment, budget-aware generation, repository-scale evaluation, and test maintenance.

AI.tldr: This survey paper (95 sources, through September 2026) presents a structured framework for understanding LLM-based software testing across four dimensions: testing objectives/artifacts, training/generation information sources, generation mechanisms, and evaluation evidence. The key contribution is clarifying how different test types (coverage-based, reference-based, requirements-based) provide distinct evidence, and how execution feedback affects the trade-off between executability and oracle independence. The paper identifies research directions in independent oracle assessment, budget-aware generation, repository-scale evaluation, and test maintenance.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the rapidly growing use of large language models (LLMs) for various testing tasks, including generating test scenarios, executable test suites, assertions, interaction sequences, and fuzzing infrastructure. However, these different testing artifacts serve distinct purposes and rely on different sources of information about correct behavior. A key insight is that tests providing coverage, tests agreeing with reference programs, and tests detecting requirements violations each provide distinct types of evidence. This diversity lacked a unified framework for understanding the field, motivating the authors to create a systematic organization of LLM-based testing research.
AI.method: The authors conducted a structured narrative survey using 95 curated source records up to 29 September 2026. They organized the field along four dimensions: (1) testing objectives and artifacts - what types of tests are generated and their purposes; (2) information available during training and generation - what knowledge sources LLMs can leverage; (3) generation and learning mechanisms - how LLMs produce tests; and (4) evaluation evidence - how test quality is assessed. The survey synthesizes work across unit and requirements-based testing, test oracles, API and GUI testing, fuzzing, and learned test generators.
AI.result: The paper presents a comprehensive framework that explains several key relationships: (1) how execution feedback can improve executability while potentially compromising oracle independence; (2) why specification provenance and training-time reference supervision are critical for meaningful comparisons; (3) how downstream code-selection gains differ from actual test correctness. The framework organizes existing benchmarks and identifies gaps in current evaluation approaches. The authors use these distinctions to derive a research agenda focusing on independent oracle assessment, budget-aware generation, repository-scale evaluation, and test maintenance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by presenting a research agenda centered on four key areas: (1) independent oracle assessment - developing methods to evaluate test quality without relying on the same mechanisms used for generation; (2) budget-aware generation - understanding the trade-offs between computational cost and test quality; (3) repository-scale evaluation - moving beyond single-function testing to evaluate LLMs across entire codebases; and (4) test maintenance - addressing the challenge of keeping LLM-generated tests valid as code evolves. The framework provides a systematic way to understand the relationships between generation processes, evidence sources, and test quality, enabling more informed research and practical applications in LLM-based testing.

title: Evolving LLM-Generated Features for Interpretable Classification
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as classifiers, yet they operate as opaque systems whose decisions are difficult to interpret, which complicates their use in regulated domains such as credit scoring or medical diagnosis. We propose an evolutionary framework that iteratively discovers natural language feature definitions (rubrics) for interpretable classification. An LLM generates candidate binary features, evaluates each sample against them, and the resulting vectors can be used to train a transparent classifier such as logistic regression. The feature set evolves over multiple iterations guided by classification errors, per-class activation rates, and feature ablation scores. We evaluate across three benchmarks, including a credit risk dataset representative of regulated domains, comparing single-shot LLM rubrics, evolved rubrics, and direct zero-shot LLM classification. Evolved features improve over single-shot rubrics by +2.9 pp on average and outperform zero-shot LLM classification on two of three tasks, while providing fully auditable decision logic. On the credit risk task, the zero-shot LLM performs at chance (50.7%) with a strong bias toward a single class, whereas evolved features achieve balanced, interpretable predictions. Crucially, this failure is invisible in aggregate accuracy and surfaces only under per-class auditing. Analysis reveals that evolution is most effective when label boundaries cannot be inferred from category names alone or when the LLM lacks reliable domain-specific reasoning.

AI.tldr: An evolutionary framework that iteratively discovers natural language feature definitions (rubrics) for interpretable classification using LLMs. The LLM generates candidate binary features, evaluates samples, and the resulting vectors train transparent classifiers like logistic regression. Features evolve over multiple iterations guided by classification errors, per-class activation rates, and feature ablation scores.
AI.motivation: Large language models are increasingly used as classifiers but operate as opaque systems whose decisions are difficult to interpret, which complicates their use in regulated domains such as credit scoring or medical diagnosis.
AI.method: An evolutionary framework where an LLM generates candidate binary features, evaluates each sample against them, and the resulting vectors train a transparent classifier (logistic regression). The feature set evolves over multiple iterations guided by classification errors, per-class activation rates, and feature ablation scores.
AI.result: Evolved features improve over single-shot rubrics by +2.9 percentage points on average and outperform zero-shot LLM classification on two of three tasks, while providing fully auditable decision logic. On the credit risk task, zero-shot LLM performs at chance (50.7%) with strong bias toward a single class, whereas evolved features achieve balanced, interpretable predictions. This failure is invisible in aggregate accuracy and surfaces only under per-class auditing.
AI.conclusion: Evolution is most effective when label boundaries cannot be inferred from category names alone or when the LLM lacks reliable domain-specific reasoning. The framework successfully creates interpretable, auditable classification features while exposing hidden failures in LLM classification that aggregate metrics miss.

title: The Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating: A Framework for Disclosing Human-AI Collaboration
summary: Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly incorporated into digital media and more generally into production workflows with which the public frequently interacts. Current provenance standards and disclosure methods frequently rely on binary categorizations, differentiating only between entirely human-authored and AI-generated content, or depend on technical watermarking that lacks user-facing clarity. However, there are very different risks and outcomes depending on the different uses of AI in the creation and consumption of end products. Therefore, we propose the Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating framework which addresses these concerns by introducing a six-tier scale (Levels 0-5) that discloses the extent of AI involvement in both product creation and user experience. This paper details the structural methodology of the REAL Rating system and the specifics of its application across text, image, audio, video, and software products.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating framework, a six-tier scale (Levels 0-5) designed to disclose the extent of AI involvement in digital media and products. The framework addresses the limitations of current binary categorization methods (human-authored vs. AI-generated) and technical watermarking approaches that lack user-facing clarity.
AI.motivation: Current provenance standards and disclosure methods rely on binary categorizations that only differentiate between entirely human-authored and AI-generated content, or depend on technical watermarking that lacks user-facing clarity. However, there are very different risks and outcomes depending on the different uses of AI in creation and consumption of end products, necessitating a more nuanced disclosure approach.
AI.method: The paper proposes a structural methodology using a six-tier scale (Levels 0-5) that discloses the extent of AI involvement in both product creation and user experience. The framework is designed for application across multiple product types: text, image, audio, video, and software.
AI.result: The REAL Rating framework introduces a graduated scale (0-5) that provides more nuanced disclosure of AI involvement compared to binary classification, addressing different risk levels and user experience implications across various content types.
AI.conclusion: The REAL Rating system provides a comprehensive solution for disclosing AI involvement in digital products, offering user-facing clarity through a standardized six-tier scale applicable across multiple media formats (text, image, audio, video, and software).

title: Verifier-Guided Synthetic Augmentation for 3D Human Shape Generation
summary: Limited training data diversity constrains generative modeling of 3D human bodies: conservative models remain close to observed examples, whereas exploratory models often violate basic body proportions. We introduce a verifier-guided augmentation framework that uses global and mode-local PCA to generate inexpensive candidates, screens them using correspondence-derived skeletal proportions and body-part geometry, and retrains a diffusion model on accepted candidates. Elastic registration provides both the modal structure used by distributed PCA and the dense anatomical correspondence needed for scalable screening without per-candidate body-model fitting. A blinded human study supports the verifier as a conservative gatekeeper, favoring verifier-accepted over rejected outputs. We evaluate full-pool verifier acceptance separately from the coverage and departure of accepted samples and combine them through EAUC. On 4,498 registered DFAUST surfaces, distributed-PCA augmentation achieves 86.32% acceptance, the highest CP-AUC (0.871), and the highest EAUC (0.752), improving EAUC by 32% over real-only and self-augmented diffusion. These results show that mode-local, verifier-guided proposals broaden diffusion generation while maintaining high agreement with calibrated body measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a verifier-guided augmentation framework for training diffusion models to generate 3D human bodies. The method uses global and mode-local PCA to generate candidate bodies, screens them using skeletal proportions and body-part geometry, and retrains the diffusion model on accepted samples. The approach achieves 86.32% acceptance rate and improves EAUC by 32% over baseline methods.
AI.motivation: Limited training data diversity in 3D human body generation causes two problems: conservative models stay too close to training examples, while exploratory models often produce physically implausible bodies with abnormal proportions. Current methods lack effective ways to balance diversity with anatomical validity.
AI.method: The framework uses: 1) Global and mode-local PCA to generate diverse candidate bodies; 2) A verifier that screens candidates using correspondence-derived skeletal proportions and body-part geometry; 3) Elastic registration to provide both modal structure for PCA and dense anatomical correspondence for scalable screening; 4) Retraining a diffusion model on verifier-accepted candidates.
AI.result: On 4,498 DFAUST surfaces: distributed-PCA augmentation achieves 86.32% acceptance rate, highest CP-AUC (0.871), and highest EAUC (0.752). This represents a 32% improvement in EAUC over real-only and self-augmented diffusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: Mode-local, verifier-guided proposals successfully broaden diffusion model generation while maintaining high agreement with calibrated body measurements. The verifier acts as a conservative gatekeeper, effectively balancing exploration with anatomical plausibility.

title: SEA-LM: Egocentric Spatial Audio Understanding for Wearable Microphone Arrays
summary: Embodied, ego-centric intelligence fundamentally requires the ability to comprehend spatial audio within complex environments. While large audio-language models excel at mono-channel reasoning, they lack spatial awareness, discarding critical spatial cues that enable sound localization and that can improve the disentanglement of overlapping sound sources. To address this, we present SEA-LM, a Spatial Audio Understanding model. First, we introduce FOACODER, a layout-flexible spatial audio encoder trained on source localization and ego-centric voice activity detection objectives to encode First Order Ambisonics derived from variable-count, variable-position smart-glasses arrays via beamforming. We train a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to understand these spatial audio embeddings through a two-stage curriculum spanning six tasks, including sound localization and spatially selective transcription in settings with multiple speakers and overlapping sounds. To prevent the transcription outputs from dominating the next token prediction loss and overwhelming the direction predictions, we introduce a Spatio-temporal Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss. On our evaluation set, SEA-LM achieves lower azimuth and elevation MAE, higher temporal IoU, lower external-source hallucination and missing-source rates, and lower WER on most transcription tasks than compared baselines, while remaining robust across 1,211 smart-glasses array configurations with 4 to 9 microphones.

AI.tldr: SEA-LM is a spatial audio understanding model that enables Large Language Models to comprehend spatial audio with spatial awareness, addressing the limitation of existing audio-language models that discard spatial cues. The system uses FOACODER for spatial audio encoding and a novel Spatio-temporal Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss to balance transcription and direction prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Current large audio-language models excel at mono-channel reasoning but lack spatial awareness, discarding critical spatial cues that enable sound localization and improve disentanglement of overlapping sound sources. This is a fundamental limitation for embodied, ego-centric intelligence that requires comprehending spatial audio in complex environments.
AI.method: 1) FOACODER: A layout-flexible spatial audio encoder trained on source localization and ego-centric voice activity detection objectives, encoding First Order Ambisonics from variable-count, variable-position smart-glasses arrays via beamforming. 2) Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) trained through a two-stage curriculum spanning six tasks (sound localization and spatially selective transcription with multiple speakers and overlapping sounds). 3) Spatio-temporal Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss to prevent transcription outputs from dominating the loss and overwhelming direction predictions.
AI.result: SEA-LM achieves: lower azimuth and elevation MAE (Mean Absolute Error), higher temporal IoU, lower external-source hallucination and missing-source rates, lower WER (Word Error Rate) on most transcription tasks, while remaining robust across 1,211 smart-glasses array configurations with 4 to 9 microphones.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SEA-LM successfully enables spatial audio understanding in MLLMs, maintaining performance across diverse microphone configurations and effectively balancing multiple tasks including sound localization and transcription in multi-speaker, overlapping sound scenarios.

title: Rethinking Tool Design for Agentic RCA: A Controlled Empirical Study
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly explored for root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems, yet empirical guidance on how to design and combine their tools remains limited. We conduct a controlled empirical study of tool abstraction and composition across models and microservice environments. We implement 24 structured tools for metric access (L1), evidence analysis (L2), and diagnosis (L3), alongside a Python-based reference setting (L0). Using 375 failure cases from three microservice systems, we evaluate eight configurations with Qwen3.7-Plus and compare four Qwen models on a shared subset of four configurations. Our results show that tool configurations affect root cause localization and failure type identification differently. With Qwen3.7-Plus, L3 achieves 82.8% top-1 localization accuracy compared with 85.4% for L0, while requiring less than half the time per case. Adding tool levels can improve type identification while reducing localization accuracy. Trajectory analysis reveals cases in which agents override correct diagnostic recommendations after consulting additional evidence. Model choice also changes tool benefits: adding L3 to L1+L2 improves diagnosis for three models but hurts Qwen3-8B, which rarely invokes L3. Tool configuration rankings further change across microservice systems. These findings provide an empirical foundation for designing and using RCA tools, guiding tool selection and composition according to the model, diagnostic objective, and target system.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a controlled empirical study on designing and combining tools for LLM agents performing root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems, evaluating 24 structured tools across 4 abstraction levels using 375 failure cases and multiple Qwen models.
AI.motivation: Large language model agents are increasingly explored for RCA in microservice systems, but there is limited empirical guidance on how to design and combine their tools effectively.
AI.method: Controlled empirical study implementing 24 structured tools across 3 levels (L1: metric access, L2: evidence analysis, L3: diagnosis) plus a Python-based reference (L0). Evaluated 8 configurations using Qwen3.7-Plus and compared 4 Qwen models on 4 configurations using 375 failure cases from 3 microservice systems.
AI.result: L3 achieves 82.8% top-1 localization accuracy vs 85.4% for L0 while requiring less than half the time. Adding tool levels improves type identification but reduces localization accuracy. Agents sometimes override correct recommendations after consulting additional evidence. Tool benefits vary by model: L3 helps 3 models but hurts Qwen3-8B. Configuration rankings change across different microservice systems.
AI.conclusion: Tool configurations significantly affect RCA outcomes. Model choice, diagnostic objectives, and target systems all influence tool selection and composition. The findings provide an empirical foundation for designing RCA tools, with guidance for practitioners on selecting appropriate tool combinations based on their specific model, goals, and system context.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: One-Step Curvature Probes Miss the Fitting Operator: Retained Capacity and Terminal Null-Space Correction for Continual Learning
summary: A one-step curvature probe evaluates an initial direction, whereas continual learners are judged after reaching comparable new-task fit. In an overparameterized linearization, projected gradient descent converges to $Δ_P=PJ^\top(JPJ^\top)^{-1}r$, and its squared-displacement inflation is exactly the reciprocal of the retained fitting capacity $c_P(r)$. More generally, the terminal old-task quadratic ratio factorizes as $1/[c_P(r)G_{\rm end}(P,r)]$, where $G_{\rm end}$ compares curvature along endpoint directions. In the rank-one case, $G_{\rm end}$ equals the one-step probe gain; for multiple outputs, the two gains can differ. The terminal quadratic also separates into a curvature-optimal fitting floor and an algorithm-dependent null-space excess, motivating terminal null-space correction, which preserves linearized new-task outputs on its Jacobian batch. Controlled checks validate the local quadratic and show that projection can greatly reduce matched-norm curvature while barely changing terminal forgetting. Across common-threshold configurations, projection yields the larger signed old-task loss change in 73/99 matched pairs, retained fitting capacity falls with rank, and fixed-rank comparisons separate terminal forgetting even when probe gain is approximately matched. On Permuted MNIST and Split CIFAR-100, terminal correction decreases signed old-task loss in 166/180 method--dataset--seed pairs under the all-seed intention-to-correct analysis; because acceptance and outcome reporting use the same held-out split, this result is descriptive and test-conditioned. Overall, terminal cost depends jointly on retained fitting capacity, endpoint-direction curvature, and the null-space component selected by optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the mechanics of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning through a linearized overparameterized lens. The authors derive that terminal old-task loss depends on three factors: retained fitting capacity, endpoint-direction curvature, and null-space component selected by optimization. They propose terminal null-space correction to preserve linearized new-task outputs and validate the theory empirically on Permuted MNIST and Split CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: The standard evaluation of continual learning methods compares final new-task performance after training on a sequence of tasks. However, this paper identifies a fundamental asymmetry: one-step curvature probes evaluate initial directions, while continual learners are judged after reaching comparable new-task fit. This motivates a deeper theoretical understanding of what determines terminal old-task performance in overparameterized models.
AI.method: The authors analyze projected gradient descent in an overparameterized linearization framework. They derive exact expressions for the squared-displacement inflation as the reciprocal of retained fitting capacity c_P(r). More generally, they show the terminal old-task quadratic ratio factorizes as 1/[c_P(r)G_end(P,r)], where G_end compares curvature along endpoint directions. They propose terminal null-space correction to preserve linearized new-task outputs on the Jacobian batch.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Projection can greatly reduce matched-norm curvature while barely changing terminal forgetting; (2) Across common-threshold configurations, projection yields larger signed old-task loss change in 73/99 matched pairs; (3) Retained fitting capacity falls with rank; (4) Fixed-rank comparisons separate terminal forgetting even when probe gain is approximately matched; (5) On Permuted MNIST and Split CIFAR-100, terminal correction decreases signed old-task loss in 166/180 method--dataset--seed pairs.
AI.conclusion: Terminal cost in continual learning depends jointly on: (1) retained fitting capacity, (2) endpoint-direction curvature, and (3) the null-space component selected by optimization. The authors provide a theoretical framework that unifies one-step probe analysis with full continual learning evaluation, and demonstrate that terminal null-space correction is an effective strategy for reducing forgetting.

title: Agent Policy-Value Audit: Separating Transition Composition from Event Selection in Financial LLM Agents
summary: Financial LLM agents are often evaluated by comparing their end-to-end returns with those of a baseline and testing the paired difference against zero. This measures whether deploying the agent changes realized performance, but it does not isolate event-selection skill. An agent that frequently changes positions from flat to long can earn a positive paired return from an upward-drifting event pool even when it selects events at random. We propose the Agent Policy-Value Audit, which holds fixed the observed count of each ordered action-change type and randomly reassigns them across eligible events. The average payoff from these reassignments is the composition benchmark; the difference between observed deployment value and this benchmark is selection value. In semi-synthetic benchmarks based on real earnings-event returns, a zero-centered paired test falsely attributes passive exposure to selection skill in $11.6\%$ of no-skill replications, while the transition-matched audit reduces this rate to $5.3\%$. Applied retrospectively to 723 earnings events at 44 U.S. consumer-facing firms, the audit decomposes the agent's gross deployment value of $+15.2$ bps/event into a $+25.8$ composition benchmark and a $-10.6$ selection value. The agent does not detectably outperform matched random assignments. Financial-agent evaluations should report deployment value separately from event-selection value.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical evaluation flaw in Financial LLM agents: standard paired return tests conflate event-selection skill with passive exposure to market drift. The authors propose the "Agent Policy-Value Audit" method that fixes the action-change count and randomly reassigns actions across events to separate composition effects from selection skill. The method reduces false positive rates from 11.6% to 5.3% in semi-synthetic tests and reveals that a deployed agent's +15.2 bps/event return is actually composed of +25.8 bps from composition (passive exposure) and -10.6 bps from actual selection skill.
AI.motivation: Standard financial agent evaluation compares end-to-end returns against a baseline, but this approach cannot distinguish whether positive returns come from genuine event-selection skill or simply from passive exposure to upward-drifting event pools. An agent that frequently changes positions from flat to long can earn positive returns even when selecting events at random, leading to false attribution of selection skill.
AI.method: The Agent Policy-Value Audit method works in three steps: (1) Categorize all ordered action-change types (e.g., flat→long, long→short); (2) Hold fixed the observed count of each action-change type and randomly reassign them across eligible events; (3) Calculate the average payoff from these random reassignments as the "composition benchmark." The difference between observed deployment value and the composition benchmark represents "selection value."
AI.result: In semi-synthetic benchmarks using real earnings-event returns, the traditional zero-centered paired test falsely attributes passive exposure to selection skill in 11.6% of no-skill replications, while the transition-matched audit reduces this false positive rate to 5.3%. Retrospective application to 723 earnings events at 44 U.S. consumer-facing firms shows the agent's gross deployment value of +15.2 bps/event decomposes into a +25.8 bps composition benchmark and a -10.6 bps selection value, indicating the agent does not detectably outperform matched random assignments.
AI.conclusion: Financial agent evaluations should report deployment value separately from event-selection value. The standard practice of comparing end-to-end returns conflates composition effects with genuine skill, leading to inflated performance estimates and false positive conclusions about agent capability. The proposed audit method provides a more accurate assessment by isolating true selection skill from passive exposure effects.

title: VolS-GS: Relightable Gaussian Splatting with Volumetric Subsurface Scattering
