AI.method: 1) WISE builds on the witness mechanism but takes expectations over sets of causes/witnesses to remain computationally feasible. 2) JuntaLearner uses gradient-based learning to rank components by causal impact across varying-sized sets. 3) Introduces metrics: faithfulness, necessity, task specificity, and circuit recognition score (CRS) that emphasizes small circuit effects.
AI.result: JuntaLearner achieves higher mean CRS compared to attribution baselines across all metrics on tasks with models of increasing size. The method scales to large models without growing cost (independent of candidate component count) while avoiding first-order approximations.
AI.conclusion: JuntaLearner provides a scalable solution for circuit discovery that accounts for set-level interactions and contextual effects, outperforming attribution baselines on multiple metrics and model sizes.

title: Towards Safer Autonomous Driving in an Open World: A Dual-Process Approach
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, Accepted for publication at the IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC), 2026
summary: Before autonomous driving systems can be deployed on public roads, it is vital that these systems comply with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms. Although neural networks trained on large amounts of driving data perform well in routine driving tasks, these models often struggle in novel situations that are not well-represented in the data. In this work, we propose a novel framework that combines a neural network for intuitive, learning-based planning in routine driving tasks with model predictive control for reasoning-based planning in unfamiliar situations, inspired by Dual Process Theory. A meta-cognitive component is designed to switch between the two, using a knowledge graph to reason about contextual risk based on explicit perceptual information and relevant traffic rules and social norms. Contextual risk is represented through risk fields, guiding both the switching mechanism in the meta-cognitive component and compliance with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms in the reasoning-based planner. The effectiveness of our framework is tested in CARLA for variations of a typical out-of-distribution situations involving (emergency) vehicles running a red light. We show that the novel architecture reduces the number of collisions in the scenarios by 89% and improves compliance with the special right-of-way rules, compared to the NN-only planner.

AI.tldr: A dual-process autonomous driving framework that combines neural networks for routine planning with model predictive control for novel situations, using a meta-cognitive component with knowledge graph-based risk reasoning to switch between planners and ensure compliance with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms.
AI.motivation: Neural networks trained on driving data perform well in routine tasks but struggle in novel out-of-distribution situations. Ensuring autonomous systems comply with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms is critical before public road deployment.
AI.method: Framework combining: (1) Neural network for intuitive learning-based planning in routine tasks; (2) Model Predictive Control for reasoning-based planning in unfamiliar situations; (3) Meta-cognitive component for switching between planners using knowledge graph to reason about contextual risk; (4) Risk fields for representing contextual risk and guiding both switching and compliance.
AI.result: In CARLA simulations with emergency vehicle red-light scenarios, the framework achieved 89% reduction in collisions and improved compliance with special right-of-way rules compared to NN-only planner.
AI.conclusion: The dual-process architecture effectively addresses out-of-distribution driving scenarios by dynamically switching between learning-based and reasoning-based planners, significantly improving safety and rule compliance in critical edge cases.

title: Dynamic Quadtree Tokenization and Transformer for Adaptive Mesh PDE Forecasting
summary: The quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) forces a trade-off between spatial resolution and rollout horizon, particularly for fine-scale PDEs where shocks, reaction fronts, and material interfaces occupy small, evolving regions of the domain. Conventional neural surrogates also lack mechanisms to adapt resolution dynamically. We propose WAMRViT, a ViT that tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using a wavelet-inspired refinement criterion, jointly encodes position and refinement level with 3D rotary positional embeddings, and regrids in cell space during inference for stable long-horizon rollouts. A multi-scale variant retains each leaf at its native source resolution and lets the model learn across resolution levels. Unlike fixed-budget adaptive-tokenization methods, WAMRViT imposes no predetermined token count and supports fully adaptive topology throughout autoregressive rollout. To our knowledge, it is the first machine-learning surrogate to natively tokenize multi-level Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. On uniform-grid benchmarks, uniform-patch WAMRViT improves finest-level region-of-interest VRMSE over a finest-patch uniform ViT while using substantially fewer tokens. The multi-scale variant achieves the lowest first-step full-field RMSE and VRMSE on both benchmarks and improves rollout-averaged full-field and refined-region accuracy at long horizons. With parallelized regridding, its end-to-end rollout cost lies between finest-patch and approximately token-matched coarser-patch ViTs. On a complex AMR combustion problem whose finest features cannot be represented natively by the evaluated uniform-grid baselines, WAMRViT operates directly on adaptive cells and substantially reduces finest-level error at matched transformer capacity. Code: https://github.com/tonyzyl/wamrvit

AI.tldr: WAMRViT is a Vision Transformer designed for solving PDEs that tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using wavelet-inspired refinement criteria, enabling fully adaptive topology throughout autoregressive rollout without predetermined token counts. It is the first ML surrogate to natively tokenize multi-level Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers (ViTs) suffer from quadratic attention cost, forcing trade-offs between spatial resolution and rollout horizon. This is particularly problematic for fine-scale PDEs where important features (shocks, reaction fronts, material interfaces) occupy small, evolving regions. Conventional neural surrogates lack mechanisms to adapt resolution dynamically.
AI.method: WAMRViT uses three key innovations: (1) Tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using a wavelet-inspired refinement criterion; (2) Jointly encodes position and refinement level with 3D rotary positional embeddings; (3) Regrids in cell space during inference for stable long-horizon rollouts. A multi-scale variant retains each leaf at its native source resolution and learns across resolution levels.
AI.result: On uniform-grid benchmarks, uniform-patch WAMRViT improves finest-level region-of-interest VRMSE over finest-patch uniform ViT while using substantially fewer tokens. The multi-scale variant achieves the lowest first-step full-field RMSE and VRMSE on both benchmarks and improves rollout-averaged accuracy at long horizons. With parallelized regridding, end-to-end rollout cost lies between finest-patch and coarser-patch ViTs. On complex AMR combustion problems, WAMRViT substantially reduces finest-level error at matched transformer capacity.
AI.conclusion: WAMRViT successfully enables fully adaptive tokenization for PDE surrogate modeling, achieving better accuracy with fewer tokens than fixed-resolution baselines. It is the first ML method to natively handle multi-level AMR data, opening new possibilities for ML-driven AMR in scientific computing.

title: AuraSE: Low-Hallucination Generative Speech Enhancement via Multimodal Flow Matching and Inference Policy Optimization
summary: Generative speech enhancement models can produce cleaner and more natural-sounding speech than conventional discriminative approaches, but may hallucinate by changing speech content or speaker identity, even with transcript conditioning. We present AuraSE, a flow-matching framework that addresses hallucination through complementary modality and inference designs. First, a double-stream-to-single-stream multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) allows transcript and acoustic representations to interact while preserving a dedicated pathway for the degraded input. Second, we find that the best decoder configuration, governed by guidance scale, sampling temperature, and step count, varies substantially across utterances. This observation motivates Inference Policy Optimization (IPO), an online, on-policy preference optimization method. IPO generates multiple candidates from the current model under different inference configurations, ranks them with a multi-objective reward, and learns from their relative preferences. AuraSE-IPO ranks first on 11 of 12 metrics across the synthetic test sets and obtains the highest DNSMOS and blind-listening scores among the evaluated systems on the real DNS blind test set. At deployment, it uses a fixed $10$-step ODE decoder without classifier-free guidance (CFG) or per-utterance configuration search.

AI.tldr: AuraSE is a flow-matching speech enhancement framework that addresses hallucination issues in generative models through a double-stream-to-single-stream multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) and an online preference optimization method called Inference Policy Optimization (IPO). The system achieves state-of-the-art results across 11 of 12 metrics while using a fixed 10-step decoder at deployment.
AI.motivation: Generative speech enhancement models can produce cleaner and more natural-sounding speech than conventional discriminative approaches, but they suffer from hallucination - changing speech content or speaker identity - even with transcript conditioning. Additionally, the optimal decoder configuration (guidance scale, sampling temperature, step count) varies substantially across different utterances, making deployment challenging.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary approaches: (1) A double-stream-to-single-stream multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) that allows transcript and acoustic representations to interact while preserving a dedicated pathway for the degraded input. (2) Inference Policy Optimization (IPO), an online on-policy preference optimization method that generates multiple candidates from the current model under different inference configurations, ranks them with a multi-objective reward, and learns from their relative preferences.
AI.result: AuraSE-IPO ranks first on 11 of 12 metrics across synthetic test sets and obtains the highest DNSMOS and blind-listening scores among evaluated systems on the real DNS blind test set. At deployment, it uses a fixed 10-step ODE decoder without classifier-free guidance (CFG) or per-utterance configuration search.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AuraSE framework successfully addresses hallucination in generative speech enhancement through novel architecture design (MMDiT) and inference optimization (IPO). The combination of multimodal representation learning and online preference optimization achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while maintaining practical deployment efficiency with a fixed decoder configuration.

title: Understanding the Hierarchical Structure and Functional Landscape of the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem
summary: AI agents increasingly rely on tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to complete user tasks. Hundreds of thousands of MCP servers are listed across marketplaces, yet they are organized only by coarse, marketplace-specific server categories. This makes it difficult for agents and users to identify tools for a given operation, find functional alternatives, and assess how those alternatives differ. We present MCPacific, the largest tool-level, cross-marketplace map of the MCP ecosystem. MCPacific collects 368,754 MCP server listings corresponding to 124,267 unique servers across 17 marketplaces, statically extracts 1,328,233 tool specifications from these servers in seven languages, and organizes them into a hierarchical functional taxonomy of 58,915 capabilities. We construct the taxonomy through an iterative LLM-driven design-test-refine process and map the full corpus to it using calibrated embedding routing. Our study reveals that MCP extends well beyond developer tooling, with 85% of tools serving other domains. Functional alternatives are widespread but unevenly distributed: 98.5% of tools have at least one alternative, yet nearly a quarter of capabilities are supported by only one tool. Functionally comparable tools also differ in security alerts, code complexity, and project maintenance, with complexity differing by more than 2.5x in 41% of comparable tool pairs. Finally, presenting candidate tools through the taxonomy rather than a flat list improves task completion rate across all four evaluated models, with gains of up to 12 percentage points in Pass@0.75 for crowded candidate sets.

AI.tldr: MCPacific is the largest cross-marketplace map of the MCP (Model Context Protocol) ecosystem, collecting 368,754 server listings across 17 marketplaces, extracting 1,328,233 tool specifications, and organizing them into a hierarchical taxonomy of 58,915 capabilities. The study reveals that 85% of MCP tools serve non-developer domains, 98.5% of tools have functional alternatives, and using the taxonomy improves task completion rates by up to 12 percentage points.
AI.motivation: The MCP ecosystem lacks fine-grained tool organization - existing marketplaces only use coarse categories, making it difficult for AI agents and users to identify appropriate tools for specific operations, find functional alternatives, and assess differences between alternatives.
AI.method: MCPacific collects MCP server listings from 17 marketplaces, statically extracts tool specifications in seven programming languages, and constructs a hierarchical functional taxonomy through an iterative LLM-driven design-test-refine process. The full corpus is mapped to this taxonomy using calibrated embedding routing. The researchers then evaluate tool alternatives across security, code complexity, and maintenance dimensions, and test whether taxonomy-based tool presentation improves task completion rates across four evaluated models.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) 85% of MCP tools serve non-developer domains; (2) 98.5% of tools have at least one functional alternative, but nearly a quarter of capabilities are supported by only one tool; (3) Functionally comparable tools differ significantly - 41% of comparable tool pairs show more than 2.5x difference in complexity; (4) Presenting candidate tools through the taxonomy rather than flat lists improves task completion rates across all four models, with gains of up to 12 percentage points in Pass@0.75 for crowded candidate sets.
AI.conclusion: MCPacific provides the first comprehensive, tool-level, cross-marketplace map of the MCP ecosystem. The hierarchical taxonomy enables better tool discovery and selection for AI agents, significantly improving task completion rates. The study highlights the importance of fine-grained tool organization and reveals that while functional alternatives are widespread, they often differ substantially in security, complexity, and maintenance characteristics.

title: LD-EnFF: Latent-Dynamics Ensemble Flow Filtering for Data Assimilation with Sparse Observations
summary: Data assimilation combines model forecasts with noisy, incomplete observations to estimate the evolving state of a dynamical system. Existing methods face two compounding challenges: high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics make repeated forward simulation computationally expensive, while sparse observations provide limited direct information about the full state. To address these challenges, we propose the Latent-Dynamics Ensemble Flow Filter (LD-EnFF), a sequential Bayesian filtering framework that performs both forecast propagation and filtering updates in a compact latent space. LD-EnFF combines a latent dynamics surrogate for ensemble propagation with a variational autoencoder (VAE)-based observation model that evaluates a state-dependent observation likelihood in latent space. At each assimilation step, an ensemble filtering update based on flow matching uses the forecast ensemble and this likelihood to generate posterior samples, jointly updating latent states and uncertain parameters. This design avoids repeated full-state simulation during forecasting and full-field reconstruction during likelihood evaluation. LD-EnFF substantially outperforms a broad range of data assimilation algorithms on benchmarks spanning Kolmogorov flow, tsunami propagation, and atmospheric modeling, all featuring complex dynamics and sparse, noisy observations.

AI.tldr: LD-EnFF is a sequential Bayesian filtering framework that performs forecast propagation and filtering updates in a compact latent space, combining a latent dynamics surrogate with a VAE-based observation model and flow matching-based ensemble filtering.
AI.motivation: Data assimilation faces two key challenges: (1) high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics make repeated forward simulation computationally expensive, and (2) sparse observations provide limited direct information about the full state.
AI.method: LD-EnFF combines: (1) a latent dynamics surrogate for ensemble propagation, (2) a VAE-based observation model that evaluates state-dependent observation likelihood in latent space, and (3) an ensemble filtering update based on flow matching to jointly update latent states and uncertain parameters.
AI.result: LD-EnFF substantially outperforms a broad range of data assimilation algorithms on benchmarks spanning Kolmogorov flow, tsunami propagation, and atmospheric modeling—all featuring complex dynamics and sparse, noisy observations.
AI.conclusion: The latent space approach avoids repeated full-state simulation during forecasting and full-field reconstruction during likelihood evaluation, enabling efficient data assimilation for complex high-dimensional systems.

title: The Independence Prior of SAEs Fragments Visual Concepts
summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose model activations into sparse combinations of interpretable dictionary atoms. Although SAEs are grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), their objective smuggles in an additional prior: concepts across patches are treated as independent, an assumption clearly violated by natural images and by the activations they induce. We therefore specialize LRH to vision through the Markov-Field Linear Representation Hypothesis (MFLRH), which adds the missing spatial dependencies to the LRH assumptions. We thus propose Spatial-SAE as an amortized MAP estimator under the MFLRH. Spatial-SAE consistently outperforms standard SAEs in concept recovery and interpretability. Across four variants, it achieves a 96% average win rate on synthetic concept recovery and improves interpretability on DINOv2 activations, at a reconstruction cost concentrated in high spatial frequencies.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a limitation in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) - their assumption of independent concepts across patches, which contradicts natural images. It proposes Spatial-SAE, an amortized MAP estimator based on the Markov-Field Linear Representation Hypothesis (MFLRH) that incorporates spatial dependencies.
AI.motivation: Standard SAEs are based on the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) but assume concepts across patches are independent - an assumption violated by natural images and their activations. This missing spatial prior limits interpretability and concept recovery.
AI.method: The paper specializes LRH to vision through the Markov-Field Linear Representation Hypothesis (MFLRH), which adds spatial dependencies. Spatial-SAE is then proposed as an amortized MAP estimator under this new framework.
AI.result: Spatial-SAE consistently outperforms standard SAEs across four variants: achieving 96% average win rate on synthetic concept recovery and improving interpretability on DINOv2 activations, with reconstruction cost concentrated in high spatial frequencies.
AI.conclusion: By incorporating spatial dependencies through MFLRH, Spatial-SAE significantly improves concept recovery and interpretability over standard SAEs, demonstrating the importance of modeling spatial relationships in vision-based representation learning.

title: ASD-FEAT: A Multi-Modal Infant Video-Derived Dataset for Early ASD Risk Prediction
summary: Accurate early screening for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a precursor to timely intervention, which is critical for improving cognitive and behavioral outcomes. We present ASD-FEAT (ASD - Feature Extraction And Tracking), a multimodal dataset derived from video recordings of infant-adult interaction sessions. The key contribution of ASD-FEAT is the combination of longitudinal coverage from infancy through 36 months, repeated interaction sessions, clinically validated developmental outcomes, expert frame-level behavioral annotations, and privacy-conscious multimodal feature representations. To the best of our knowledge, existing ASD behavioral datasets do not jointly provide these characteristics at comparable scale. To demonstrate the utility of ASD-FEAT, we use it to evaluate a computer-vision-based end-to-end pipeline relying on machine learning techniques to automatically identify ASD risk. ASD-FEAT integrates both expert-defined and deep-learned features, including face and eye landmarks, facial action units, gaze direction, head position, mel-spectrogram audio representations, and optical flow, to identify behavioral markers of social interaction. Our automated pipeline achieves an ASD classification accuracy of 76.2% and an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) of 0.82, compared to classifiers trained on manually labeled behaviors, which yielded 81.3% accuracy and an AUROC of 0.88. We further introduce a within-visit partner contrast: a per-visit signal contrasting examiner-directed and parent-directed social behavior which, when added to the classifier, lifts the fully automated Look Face + Smile and Look Face + Vocal configurations to Matthews correlations of 0.49 and 0.45 respectively, exceeding the human-coded single-partner baseline of 0.42.

AI.tldr: ASD-FEAT is a novel multimodal dataset for early Autism Spectrum Disorder screening derived from video recordings of infant-adult interactions, combining longitudinal coverage (birth to 36 months), repeated sessions, clinical validation, and privacy-conscious features. The automated pipeline achieves 76.2% accuracy and 0.82 AUROC, while a new "within-visit partner contrast" metric improves performance beyond human-coded baselines.
AI.motivation: Early screening for ASD is critical for timely intervention and improved cognitive/behavioral outcomes. Existing datasets lack the combination of longitudinal coverage, repeated interaction sessions, clinical validation, expert annotations, and privacy-conscious multimodal features at scale. This limits the development and evaluation of automated screening tools.
AI.method: The study presents ASD-FEAT dataset and evaluates a computer-vision-based end-to-end pipeline using machine learning. Features integrated include: face and eye landmarks, facial action units, gaze direction, head position, mel-spectrogram audio representations, and optical flow. A novel "within-visit partner contrast" metric was introduced comparing examiner-directed vs parent-directed social behavior.
AI.result: Automated pipeline achieved 76.2% ASD classification accuracy with AUROC of 0.82. Classifiers trained on manually labeled behaviors achieved 81.3% accuracy and 0.88 AUROC. The within-visit partner contrast added to Look Face + Smile and Look Face + Vocal configurations achieved Matthews correlations of 0.49 and 0.45 respectively, exceeding the human-coded single-partner baseline of 0.42.
AI.conclusion: ASD-FEAT addresses a significant gap in ASD behavioral datasets by providing comprehensive longitudinal, multimodal data with clinical validation. The automated pipeline demonstrates promising ASD risk identification capabilities (76.2% accuracy, 0.82 AUROC), approaching human-coded performance (81.3% accuracy, 0.88 AUROC). The novel within-visit partner contrast metric successfully captures differential social behavior patterns and improves automated classification performance beyond human-coded baselines.

title: Revisiting Label-Free Speaker Embedding Enhancement with vMF Profile Likelihood
summary: Embedding enhancement improves speaker verification under acoustic mismatch without modifying a frozen backbone. Recent work has established a practical label-free setting for this task, but often adopts increasingly structured formulations. Here, the clean target is directly observed during training, making enhancement a matching problem on the unit hypersphere. We model the clean target with a von Mises--Fisher (vMF) likelihood and profile out a sample-wise concentration parameter, yielding a simple closed-form objective with adaptive weighting. Across VoxCeleb1, VoxSRC23, CN-Celeb, VOiCES, and VC-Mix, the proposed method largely preserves the baseline and gives clearer gains on challenging mismatch sets. It also remains stable under a broad single-view recipe, where a recent diffusion baseline becomes less reliable in controlled comparisons. These results suggest that effective label-free embedding enhancement in this setting does not require a highly structured formulation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a simple label-free embedding enhancement method for speaker verification under acoustic mismatch. It uses a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) likelihood model with sample-wise concentration parameter profiling, yielding a closed-form objective with adaptive weighting. The method preserves baseline performance while gaining improvements on challenging mismatch sets, and remains stable under a broad single-view recipe.
AI.motivation: Current label-free embedding enhancement methods for speaker verification under acoustic mismatch often adopt increasingly structured formulations. The authors seek a simpler approach that doesn't require highly structured formulations while still effectively handling acoustic mismatch when the clean target is directly observed during training.
AI.method: The method models the clean target with a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) likelihood and profiles out a sample-wise concentration parameter, yielding a simple closed-form objective with adaptive weighting. The approach treats enhancement as a matching problem on the unit hypersphere without modifying the frozen backbone.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets (VoxCeleb1, VoxSRC23, CN-Celeb, VOiCES, and VC-Mix), the proposed method largely preserves the baseline performance and gives clearer gains on challenging mismatch sets. It also remains stable under a broad single-view recipe, where a recent diffusion baseline becomes less reliable in controlled comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Effective label-free embedding enhancement in speaker verification does not require a highly structured formulation. The simple vMF-based approach achieves competitive or better results than more complex methods while offering improved stability and simplicity.

title: Adaptive Code Revision Attacks on AI Pull Request Reviewers
summary:
Pull-request review protects software before new code reaches users, helping prevent vulnerabilities that could expose users to attacks. AI agents increasingly perform these reviews and explain which problems need fixing. However, for an attacker submitting vulnerable code, this feedback also reveals what changes may secure approval. Existing PR attacks seek such approval through persuasive text and comments while keeping executable code fixed. This leaves unclear whether an attacker can use the feedback to repair the reported problem while preserving a vulnerability in the revised code. We therefore conduct an empirical study of this threat using AFCRA (Adaptive Feedback-guided Code Revision Attack). To distinguish successful attacks from genuine repairs, we construct AFCRA-Bench from 159 disclosed vulnerabilities, with executable exploits to verify vulnerabilities in code.
  Across five-round interactions with Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.5 reviewers, AFCRA reaches success rates 2.5x and 12.5x those of the strongest evaluated text- or comment-based attack. Case studies of these successes show how reviewers accept repairs of reported problems while overlooking surviving vulnerabilities. These findings establish feedback-guided code revision as a threat to automated PR review. To address this threat, we derive actionable implications for researchers, AI providers, PR reviewers, and PR authors on securing AI-assisted development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AFCRA (Adaptive Feedback-guided Code Revision Attack), a novel threat where attackers use AI code review feedback to fix reported vulnerabilities while preserving other vulnerabilities. The study uses AFCRA-Bench with 159 disclosed vulnerabilities and achieves 2.5x-12.5x higher success rates than previous text/comment-based attacks against AI reviewers like Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.5.
AI.motivation: Pull-request reviews help prevent vulnerabilities, but AI agents providing feedback inadvertently reveal what needs fixing. This creates a new attack vector: attackers can exploit the feedback to make superficial repairs that satisfy reviewers while keeping malicious code intact. Prior attacks only used persuasive text/comments without modifying executable code, leaving unclear whether attackers could use feedback to repair reported issues while preserving vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The researchers conducted an empirical study using AFCRA with AFCRA-Bench (159 disclosed vulnerabilities with executable exploits to verify vulnerabilities). They tested across five-round interactions with two AI reviewers: Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.5. They compared against text-based and comment-based attack baselines.
AI.result: AFCRA achieved success rates 2.5x higher than the strongest text-based attack and 12.5x higher than the strongest comment-based attack when evaluated against Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.5 reviewers. Case studies demonstrated how reviewers accepted repairs of reported problems while overlooking surviving vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-guided code revision represents a concrete threat to automated PR review systems. The findings provide actionable implications for researchers (developing better detection), AI providers (improving review robustness), PR reviewers (implementing holistic security checks), and PR authors (understanding AI-assisted development risks).

title: Protecting Sensitive Data in Image Synthesis via PAC-Private Adaptation for Diffusion Models
summary: Synthetic data are increasingly used as an alternative to sharing sensitive records. However, synthetic data generation does not guarantee privacy, as diffusion models trained or adapted on sensitive data remain susceptible to reconstruction attacks. Moreover, while approaches that use differential privacy (DP), such as DP-SGD, achieve provably private diffusion model training, the repeated gradient clipping and noise injection they require result in significant utility loss. An important limitation of DP-based privacy is that, although it has a provable relationship to reconstruction privacy (RP), that relationship is indirect. RP is defined in terms of limiting how much an adversary's posterior distribution over sensitive data differs from the prior, whereas DP provides guarantees by bounding the sensitivity of outputs to changes in individual records. This indirection is an important source of the utility loss. To address this, we propose a PAC-private diffusion model adaptation to achieve reconstruction privacy. Since PAC-privacy is defined directly with respect to posterior advantage over the prior, it directly implicates RP. To obtain scalable PAC privatization in high dimensions, we first learn a compact data-dependent diffusion model component using LoRA or Textual Inversion, and then calibrate anisotropic Gaussian noise from the covariance of repeated mechanism outputs. Unlike DP-SGD, our method perturbs the learned component only once after optimization, thereby avoiding privacy composition across gradient updates. We evaluate the framework on few-shot concept personalization and full-dataset image synthesis, and show that the proposed approach better preserves subject identity, generation quality, and downstream classification accuracy than DP while achieving the same reconstruction privacy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PAC-private diffusion model adaptation as an alternative to differential privacy (DP) for achieving reconstruction privacy in synthetic data generation. The method uses LoRA/Textual Inversion to learn compact data-dependent components, then calibrates anisotropic Gaussian noise once after optimization, avoiding privacy composition across gradient updates.
AI.motivation: Address the utility-privacy tradeoff in synthetic data generation. DP-based approaches like DP-SGD suffer from significant utility loss due to repeated gradient clipping and noise injection. Additionally, the indirect relationship between DP and reconstruction privacy (RP) is an important source of utility loss, as DP bounds output sensitivity rather than directly targeting posterior advantage over the prior.
AI.method: 1) Learn compact data-dependent diffusion model components using LoRA or Textual Inversion; 2) Calibrate anisotropic Gaussian noise from the covariance of repeated mechanism outputs; 3) Perturb the learned component only once after optimization to avoid privacy composition across gradient updates.
AI.result: The proposed approach better preserves subject identity, generation quality, and downstream classification accuracy compared to DP, while achieving the same reconstruction privacy.
AI.conclusion: PAC-privacy provides a more direct path to reconstruction privacy than DP, resulting in better utility preservation. The single-round noise injection after optimization avoids the累积 privacy loss from multiple gradient updates, making it more suitable for high-dimensional synthetic data generation tasks.

title: CUAWright: A Minimal Unified Interface for Digital Agents
summary: The prevailing approach to computer-use agents couples a model with a domain-specific harness: a browser or desktop environment equipped with human engineered tools that are fixed before task execution. As models' coding capabilities improve, the GUI native and static harness prevents them from direct programmatic operation on system state, as well as flexible construction of tools. To this end, we introduce CUAWright, a minimal terminal harness of roughly 3K lines of code that uses bash commands as its sole action interface, and a file system as its evolvable space for dynamically creating tools and managing the context. We conduct comprehensive experiments across a wide range of digital tasks, and demonstrate that by giving the agent a minimal, programmable interface, it achieves substantially stronger results compared to their GUI or hybrid CLI interface across a wide range of tasks. On OSWorld 2.0, CUAWright delivers a 33.2% relative improvement in partial reward while reducing estimated cost by 37.5% compared with the published GPT-5.5 baseline. On Online-Mind2Web and the long horizon Odysseys benchmark, CUAWright substantially outperforms GUI native harness by 4.7% and 44.0% in success rate, respectively. Furthermore, we found the gains extend to CAD applications that require accurate visual understanding and CLI interaction: on CADGenBench and BenchCAD, our unified harness yields 8.1%-41.6% relative improvements over other CLI based harnesses with GPT-5.5. Together, these results suggest digital environments are far more programmable than their GUI interfaces imply, and a minimal terminal-focused harness is the key for better performance and efficiency.

AI.tldr: CUAWright is a minimal terminal harness (~3K LOC) that uses bash commands as the sole action interface, allowing agents to dynamically create tools via the file system. It outperforms GUI-based and hybrid CLI harnesses across multiple benchmarks (OSWorld 2.0, Online-Mind2Web, Odysseys, CADGenBench, BenchCAD) with 4.7%-44.0% improvements in success rate and 37.5% cost reduction.
AI.motivation: Current computer-use agents rely on GUI-based harnesses with fixed, human-engineered tools that prevent models from direct programmatic operation on system state and flexible tool construction. As models' coding capabilities improve, the static GUI harness becomes a limitation.
AI.method: CUAWright uses bash commands as the sole action interface and leverages the file system as an evolvable space for dynamically creating tools and managing context. This minimal terminal harness (~3K lines of code) provides a programmable interface instead of GUI-based tools.
AI.result:
- OSWorld 2.0: 33.2% relative improvement in partial reward, 37.5% cost reduction vs GPT-5.5 baseline
- Online-Mind2Web: 4.7% improvement in success rate over GUI native harness
- Odysseys (long horizon): 44.0% improvement in success rate over GUI native harness
- CADGenBench and BenchCAD: 8.1%-41.6% relative improvements over other CLI harnesses with GPT-5.5
AI.conclusion: Digital environments are far more programmable than their GUI interfaces imply. A minimal terminal-focused harness is the key for better performance and efficiency in computer-use agents.

title: A Theory of Shape Reconstruction from Heat Conduction and Shading
summary: Shape from shading using a single image of a Lam- bertian surface is inherently ambiguous. When the light source direction is known, the surface normal estimation has a cone- ambiguity, which worsens when the source is unknown. Recently, shape from heat conduction has emerged as an approach that leverages heat transport equations to estimate the Shape Lapla- cian operator, an intrinsic measure of shape. However, deriving surface normals from the Laplacian operator encounters a local binary convex/concave ambiguity. Our contribution introduces a novel theory to resolve these local shape ambiguities (excluding a few degeneracies) without relying on priors like smoothness, by combining the cues from shading and heat conduction. Our method ensures the mathematical constraints of both shading and the Laplacian are satisfied simultaneously, even with an unknown light source. We validate our theory through simulations of complex shapes and analyze its performance in the presence of noise, as well as on a noisy single thermal video of real-world objects with complex shapes and material properties, including varying albedo.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel theory combining shading and heat conduction cues to resolve local shape ambiguities (cone ambiguity and convex/concave ambiguity) in surface normal estimation from a single image, without requiring priors like smoothness, and works even with unknown light source direction.
AI.motivation: Shape from shading using a single image of a Lambertian surface is inherently ambiguous. With known light source, there's a cone-ambiguity; with unknown light source, the ambiguity worsens. Shape from heat conduction can estimate the Shape Laplacian operator but encounters local binary convex/concave ambiguity. Existing methods rely on priors like smoothness, which this work avoids.
AI.method: The proposed method combines cues from shading and heat conduction to resolve local shape ambiguities. It ensures mathematical constraints of both shading and the Laplacian are satisfied simultaneously, even with an unknown light source. Validation is done through simulations of complex shapes, noise analysis, and testing on a noisy single thermal video of real-world objects with complex shapes and material properties including varying albedo.
AI.result: The theory successfully resolves local shape ambiguities (excluding a few degeneracies) without relying on priors like smoothness, while satisfying both shading and Laplacian constraints simultaneously with unknown light source.
AI.conclusion: The combination of shading and heat conduction cues provides a promising approach to resolve shape ambiguities in computer vision, validated on both simulated complex shapes and real-world thermal video data with varying material properties.

title: Paradee: Distilling Kokoro-82M into an 8M-Parameter Single-Voice Text-to-Speech Model
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Code: https://github.com/sahilmahendrakar/paradee. Model and audio samples: https://huggingface.co/sahilmahendrakar/Paradee-8M-v1.0
summary: We distill Kokoro-82M, a widely used open text-to-speech model with 54 voices, into Paradee, an 8.07M-parameter model that speaks one of them. Paradee keeps Kokoro's architecture with much narrower layers, and each of its two halves is trained separately against the frozen teacher. It has 10x fewer parameters and needs 15x less compute. We first synthesize a corpus with the teacher and keep its durations, pitch, energy and phoneme features. We then train a small text side to predict these values, and a small decoder to turn the teacher's saved values into the teacher's audio, first with spectral losses and then adversarially. Finally, we connect the two halves and quantize the weights to int8. It needs no alignment learning and no joint training, and it runs on one laptop. Stored in int8, Paradee is 8.5 MB, runs 25x faster than real time on one CPU thread, and scores 4.41 on UTMOS against the teacher's 4.52. The student initially kept a slight buzz, which we trace to the phase of voiced speech between 2 and 8 kHz. A phase-locking filter applied after synthesis removes most of it, with no training and no extra parameters. Code, model files and audio samples are at https://github.com/sahilmahendrakar/paradee

AI.tldr: The paper presents Paradee, a distilled 8.07M-parameter text-to-speech model derived from the 82M-parameter Kokoro-82M teacher model. The distillation process uses separate training for text encoder and decoder halves, with spectral and adversarial losses, followed by int8 quantization. The resulting model achieves 4.41 UTMOS (vs 4.52 teacher), runs 25x faster than real-time on a single CPU thread, and requires no alignment learning or joint training.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create a compact, efficient text-to-speech model that can run on a laptop while maintaining acceptable quality compared to the large teacher model. The goal is to reduce model size by 10x and compute requirements by 15x while preserving most of the voice quality.
AI.method: The method involves: 1) Synthesizing a corpus using the frozen teacher model and preserving durations, pitch, energy, and phoneme features; 2) Training a small text encoder to predict these acoustic features; 3) Training a small decoder to convert teacher's saved values to audio using spectral and adversarial losses; 4) Connecting both halves and quantizing weights to int8; 5) Applying a post-synthesis phase-locking filter to remove buzz artifacts in the 2-8 kHz frequency range.
AI.result: Paradee achieves 4.41 UTMOS score against the teacher's 4.52, runs 25x faster than real-time on a single CPU thread, and is only 8.5 MB when stored in int8 format. The model has 10x fewer parameters (8.07M vs 82M) and requires 15x less compute. The phase-locking filter effectively removes most of the buzz artifact without additional parameters or training.
AI.conclusion: The authors successfully distilled a large TTS model into a compact version that maintains high quality (UTMOS 4.41 vs 4.52) while being extremely efficient (25x faster than real-time on CPU). The key innovations include separate training of encoder/decoder halves, using teacher's acoustic features as training targets, and a simple post-processing filter for artifact removal. The approach requires no alignment learning or joint training, making it practical for deployment on consumer hardware.

title: UndoBench: Separating Task Competence from Recovery Capability in Tool-Using AI Agents
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures. Code and benchmark available at https://github.com/tradertanmay/undobench
summary: Tool-using AI agents are increasingly deployed across enterprise software systems, yet widely used benchmarks primarily evaluate nominal task completion, conflating baseline planning competence with operational fault recovery. We introduce UndoBench, a benchmark spanning 36 base workflows and 36 fault scenarios across 8 enterprise domains, decoupling task competence from recovery capability via counterfactual paired trials under identical seeds alongside wire-level effect-history and environment-state oracles. On 12 held-out TEST workflows across two open-weight models, two frameworks, and three recovery paradigms (5,760 executions / 2,880 paired trials) in the frozen lost-acknowledgment study, nominal competence reached 83.54% while conditional recovery success rate (CRSR) fell to 46.72%, with naive retry producing duplicate external effects in 53.33% of trials. Extensions to commercial API models reproduced this competence-recovery separation. Evaluations across complementary execution boundaries show that recovery is phase-dependent: before mutation, methods perform similarly without duplicate effects among capable trials; during partial mutation, naive retry, per-call idempotency, and zero-privilege journaling collapse on the evaluated composite workflows; after commit but before acknowledgment, verification and server-side idempotency substantially improve safety. These findings demonstrate that evaluating nominal completion alone masks critical, phase-dependent recovery vulnerabilities in autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces UndoBench, a benchmark that separates task completion evaluation from fault recovery capability in AI agents. The key finding is a significant gap between nominal task success (83.54%) and actual recovery success (46.72%), with recovery effectiveness being highly dependent on the execution phase.
AI.motivation: Current enterprise AI benchmarks conflate baseline planning competence with operational fault recovery capabilities. This masks critical vulnerabilities in autonomous agents when failures occur during task execution.
AI.method: UndoBench uses 36 base workflows and 36 fault scenarios across 8 enterprise domains with counterfactual paired trials under identical seeds, wire-level effect-history, and environment-state oracles. Testing involved 5,760 executions across 12 held-out workflows, 2 open-weight models, 2 frameworks, and 3 recovery paradigms (naive retry, per-call idempotency, zero-privilege journaling, verification, server-side idempotency).
AI.result: Nominal competence reached 83.54% while conditional recovery success rate (CRSR) dropped to 46.72%. Naive retry produced duplicate external effects in 53.33% of trials. Recovery effectiveness is phase-dependent: before mutation all methods perform similarly; during partial mutation all methods fail; after commit but before acknowledgment, verification and server-side idempotency substantially improve safety.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating nominal completion alone masks critical, phase-dependent recovery vulnerabilities in autonomous agents. The competence-recovery separation is a fundamental issue that commercial API models also exhibit, suggesting a need for benchmarks that explicitly evaluate fault recovery capabilities.

authors: A. M. C. M. van Gils
title: On architectural choices for interpretability and thermodynamic consistency in Physically Recurrent Neural Networks in the low-data regime
summary: In this paper, we unravel the effect of different decoder architectures on the interpretability of the latent space of the Physically Recurrent Neural Network. Particular emphasis is given to a new weight normalization constraint, which acts as a regularization technique and enables robust training in the low-data regime. A brief visual exploration illustrates how these changes impact the latent space and how the fictitious stress can align with the true state of the RVE without explicit training. Reaping the benefits of a meaningful latent space, a case study illustrates how information from the microscopic level can be retrieved and incorporated into a multi-task approach that does not require extra parameters or larger training sets. Another key contribution shows that a specific architectural choice can naturally lead to a thermodynamically consistent formulation. By enforcing an adjoint encoder-decoder structure with positive scalar contributions, this modification ensures energy consistency across scales and non-negative dissipation, leading to even lower training requirements. This alternative completes the study on interpretability, inductive bias, and thermodynamic consistency, and demonstrates that data efficiency can be improved with careful architectural choices rooted in the underlying physics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates decoder architectures in Physically Recurrent Neural Networks (PhysRNN), introducing a weight normalization constraint for robust training in low-data regimes. The study demonstrates how specific architectural choices can lead to interpretable latent spaces that align with physical states, enable multi-task learning without extra parameters, and ensure thermodynamic consistency through an adjoint encoder-decoder structure with positive scalar contributions.
AI.motivation: Improve interpretability of latent space in PhysRNN, enable robust training with limited data, and ensure thermodynamic consistency across scales through architectural design rather than explicit constraints.
AI.method: Novel weight normalization constraint as regularization technique; adjoint encoder-decoder structure with positive scalar contributions to enforce energy consistency and non-negative dissipation.
AI.result: Weight normalization constraint enables robust training in low-data regime; latent space becomes interpretable with stress aligning to true RVE state; microscopic information can be retrieved for multi-task learning without extra parameters; thermodynamic consistency achieved with energy consistency across scales and non-negative dissipation, leading to lower training requirements.
AI.conclusion: Data efficiency in physics-informed neural networks can be significantly improved through careful architectural choices rooted in underlying physics, specifically by enforcing thermodynamic consistency via adjoint encoder-decoder structures with positive scalar contributions.

title: InvestigationWorlds: An Agentic Environment for Legal Investigation
summary: We introduce InvestigationWorlds, an agentic environment for legal investigation. We build on an underused artifact of U.S. civil litigation: the summary judgment motion. This motion relies upon a record composed of real evidence exhibits, and results in a court-adopted hypothesis that is treated as ground truth for the purposes of deciding the motion. Each environment is built from a real U.S. Federal Court case retrieved from Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) and augmented by an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes role-tagged documents around the original record. The resulting corpus admits multiple coherent factual readings, only one of which matches the court-adopted hypothesis. Evaluating on 100 cases, we find agents often commit to incorrect hypotheses despite retrieving relevant evidence, struggling to distinguish the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative hypotheses.

AI.tldr: InvestigationWorlds is a novel agentic environment for evaluating legal investigation AI, built from real PACER cases with attorney-validated document synthesis. On 100 cases, agents struggle to identify the correct court-adopted hypothesis among multiple plausible alternatives, even when retrieving relevant evidence.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a critical gap in legal AI research: the lack of realistic, complex environments for evaluating AI agents on legal investigation tasks. The authors identify the summary judgment motion in U.S. civil litigation as an underused but valuable artifact—it relies on real evidence exhibits and produces a court-adopted hypothesis treated as ground truth. This creates a unique evaluation benchmark where agents must distinguish the correct (court-adopted) hypothesis from multiple plausible alternative interpretations.
AI.method: The authors built InvestigationWorlds by: (1) retrieving real U.S. Federal Court cases from PACER, (2) augmenting them via an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes role-tagged documents around the original court record. This produces environments with multiple coherent factual readings, only one matching the court-adopted hypothesis. Evaluation was conducted on 100 cases.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals a significant finding: AI agents often commit to incorrect hypotheses even when they retrieve relevant evidence. The core challenge lies not in evidence retrieval but in distinguishing the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative hypotheses—suggesting limitations in reasoning about competing factual narratives.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that current AI agents can retrieve relevant evidence but fail at the higher-order task of distinguishing correct from incorrect factual interpretations in complex legal scenarios. This highlights a key limitation in legal reasoning AI and provides a valuable benchmark for future research on adversarial legal reasoning and hypothesis discrimination.

title: Evaluating Zone-Guided Front Extraction for Glacier Calving-Front Delineation in SAR Imagery
comment: Accepted in ICMLA 2026 as short paper. 4 pages, 1 figure
summary: Automatic calving-front delineation from synthetic aperture radar imagery is challenging because the front is a thin and often ambiguous boundary between glacier ice, ocean, and surrounding rock or terrain. The CAlving Fronts and where to Find thEm (CaFFe) dataset provides both binary calving-front masks and broader semantic zone masks, making it possible to study whether zone-level supervision can support front recovery. In this paper, we compare direct front prediction with zone-guided front extraction using U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and SegFormer-B0 under the same bounding-box-cropped CaFFe setting. In the direct setting, models predict the binary calving-front mask. In the zone-guided setting, the model first predicts four semantic zone classes, and the front is then extracted from the predicted glacier-ocean boundary. We evaluate both zone-level and front-level performance, include a ground-truth-zone boundary check, and examine lightweight test-time adaptation on sensor-specific and glacier-specific subsets. The results show that zone labels contain useful front-boundary information: extracting the front from ground-truth zones gives the lowest mean distance error. However, fronts extracted from model-predicted zones remain weak, even when zone segmentation scores are moderate. Test-time adaptation also does not consistently improve zone-guided front recovery. These results indicate that zone segmentation performance should not be treated as a substitute for front-level evaluation and that effective use of zone labels may require boundary-aware training, label fusion, or explicit front supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether zone-level supervision can improve calving front delineation from SAR imagery. While extracting fronts from ground-truth zones achieves the lowest error, fronts derived from model-predicted zones remain weak, and test-time adaptation does not consistently help. The study concludes that zone segmentation performance cannot substitute front-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: Automatic calving-front delineation from SAR imagery is challenging due to the thin, ambiguous nature of the front boundary. The CaFFe dataset provides both binary front masks and semantic zone masks, enabling investigation of whether zone-guided supervision can improve front recovery compared to direct front prediction.
AI.method: The study compares direct front prediction versus zone-guided front extraction using three architectures (U-Net, DeepLabV3+, SegFormer-B0) under identical bounding-box-cropped settings. In the direct setting, models predict binary calving-front masks. In the zone-guided setting, models first predict four semantic zone classes, then the front is extracted from the predicted glacier-ocean boundary. Evaluations include zone-level and front-level performance, ground-truth zone boundary checks, and lightweight test-time adaptation on sensor-specific and glacier-specific subsets.
AI.result: Zone labels contain useful front-boundary information: extracting the front from ground-truth zones yields the lowest mean distance error. However, fronts extracted from model-predicted zones remain weak, even when zone segmentation scores are moderate. Test-time adaptation also does not consistently improve zone-guided front recovery.
AI.conclusion: Zone segmentation performance should not be treated as a substitute for front-level evaluation. Effective use of zone labels may require boundary-aware training, label fusion, or explicit front supervision to improve calving front extraction.

title: Finite State Machine-Based Traffic Orchestration for Multi-Engine Analysis Platforms
summary: Modern application-security platforms route live traffic from a single proxy into several independent analysis engines -- behavioral anomaly detection, authentication analysis, resource discovery, access-control inspection, among others. Each engine's appetite for traffic changes on its own schedule, yet the proxy can honor only one forwarding instruction per resource. We present a traffic-orchestration method that models the combined needs of all engines as a single composite finite state machine (FSM) whose state space is the Cartesian product of per-engine states. Every reachable composite state pre-maps to one forwarding configuration, so runtime reduces to a lookup rather than a negotiation. We add two refinements: time-based expiry treated as a first-class FSM transition enabling declarative traffic decay, and per-state multi-tier outputs that let one machine serve every service level. The design is fully declarative, engine-agnostic, and scales to N engines without re-architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a traffic-orchestration method for modern application-security platforms that need to route live traffic from a single proxy to multiple independent analysis engines (behavioral anomaly detection, authentication analysis, resource discovery, access-control inspection). The solution models combined engine needs as a composite finite state machine (FSM) whose state space is the Cartesian product of per-engine states, enabling runtime lookup rather than negotiation.
AI.motivation: Application-security platforms require routing traffic to multiple independent analysis engines, but each engine has different traffic appetite on its own schedule. The proxy can honor only one forwarding instruction per resource, creating a fundamental routing conflict that needed a scalable solution.
AI.method: The authors model the combined needs of all analysis engines as a single composite FSM where state space = Cartesian product of per-engine states. Every reachable composite state pre-maps to one forwarding configuration. They add two refinements: (1) time-based expiry treated as a first-class FSM transition for declarative traffic decay, and (2) per-state multi-tier outputs enabling one machine to serve every service level.
AI.result: The design achieves: (1) runtime reduction to a simple lookup instead of negotiation, (2) fully declarative and engine-agnostic operation, (3) scalability to N engines without re-architecture.
AI.conclusion: The proposed composite FSM approach provides a scalable, declarative solution for traffic orchestration in multi-engine security platforms, eliminating runtime negotiation while supporting time-based expiry and multi-tier service levels.

title: Articulatory Entrainment and Coordination Complexity in Spontaneous Autistic and Non-autistic Dialogue
comment: Accepted to be published in Interspeech 2026
summary: Articulatory entrainment, the adaptation of vocal tract coordination to facilitate interaction remains underexplored in spontaneous dialogue, particularly among autistic speakers. Many prior studies have utilized task-based, phoneme-level analyses with invasive measurement techniques. Here, we introduce a speaker-independent framework to quantify articulatory entrainment in spontaneous dyadic conversations among autistic and non-autistic adults using acoustic-to-articulatory inversion and coordination complexity metrics. We examine temporal changes in articulatory coordination across interaction. Non-autistic dyads exhibit increasing coordination complexity and stronger entrainment over time, autistic dyads show moderate effects, and mixed dyads demonstrate the least alignment. Greater articulatory entrainment correlates with higher self-reported conversational success, indicating increase in coordination complexity as a marker of effective social interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a speaker-independent framework using acoustic-to-articulatory inversion to measure articulatory entrainment in spontaneous dyadic conversations among autistic and non-autistic adults. Non-autistic dyads show increasing coordination complexity and stronger entrainment over time, while autistic and mixed dyads show less alignment.
AI.motivation: Prior studies on articulatory entrainment have relied on task-based, phoneme-level analyses with invasive measurement techniques, leaving spontaneous dialogue and autistic speakers underexplored.
AI.method: The study uses acoustic-to-articulatory inversion and coordination complexity metrics to quantify articulatory entrainment in spontaneous dyadic conversations among autistic and non-autistic adults, examining temporal changes across interaction.
AI.result: Non-autistic dyads exhibit increasing coordination complexity and stronger entrainment over time; autistic dyads show moderate effects; mixed dyads demonstrate the least alignment. Greater articulatory entrainment correlates with higher self-reported conversational success.
AI.conclusion: Increased coordination complexity serves as a marker of effective social interaction, suggesting articulatory entrainment is a valuable metric for understanding social communication dynamics.

title: Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the Agentic AI for Biological Discovery Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to scientific discovery and hypothesis generation. Both the effect of refinement and the diversity of the delivered set are hard to interpret before experimental ground truth exists, and both are typically reported by deciding whether pairs of generated hypotheses describe the same underlying mechanism. We study two evaluation questions that rest on this pairwise equivalence judgment: (1) how much self-critique changes delivered hypotheses beyond run-to-run variability, and (2) how the equivalence rule used to group hypotheses affects measured diversity. Across four proprietary instances, we hold opening hypotheses fixed, rerun the downstream workflow with 0, 1, and 5 critique rounds, and score matched hypothesis pairs with an LLM-as-a-judge. Relative to matched same-depth reruns, moving from 0 to 1 round produces 34.5 percentage points (pp) of additional mechanism-level divergence, whereas 1 to 5 rounds adds 1.3 pp. We then compare three equivalence rules: term frequency--inverse document frequency (TF--IDF) similarity, dense embeddings, and the same LLM-as-a-judge. We construct controlled hypothesis pairs that either preserve the causal explanation through wording or biological-terminology changes, or replace one component of the causal chain while holding the rest fixed. All three rules are invariant to meaning-preserving edits, but when the initiating event is replaced, the LLM-as-a-judge identifies 83% of valid pairs as different mechanisms, versus 0% for TF--IDF and 8% for embeddings; varying only the rubric that defines same mechanism moves this figure from 38% to 96%. Together, these results show that pairwise equivalence judgments are a measurement choice: how mechanism equivalence is defined affects both the estimated effect of self-critique and the measured diversity of generated hypotheses.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how to evaluate hypotheses generated by LLM-based multi-agent systems for scientific discovery. The authors investigate two key questions: (1) the impact of self-critique on hypothesis quality beyond natural variability, and (2) how different equivalence rules affect measured diversity. They find that the first critique round adds 34.5 percentage points of mechanism-level divergence, but subsequent rounds add minimal gain. The choice of equivalence rule (TF-IDF, embeddings, or LLM-as-a-judge) dramatically affects diversity measurements, with the LLM-as-a-judge being most sensitive to causal mechanism changes (83% detection vs 0-8% for others).
AI.motivation: The researchers aimed to address a fundamental challenge in evaluating LLM-generated scientific hypotheses: the lack of ground truth makes it difficult to assess whether refinement improves hypotheses or whether generated hypotheses are truly diverse. The core problem is that both metrics depend on judging whether pairs of hypotheses describe the same underlying mechanism, and this judgment itself is variable depending on the method used.
AI.method: The study used four proprietary LLM instances. They fixed initial hypotheses and reran the generation workflow with 0, 1, and 5 critique rounds. They then compared three equivalence rules: TF-IDF similarity, dense embeddings, and LLM-as-a-judge, using controlled hypothesis pairs that either preserved causal explanations or replaced specific components of the causal chain.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The first critique round produces 34.5 percentage points of additional mechanism-level divergence relative to natural variability, but additional rounds (1 to 5) add only 1.3 pp. (2) All three equivalence rules are invariant to meaning-preserving edits (wording/terminology changes). (3) When the initiating event is replaced, LLM-as-a-judge identifies 83% as different mechanisms, while TF-IDF detects 0% and embeddings detect 8%. (4) Changing the rubric definition of "same mechanism" shifts detection rates from 38% to 96%.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that pairwise equivalence judgments are fundamentally a measurement choice. How mechanism equivalence is defined significantly impacts both the estimated effect of self-critique and the measured diversity of generated hypotheses. This has important implications for evaluating LLM-based scientific discovery systems, as different evaluation methods may yield contradictory conclusions about system performance.

title: Why Convolution Still Matters: Evaluating Inductive Biases in Cryospheric Image Classification
comment: Accepted at IEEE IGARSS 2026, 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Recent advances in attention-based deep learning have motivated their adoption for remote sensing image classification; however, their benefits for cryospheric imagery, where surface states are dominated by fine-grained textures and class imbalance, remain unclear. In this work, we revisit a benchmark Greenland Ice Sheet image dataset, previously shown to favor convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to examine whether modern attention-based and hybrid architectures improve class-wise reliability. We conduct a controlled comparison between a classical CNN (AlexNet), a modern CNN (ConvNeXt-Tiny), a pure attention-based model (Swin-Tiny), and a hybrid convolution-attention model (CoAtNet-0) under identical training and evaluation protocols. Results show that AlexNet achieves the highest accuracy and the strongest balanced performance as measured by macro-averaged F1, while ConvNeXt-Tiny exhibits the highest macro-averaged AUC, indicating strong class separability but less consistent final decision quality. Class-wise analysis reveals that hybrid architectures improve recall for rare and structurally distinct surface classes, whereas convolutional models remain more reliable for texture-dominated categories. These findings highlight the importance of aligning architectural inductive bias with cryospheric data characteristics and suggest that increased model complexity does not necessarily translate to improved reliability for ice-sheet surface classification.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether modern attention-based deep learning architectures improve classification performance on cryospheric imagery (Greenland Ice Sheet), comparing AlexNet, ConvNeXt-Tiny, Swin-Tiny, and CoAtNet-0 under identical protocols. Surprisingly, the classical CNN (AlexNet) achieves highest accuracy and balanced F1, while ConvNeXt-Tiny leads in macro-averaged AUC. Hybrid architectures improve recall for rare classes, but convolutional models remain more reliable for texture-dominated categories.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the gap in knowledge about whether attention-based deep learning benefits cryospheric imagery classification, where surface states are characterized by fine-grained textures and class imbalance. The benchmark Greenland Ice Sheet dataset previously favored CNNs, prompting a re-examination with modern architectures.
AI.method: A controlled comparison was conducted using four architectures: (1) classical CNN (AlexNet), (2) modern CNN (ConvNeXt-Tiny), (3) pure attention-based model (Swin-Tiny), and (4) hybrid convolution-attention model (CoAtNet-0). All models were trained and evaluated under identical protocols on a benchmark Greenland Ice Sheet image dataset.
AI.result: AlexNet achieved highest accuracy and strongest balanced performance (macro-averaged F1). ConvNeXt-Tiny showed highest macro-averaged AUC, indicating strong class separability but less consistent final decisions. Hybrid architectures improved recall for rare and structurally distinct surface classes, while convolutional models remained more reliable for texture-dominated categories.
AI.conclusion: Increased model complexity does not necessarily translate to improved reliability for ice-sheet surface classification. Architectural inductive bias should align with cryospheric data characteristics. The classical CNN (AlexNet) surprisingly outperforms modern attention-based architectures on this specific benchmark.

title: PreMaQ: Predicting Maintainability-Related Quality of LLM-Generated Code Before Generation
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable of code generation, adopting generated code in software development requires assessing not only its functional correctness but also its maintainability-related quality. If such quality could be estimated before generation, developers could avoid the cost of generating, reviewing, and discarding low-quality code. Although prior work has shown that the functional correctness of the LLM-generated code can be predicted in advance, it remains unclear whether maintainability-related quality is similarly predictable. We introduce Pre-Generation Maintainability-Related Quality Prediction (PreMaQ), which predicts the Code Smell Score (CSS) and Maintainability Index (MI) of generated code from the internal representations of LLMs before generation. Our evaluation covers four open-weight LLMs and four Python code generation benchmarks, comprising 2,695 tasks in total. Our results show that predicted CSS and MI consistently correlate with their observed values across all 16 model-benchmark combinations, achieving mean Spearman rank correlations of 0.57 and 0.65, respectively. When used for model selection, PreMaQ achieves 59.5% of the maintainability-related quality improvement attainable by an ideal maintainability-based selector over random selection on tasks for which multiple models generate functionally correct code. Combining predictions from PreMaQ and prompt embeddings increases this proportion to 60.7%, indicating that the two signals are complementary. These findings suggest that PreMaQ can be used to predict and improve the maintainability-related quality of LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: PreMaQ predicts the maintainability quality (CSS and MI) of LLM-generated code from internal model representations before generation. Evaluated on 2,695 tasks across 4 LLMs and 4 benchmarks, achieving mean Spearman correlations of 0.57 and 0.65 respectively. When used for model selection, it achieves 59.5% of ideal improvement, rising to 60.7% when combined with prompt embeddings.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become capable of code generation, developers need to assess not only functional correctness but also maintainability. Current approaches generate code first then evaluate, which is costly. Predicting maintainability before generation could help developers avoid low-quality code and select better models for their tasks.
AI.method: PreMaQ uses internal representations of LLMs to predict Code Smell Score (CSS) and Maintainability Index (MI) before code generation. Evaluation covers 4 open-weight LLMs and 4 Python code generation benchmarks (2,695 tasks total). Predictions are evaluated using Spearman rank correlation, and a model selection approach tests practical utility.
AI.result: Predicted CSS and MI consistently correlate with observed values across all 16 model-benchmark combinations, with mean Spearman correlations of 0.57 (CSS) and 0.65 (MI). For model selection, PreMaQ achieves 59.5% of the maintainability improvement attainable by an ideal selector. Combining PreMaQ predictions with prompt embeddings increases this to 60.7%, showing complementary signals.
AI.conclusion: PreMaQ can effectively predict maintainability-related quality of LLM-generated code before generation. This enables developers to select better models and improve code quality proactively. The complementary nature of PreMaQ and prompt embeddings suggests potential for further improvement through combined approaches.

title: DUET: Co-Evolving Solver and Grader Agents
summary: Agentic workflows are increasingly used across domains such as technology, finance, and enterprise operations. As these agents become more widely deployed, continually improving them becomes increasingly important. This raises an immediate challenge: How should the agent evolve? This evolution requires effective evaluation that can assess outcomes and provide useful feedback for optimization. As the agent evolves, its behaviors and failure modes may also change, making a fixed evaluator increasingly inadequate. Another fundamental question: How should we evaluate an evolving agent? These two challenges are inherently coupled; changes in agent behavior can expose limitations of the current evaluator, while a stronger evaluator provides more informative feedback for improving the agent. Motivated by this interaction, we introduce DUET, a framework that jointly optimizes a solver agent and a grader agent to improve both. DUET iteratively selects training tasks, executes them with the solver, evaluates the resulting outcomes with the grader, and uses a tool-using update module to revise the solver and the grader, alternating between the two across rounds. By updating the grader within the optimization loop, DUET turns evaluation from a fixed source of feedback into a first-class optimization objective that adapts alongside the solver. Experiments across four agent benchmarks show that DUET improves both solver and grader performance and consistently outperforms baselines that optimize the solver with a fixed grader.

AI.tldr: DUET is a framework that jointly optimizes a solver agent and a grader agent in an iterative loop, addressing the challenge of evaluating evolving AI agents. By updating the grader alongside the solver, DUET turns evaluation from a fixed feedback source into a first-class optimization objective.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that as agentic workflows evolve, their behaviors and failure modes change, making fixed evaluators increasingly inadequate. The authors recognize that evaluation and agent improvement are inherently coupled: changing agent behavior exposes evaluator limitations, while stronger evaluators provide better feedback for optimization.
AI.method: DUET uses an iterative process that: (1) selects training tasks, (2) executes them with the solver agent, (3) evaluates outcomes with the grader agent, and (4) uses a tool-using update module to revise both the solver and grader, alternating between them across rounds.
AI.result: Experiments across four agent benchmarks show that DUET improves both solver and grader performance, consistently outperforming baselines that optimize the solver with a fixed grader.
AI.conclusion: The co-evolution of solver and grader is essential for effective agent optimization. By treating evaluation as a dynamic, optimizable component rather than a fixed benchmark, DUET enables more robust improvement cycles for agentic systems.

title: Agentic Cognitive Depth: Operational Criteria for Evaluating LLM Agents
comment: The 5th International Conference on Human and Artificial Rationalities
summary: Agentic large language model (LLM) systems are commonly implemented as an LLM in a loop with Planning, Memory, Tools, and Control Flow. This application-focused view connects agentic LLM research with deployable systems and leaves open how such systems should be evaluated beyond end-to-end task success. Building on this view, we define agentic cognitive depth as a trajectory-level profile across five operational criteria. The profile contains context sensitivity ($C$), temporal continuity ($T$), multimodal coordination ($M$), adaptive interaction ($A$), and metacognitive monitoring ($Mc$). The first four criteria measure how well Control Flow, Memory, Tools, and Planning are used across a trajectory. The fifth measures whether the system monitors and regulates the full run. For each criterion, we give operational proxies and a perturbation procedure, then connect the profile to the agent's world model. We provide the structure needed to extend benchmarks such as GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, and TRIP-Bench with per-criterion diagnostics. Symbolic verifiers, structured memory, planner coupling, and tool constraints provide practical ways to build and test these capacities.

AI.tldr: This paper defines "agentic cognitive depth" as a trajectory-level evaluation framework for agentic LLM systems, comprising five operational criteria: context sensitivity, temporal continuity, multimodal coordination, adaptive interaction, and metacognitive monitoring. The framework extends beyond end-to-end task success to diagnose specific capabilities of LLM agents across Planning, Memory, Tools, and Control Flow components.
