AI.motivation: Current evaluation of agentic LLM systems focuses primarily on end-to-end task success, leaving open how such systems should be evaluated beyond this metric. The authors aim to provide a more nuanced, diagnostic approach to assess the specific capabilities of agentic LLM systems.
AI.method: The authors define five operational criteria with operational proxies and perturbation procedures: (1) Context sensitivity (C) - measures Control Flow usage, (2) Temporal continuity (T) - measures Memory usage, (3) Multimodal coordination (M) - measures Tools usage, (4) Adaptive interaction (A) - measures Planning usage, and (5) Metacognitive monitoring (Mc) - measures whether the system monitors and regulates the full run. They connect these criteria to the agent's world model and provide methods to extend existing benchmarks (GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, TRIP-Bench) with per-criterion diagnostics.
AI.result: The paper provides a structured framework for evaluating agentic LLM systems with five diagnostic criteria, along with practical implementation approaches using symbolic verifiers, structured memory, planner coupling, and tool constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed agentic cognitive depth framework offers a comprehensive approach to evaluating agentic LLM systems beyond end-to-end task success, enabling per-criterion diagnostics through existing benchmarks and practical implementation methods.

title: VCURF: Virtual Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields
summary: Radiance fields, implemented with either implicit (NeRF) or explicit (Gaussian Splatting) representations, are advancing the state of the art in novel view synthesis at a rapid pace. Even though the rendered views they generate are often compelling, they are not free of errors. In this paper, we propose a new approach for pixel-wise uncertainty quantification based on measuring the inconsistencies among renderings by the radiance field model in virtual cameras sampled near the target viewpoint. We named our approach VCURF for Virtual Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields. VCURF treats the radiance field model as a black box, only assuming that it is capable of rendering color and depth on demand. This property makes our approach applicable to both NeRF and GS models without any modification. Our experiments on a combination of datasets, radiance field models and baselines demonstrate VCURF's effectiveness in pixel-wise uncertainty estimation. We conclude the paper with findings that question the way view selection is tackled by the majority of the current literature.

AI.tldr: VCURF is a novel pixel-wise uncertainty quantification method for radiance fields (NeRF and Gaussian Splatting) that measures inconsistencies among renderings from virtual cameras near the target viewpoint, treating the radiance field as a black box.
AI.motivation: Radiance field methods (NeRF and Gaussian Splatting) generate compelling novel views but contain errors. The literature lacks effective pixel-wise uncertainty estimation approaches, and current view selection methods may be flawed.
AI.method: VCURF renders the scene from virtual cameras sampled near the target viewpoint and measures inconsistencies among these renderings to quantify pixel-wise uncertainty. It treats the radiance field as a black box, only requiring the ability to render color and depth on demand.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets, radiance field models, and baselines demonstrate VCURF's effectiveness in pixel-wise uncertainty estimation.
AI.conclusion: The findings question the way view selection is tackled by the majority of current literature, suggesting a need to reconsider existing approaches.

title: Adopting InnerSource in a Public Sector Organization: A Case Study
summary: InnerSource (IS) is increasingly viewed as a way to improve large-scale software development. However, evidence on its adoption in public sector organizations remains limited. This paper reports a study of IS adoption in a Swedish Public Sector Organization. Drawing on nine semi-structured interviews and an internal workshop with 13 participants, we examine motivations, challenges, and improvement strategies for IS adoption. The results show that the main motivations are improving reuse, strengthening cross-team collaboration, and enabling faster and more cost-efficient development. Key challenges relate to a lack of an open culture and mindset, management of reusable assets (e.g., ownership, documentation, and code visibility), and ways of working (e.g., siloed practices and limited time for contributions). The study also identified improvements to address challenges, including fostering an enabling culture and mindset for IS and knowledge sharing, strengthening management support, and establishing internal platforms and governance for reusable assets.

AI.tldr: This study examines InnerSource adoption in a Swedish Public Sector Organization through interviews and workshop data, identifying key motivations (reuse, collaboration, efficiency), challenges (culture, asset management, siloed practices), and improvement strategies (culture, management support, governance).
AI.motivation: InnerSource is increasingly viewed as a way to improve large-scale software development, but evidence on its adoption in public sector organizations remains limited. This study addresses this gap by investigating IS adoption in a Swedish public sector context.
AI.method: The study employed a qualitative approach using nine semi-structured interviews and an internal workshop with 13 participants to examine motivations, challenges, and improvement strategies for InnerSource adoption.
AI.result: Main motivations include improving reuse, strengthening cross-team collaboration, and enabling faster and more cost-efficient development. Key challenges relate to: 1) lack of open culture and mindset, 2) management of reusable assets (ownership, documentation, code visibility), and 3) ways of working (siloed practices, limited time for contributions). Improvement strategies identified include fostering enabling culture and mindset, strengthening management support, and establishing internal platforms and governance for reusable assets.
AI.conclusion: The study provides empirical evidence on InnerSource adoption in public sector, highlighting that successful adoption requires not just technical solutions but significant cultural and organizational changes, including management support, governance frameworks, and platforms to support reusable assets.

title: Pareto-Dominant Clarification: Post-Training Coding LLMs via PPO-Lagrangian Budget Constraints
comment: Accepted to the LMP Workshop at EMNLP 2026. 17 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Abhinav Rajput and Acey Vogelstein contributed equally. Code: https://github.com/Abhinav0710rajput/coding_llms_cmdp
summary: Coding agents operating under ambiguous instructions or user prompts must decide whether to ask clarifying questions or attempt a solution directly. While clarification from the user may improve the correctness of the agent's solution, each back-and-forth interaction incurs user and system costs, forming an explicit accuracy vs. efficiency tradeoff. Existing works study clarification behavior but do not train policies under enforceable clarification budgets; penalty-based approaches typically require separate coefficient tuning swept across all clarification budget levels. We formulate clarification as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and post-train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with PPO-Lagrangian to optimize coding accuracy, subject to an expected question-budget constraint. Evaluated on HumanEvalComm with a GPT-4o-mini oracle simulator, the resulting policies reveal that untuned clarification behavior is Pareto-inefficient: budget-constrained policies can simultaneously achieve higher accuracy and lower clarification rates than the baseline model. Across budget levels, we observe a log-shaped Pareto frontier with diminishing returns to additional clarification. Gains arise not from simply asking more questions overall, but from improved question targeting and better code generation under ambiguity. Without explicit supervision, trained policies learn to allocate clarification budget non-uniformly, asking more frequently on tougher (multi-degradation) tasks. These results suggest that unconstrained interactive LLM systems may systematically use clarification inefficiently.

AI.tldr: This paper trains coding agents to decide when to ask clarifying questions vs. attempting solutions directly, formulating clarification as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). Using PPO-Lagrangian on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, they show budget-constrained policies outperform unconstrained baselines, achieving higher accuracy with lower clarification rates through improved question targeting.
AI.motivation: Coding agents face ambiguous instructions and must balance between asking clarifying questions (which improves accuracy but incurs costs) versus attempting solutions directly. Existing works study clarification but don't enforce clarification budgets, and penalty-based approaches require separate tuning for each budget level.
AI.method: Formulated clarification as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and post-trained Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct using PPO-Lagrangian to optimize coding accuracy under an expected question-budget constraint. Evaluated on HumanEvalComm with a GPT-4o-mini oracle simulator.
AI.result: Budget-constrained policies simultaneously achieve higher accuracy and lower clarification rates than baseline models. A log-shaped Pareto frontier shows diminishing returns to additional clarification. Gains come from improved question targeting and better code generation under ambiguity, not from asking more questions overall. Trained policies learn to allocate clarification budget non-uniformly, asking more questions on tougher (multi-degradation) tasks.
AI.conclusion: Unconstrained interactive LLM systems may systematically use clarification inefficiently. The CMDP framework with PPO-Lagrangian provides an effective approach for training clarification policies that balance accuracy and efficiency under enforceable budget constraints.

title: SHarP: Saliency-based Pruning of Agent Harnesses
summary: Agent harnesses are systems that coordinate model calls, tool use, and task execution to help large language models complete complex tasks. To meet task requirements and address failures, these systems are often iteratively refined by amending and patching their instructions, tools, and workflows, continuously increasing harness complexity. It is therefore unclear whether some resulting harness modules are redundant, introducing substantial token overhead with little, if any, performance gain. Inspired by neural network pruning, in this paper, we study harness pruning as a means of striking a better balance between task performance and token cost. We propose SHarP (Saliency-based Harness Pruning), a simple yet effective pruning strategy based on the saliency of each harness module with respect to performance and efficiency. Specifically, we first identify tools, instructions, and supporting mechanisms as components that can be individually disabled. We then estimate the saliency of each module by ablating it and assessing its task performance and token cost relative to the full set of single-module ablations. Modules with the smallest contribution to performance or largest computational overhead are subsequently pruned. Our evaluation across various harnesses on held-out validation sets reveals a surprising finding: most harnesses that we studied are highly redundant and can maintain comparable performance and efficiency even after a substantial portion of their modules are pruned. Our pruning approach and empirical findings provide new perspectives on agent harness design and optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SHarP (Saliency-based Harness Pruning), a method to reduce complexity in LLM agent systems by identifying and removing redundant modules. The approach ablates each harness component (tools, instructions, workflows) to measure its saliency—contribution to performance versus token cost. Evaluation shows most agent harnesses are highly redundant, maintaining performance even after substantial pruning.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses (systems coordinating LLM model calls, tool use, and task execution) become increasingly complex through iterative refinement and patching. This leads to potential redundancy where some modules add token overhead without proportional performance gains. The authors seek to balance task performance with token cost efficiency.
AI.method: The proposed SHarP method: (1) Identifies removable components: tools, instructions, and supporting mechanisms; (2) Estimates saliency by ablating each module individually and measuring impact on task performance and token cost relative to full single-module ablations; (3) Prunes modules with smallest performance contribution or largest computational overhead.
AI.result: Evaluation across various harnesses on held-out validation sets reveals that most harnesses studied are highly redundant—substantial portions of modules can be pruned while maintaining comparable performance and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: SHarP provides a simple yet effective pruning strategy for agent harness optimization. The surprising finding that most harnesses are highly redundant offers new perspectives on agent harness design, suggesting that iterative refinement often introduces unnecessary complexity. This work opens new avenues for understanding and optimizing LLM agent systems.

title: Dependable AI-Assisted Engineering: A Formal Framework for AI Participation and Assurance in Safety-Critical Workflows
summary: Generative AI can produce engineering artefacts, but generation alone does not determine whether or how those artefacts should enter safety-critical workflows. This paper develops a formal framework for assigning AI participation and assurance at the level of individual workflow units. Each unit has a participation and assurance record covering its engineering requirement, an approved operational formalization where applicable, the applicable mechanism, fallback where applicable, evidence obligations and the applicable guarantee, plus a deployment-readiness status. The framework distinguishes deterministic verification, statistically calibrated admission, authorized human judgement supported by AI advice, authorized human adjudication of AI-produced artefacts, retained deterministic tool paths and explicit non-participation; these arrangements carry different kinds of guarantee rather than levels on a common scale. The framework also separates formalization fidelity from verifier soundness, provides a staged classification and readiness procedure, and derives conditions for comparing a gated AI-assisted unit with an incumbent process under recurring-population assumptions. We instantiate and apply the framework in an executed 17-unit wing-spar structural-analysis workflow combining deterministically gated AI-generated CAD, retained deterministic computation and human judgement. The AI-generated CAD program passed all 23 deterministic checks and was admitted at the first attempt. Favourable stress magnitudes did not suffice to pass the stress criteria where the predeclared mesh-convergence evidence was insufficient; those criteria were instead referred to engineering judgement. The case demonstrates selective AI participation and explicit evidence handling at unit level; no claim is made of workflow-level dependability, certification, structural safety or productivity.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a formal framework for assigning AI participation and assurance levels at individual workflow units in safety-critical engineering. It distinguishes six different arrangements (deterministic verification, statistical admission, human judgement with AI advice, human adjudication, retained deterministic paths, and non-participation) rather than treating assurance as a single scale. The framework is applied to a 17-unit wing-spar structural analysis workflow, demonstrating selective AI participation with explicit evidence handling.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the gap between AI's ability to generate engineering artefacts and the lack of formal methods for determining how those artefacts should enter safety-critical workflows. Existing approaches lack structured ways to assign AI participation and assurance at granular workflow levels.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) developing a formal framework defining participation and assurance records for each workflow unit (requirements, formalization, mechanism, fallback, evidence obligations, guarantee, deployment-readiness); (2) distinguishing six different assurance arrangements with different guarantee types; (3) separating formalization fidelity from verifier soundness; (4) providing staged classification and readiness procedures; (5) instantiating the framework in a 17-unit wing-spar structural-analysis workflow combining AI-generated CAD, deterministic computation, and human judgement.
AI.result: The AI-generated CAD program passed all 23 deterministic checks and was admitted at the first attempt. However, stress criteria could not be met through favourable stress magnitudes alone due to insufficient mesh-convergence evidence, requiring referral to engineering judgement. The case demonstrates selective AI participation and explicit evidence handling at unit level, though no workflow-level dependability, certification, structural safety, or productivity claims are made.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to assign and distinguish AI participation mechanisms in safety-critical workflows. It emphasizes that different arrangements (verification, statistical admission, human judgement, etc.) carry fundamentally different guarantee types rather than representing different points on a common scale. The case study demonstrates practical application but explicitly disclaims any claims of overall workflow safety or certification readiness.

title: Mechanizing the User's Eye: Pre-Registered Deployment of a Sabotage-Validated Fail-Plausible Observer in a Production LLM Agent Runtime
comment: Follow-up to arXiv:2606.14589. 20 pages, 4 figures. Labeled incident corpus, detector source, sabotage-validation harness, and pre-registration texts publicly available at https://github.com/bisdom-cell/openclaw-model-bridge
summary: A prior longitudinal study of silent failures in a production LLM agent runtime (arXiv:2606.14589) found that about 70% were discovered by a human looking at the product as a user while thousands of tests and governance checks stayed green, and posed mechanizing part of what the human eye does as an open problem. This paper reports our attempt. We built an automated user-viewpoint observer targeting the most dangerous class, fail-plausible failure, in which an internal error becomes fluent, plausible output to the user. It is a two-layer pipeline: five deterministic signals distilled from incident postmortems escalate to an LLM judge whose verdicts must cite verbatim evidence or be discarded. Ground truth is 24 labeled production postmortems with explicit honesty boundaries: 16 of 24 are structurally invisible to any content-reading observer, and we say so. Offline, the deterministic layer achieves 6/6 regression detection with 0/4 false positives, each detector proven load-bearing by sabotage; held-out recall on novel patterns is 0/4. It is, so far, a regression engine. Deployment followed pre-registration: shadow mode caught and retired one systematic false positive on its first run, the 26-day shadow window then ran clean, flip criteria were fixed before the shadow data was read, and the analysis protocol was frozen before the enforcing-mode window opened. That window (12 observed days) fired zero verdicts; per the pre-registered path we report live precision as undefined rather than narrating quiet as success. The observer also produced ten silent failures of its own, confirming that the judge inherits the taxonomy it judges. We release the corpus, detector, and scorecard as a runnable bench: mechanization today retires the human's regression scanning so the eye can specialize in novelty; prediction remains open but is now measurable under frozen rules.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of automating human detection of "fail-plausible failures" in LLM agent runtimes—cases where internal errors manifest as fluent, plausible outputs that bypass traditional tests. The authors built a two-layer detection pipeline: five deterministic signals escalate to an LLM judge requiring verbatim evidence. Against 24 labeled postmortems (16 invisible to content-reading observers), the deterministic layer achieved 6/6 regression detection with 0/4 false positives, but 0/4 held-out recall on novel patterns. Deployment in shadow mode caught one systematic false positive, then ran clean; a 12-day enforcement window fired zero verdicts. The observer also produced ten silent failures of its own, confirming the judge inherits the taxonomy it judges.
AI.motivation: Prior work found ~70% of silent failures in production LLM agents were discovered by humans using the product, while thousands of tests stayed green. This paper attempts to mechanize part of what the human eye does—specifically detecting "fail-plausible failures" where internal errors become fluent, plausible output to users.
AI.method: Two-layer pipeline: (1) Five deterministic signals distilled from incident postmortems for initial escalation; (2) LLM judge whose verdicts must cite verbatim evidence or be discarded. Ground truth is 24 labeled production postmortems with explicit honesty boundaries (16/24 structurally invisible to content-reading observers). Deployment followed pre-registration: shadow mode, flip criteria fixed before reading shadow data, analysis protocol frozen before enforcement mode.
AI.result: Offline deterministic layer: 6/6 regression detection with 0/4 false positives, each detector proven load-bearing by sabotage. Held-out recall on novel patterns: 0/4—it functions as a regression engine only. Deployment: 26-day shadow window caught and retired one systematic false positive, then ran clean. 12-day enforcement window fired zero verdicts (precision undefined per pre-registration). The observer also produced ten silent failures of its own, confirming the judge inherits the taxonomy it judges.
AI.conclusion: The authors release the corpus, detector, and scorecard as a runnable benchmark. Mechanization successfully retires human regression scanning so the human eye can specialize in novelty detection. Prediction (detecting novel fail-plausible patterns) remains open but is now measurable under frozen rules. The work demonstrates both the feasibility of regression detection and the current impossibility of novel failure prediction.

title: Robust blind unmixing: A geometric approach to overcoming basis variation
summary: Signal separation problems are common in science. A prominent example of this occurs during the use of diffraction or spectroscopy to identify the individual components of a mixture by measuring it. In the simplest case, the measured signal is a linear combination of basis patterns corresponding to the constituent parts. The unmixing problem is to infer all or some of these basis patterns and abundances of components from measurements of distinct mixtures. One of the core challenges of this task is the variation of the basis from mixture to mixture due to noise and the exact physics of the measurement process. This is usually addressed with tailored model-based and parametric methods that are then limited in use to specific application domains by the nature of the assumptions made. We propose a novel geometric approach to unmixing problems which views the generation of data during measurement through a metric space lens, thereby shifting the focus from parametrised models to a general relationship between basis transformations and the corresponding geometry. We take advantage of the optimal transport distances to capture commonly occurring basis variations, and use minimisation of in-class variance of candidate solutions to drive the optimisation. We pay special attention to the one-dimensional case due to its practical importance and availability of efficient distance and transport map routines. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on a range of unmixing tasks using random Gaussian mixture models, simulated powder X-ray diffraction, and laboratory hyperspectral imaging datasets.

AI.tldr: A novel geometric approach to signal unmixing problems that uses optimal transport distances to capture basis variations, shifting focus from parametric models to the relationship between basis transformations and geometry.
AI.motivation: Traditional model-based unmixing methods are limited to specific application domains by their assumptions. The core challenge is handling variation of basis patterns from mixture to mixture due to noise and measurement physics.
AI.method: The approach uses optimal transport distances to capture commonly occurring basis variations and minimizes in-class variance of candidate solutions to drive optimization. Special attention is given to the 1D case due to practical importance and availability of efficient distance and transport map routines.
AI.result: The method was demonstrated effective on various unmixing tasks using random Gaussian mixture models, simulated powder X-ray diffraction, and laboratory hyperspectral imaging datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometric framework provides a general solution for unmixing problems by viewing data generation through a metric space lens, applicable across different domains without requiring domain-specific parametric assumptions.

title: Language Model Activations Inhabit Privileged Error-Correcting Basins
summary: Language models exhibit remarkable robustness, continuing to produce coherent text even when their activations are perturbed by interventions like linear steering. We hypothesize that this robustness is a result of passive dynamics, i.e., constraining mechanisms in the forward pass that funnel activations toward "good" regions that produce coherent outputs. To investigate these hypothesized error-correcting mechanisms, we probe the geometry of language model activation space by observing the action of model layers on low-dimensional curves. In doing so, we discover that model activations occur within a cluster of distinct attracting basins, which differentiate natural activations geometrically from distributionally similar synthetic activations. Applying this lens to language model steering, we observe feature-specific basins along semantic steering directions, and find that steering moves activations between these basins. To demonstrate the active role of this geometry in neural computation, we show that adaptively modulating steering strength to transport activations across basins improves inter-language steering, significantly increasing the probability of sampling tokens from the target language compared to fixed-strength steering. Our findings establish analysis of activation space geometry as a promising approach to interpreting and controlling language models.

AI.tldr: Language models remain coherent even when their activations are perturbed (e.g., by linear steering), due to passive dynamics that constrain activations toward "good" regions. By probing activation space geometry through low-dimensional curves, the authors discover distinct attracting basins that differentiate natural from synthetic activations. Semantic steering directions contain feature-specific basins, and steering moves activations between these basins. Adaptive modulation of steering strength improves inter-language steering, increasing target language token probability compared to fixed-strength steering.
AI.motivation: To understand why language models are robust to interventions like linear steering, and to investigate the error-correcting mechanisms (passive dynamics) that funnel activations toward coherent outputs.
AI.method: Probe the geometry of language model activation space by observing model layers' action on low-dimensional curves; analyze basins along semantic steering directions; implement adaptive modulation of steering strength to transport activations across basins.
AI.result: Model activations exist within distinct attracting basins that geometrically separate natural activations from distributionally similar synthetic ones. Steering moves activations between these feature-specific basins. Adaptive steering that modulates strength to cross basin boundaries significantly improves inter-language steering, increasing target language token probability over fixed-strength steering.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing activation space geometry is a promising approach for interpreting and controlling language models, revealing the active role of this geometry in neural computation.

title: From Trust-by-Design to Continuous Trust in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
comment: 9 pages, 16 figures, submitted to the PoEM 2026 Forum as part of the 19th IFIP WG 8.1 Working Conference on the Practice of Enterprise Modeling (PoEM 2026), December 1-3, 2026, Mytilene, Lesvos, Greece
summary: Trust is crucial in the digital world, particularly in the age of systems based on artificial intelligence. Traditionally, system correctness is demonstrated by proving that the system satisfies the required properties. However, digital systems involve humans, who can make mistakes, break rules, or even intentionally cheat the system. Technical devices may also malfunction or cause errors. Therefore, external stakeholders need to trust a system throughout its operation. To address this challenge, we propose the concept of continuous trust. In this paper, we present a detailed explanation of this concept, based on a running example of a business's refund department. The paper concludes with a discussion of related work, such as compliance checking and certification, as well as an outlook on further questions regarding the formalization and the necessary tool support.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the concept of "continuous trust" to address the gap between traditional system correctness proofs and the need for external stakeholders to trust AI-based systems throughout their operation, using a business refund department as a running example.
AI.motivation: Traditional system correctness is demonstrated through property verification, but this is insufficient because digital systems involve humans who can make mistakes, break rules, or cheat, and technical devices that can malfunction. External stakeholders need ongoing trust in systems during operation, not just initial correctness proofs.
AI.method: The paper presents a detailed explanation of the "continuous trust" concept through a running example of a business's refund department, and discusses related work including compliance checking and certification.
AI.result: The paper provides a conceptual framework for continuous trust with detailed explanation and examples, along with discussion of related approaches and future directions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes with discussion of related work (compliance checking, certification) and an outlook on further questions regarding formalization and necessary tool support for continuous trust.

title: Beyond Masked Sparsity: SNACK Enables Truly Sparse Neural Networks on GPU
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 23 pages, 9 figures. Code: https://github.com/JafarBadour/Snack-SNN
summary: Deep neural networks continue to grow in parameter count, driving up training and inference cost on GPUs. Sparse neural networks and Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) promise to reduce these costs, but most implementations rely on binary masks over dense tensors and recover little of the theoretical compute, memory, or energy savings. We propose SNACK, a truly sparse GPU layer that stores and computes only non-zero connections. SNACK exposes a simple PyTorch API for restructuring connections and backpropagating gradients entirely in the sparse paradigm, and ships SNACK-COO, a custom COO-format SpMM CUDA kernel with a batch-to-Streaming-Multiprocessor mapping tuned for the small-batch, high-sparsity regime typical of large-model training and single-stream inference. At the kernel level, SNACK is up to 7x faster than the masked dense baseline (Dense+Mask) and competitive with cuSPARSE, Sputnik, and FlashSparse at 95% sparsity. At 90% sparsity, a single SNACK layer accelerates training by 8x and 3.7x, and inference by 4x and 2x, over Dense+Mask and fully dense layers, respectively, while using 72% less memory than dense and substantially less energy. End-to-end, SNACK reduces GPT-2 peak training memory by up to 40% and graph-style inference latency by 4.8x over Dense+Mask at 99% sparsity.

AI.tldr: SNACK is a truly sparse GPU layer that stores and computes only non-zero connections, addressing the inefficiency of binary mask-based sparse neural network implementations. It provides a PyTorch API and includes a custom COO-format SpMM CUDA kernel optimized for small-batch, high-sparsity regimes.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks continue to grow in parameter count, driving up training and inference costs on GPUs. Existing sparse neural networks and Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) implementations rely on binary masks over dense tensors and recover little of the theoretical compute, memory, or energy savings.
AI.method: SNACK exposes a simple PyTorch API for restructuring connections and backpropagating gradients entirely in the sparse paradigm. It ships SNACK-COO, a custom COO-format SpMM CUDA kernel with a batch-to-Streaming-Multiprocessor mapping tuned for the small-batch, high-sparsity regime typical of large-model training and single-stream inference.
AI.result: At the kernel level, SNACK is up to 7x faster than the masked dense baseline (Dense+Mask) and competitive with cuSPARSE, Sputnik, and FlashSparse at 95% sparsity. At 90% sparsity, a single SNACK layer accelerates training by 8x and 3.7x, and inference by 4x and 2x, over Dense+Mask and fully dense layers, respectively, while using 72% less memory than dense. End-to-end, SNACK reduces GPT-2 peak training memory by up to 40% and graph-style inference latency by 4.8x over Dense+Mask at 99% sparsity.
AI.conclusion: SNACK demonstrates that truly sparse GPU layers can achieve significant speedups (up to 8x in training, 4x in inference) and memory savings (72% less than dense) while maintaining competitive performance with existing sparse libraries. It successfully reduces GPT-2 training memory by 40% and inference latency by 4.8x at high sparsity levels.

title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Design Their Own Evaluations?
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75\% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91\% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.

AI.tldr: EvalResearchBench (ERB) is introduced to study whether AI agents can autonomously design evaluation benchmarks. Given constraints (budget, materials, references), AI "researcher" agents select/synthesize tasks, implement graders, and iterate via pilot testing before freezing evaluators. The best evaluators achieve ~75% pairwise agreement with target benchmarks, below the 91% ceiling set by target disagreements. Human-designed baselines remain strong, and lower execution cost correlates with higher agreement.
AI.motivation: Running complex benchmarks repeatedly is costly and slows iteration in recursive self-improvement (RSI). While human experts can design compact evaluation suites, this paper investigates whether AI agents can automate this benchmark design process, similar to how human experts would select or design evaluation tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB) as a testbed. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time/API budgets, an AI "researcher" agent selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, revises them through pilot tests, and freezes an executable evaluator. The study evaluates 9 researchers and 13 candidate models, comparing frozen evaluators against 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement.
AI.result: Best evaluators order ~75% of candidate pairs correctly (matching target benchmarks), but this falls below the 91% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets themselves. No single researcher dominates all metrics. The best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed (hidden) targets. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline. The evaluator with the lowest execution cost achieves the highest pairwise agreement. Agents can still produce issues: truncated answers, exhausted evaluation budgets, or questions dominating domain scores.
AI.conclusion: AI agents can partially automate evaluation benchmark design but remain limited—best agreement is 75% vs. 91% theoretical ceiling. Human-designed baselines remain competitive. Lower computational cost correlates with better performance, suggesting efficiency in evaluation design. Key issues (answer truncation, budget exhaustion, question dominance) indicate that agent-designed evaluators still require oversight.

title: Scaling 3D Visual Grounding in Abdominal CT
summary: Visual grounding models can enhance radiology workflows by linking report findings to image regions. This is particularly valuable for 3D CT, where findings often occupy a tiny fraction of the volume. Training 3D grounding models requires large sets of paired phrases and regions, and building such datasets is expensive, requiring radiologists to annotate images by hand. We posit that this supervision is already created implicitly during routine reporting, as radiologists frequently place 2D annotations (e.g., distance measurement, arrows) on key images to make measurements and to support report interpretation. We introduce an automated pipeline that converts these routine clinical annotations into large-scale phrase-region supervision for 3D visual grounding. The pipeline links each annotation to the corresponding finding in the report through metadata matching, then uses a promptable 3D segmentation model to convert the 2D annotation into a volumetric mask. This produces phrase-mask-volume datasets without requiring additional radiologist annotation. Applied to a single institution's clinical picture archiving and communication system (PACS), our approach generated 105K phrase-mask-volume triplets from 59K abdominal CT exams. We also introduce two abdominal CT grounding benchmarks, LocusBench-Onc and LocusBench-ED, which comprise 240 oncology and 260 emergency-department radiologist-reviewed phrase-mask-volume triplets, respectively, with the latter spanning 13 distinct categories such as appendicitis, hematoma, and hernia. We further introduce LocusCT, a 3D visual grounding model trained on this dataset, which achieves hit rates of 0.725 on LocusBench-Onc and 0.773 on LocusBench-ED, substantially outperforming comparator models. These results show that routine PACS annotations are a scalable, previously unused source of supervision for 3D visual grounding.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a scalable method to create training data for 3D visual grounding in radiology by repurposing routine clinical annotations from PACS. The approach generated 105K phrase-mask-volume triplets from 59K CT exams without additional radiologist annotation, and the resulting LocusCT model achieves state-of-the-art performance on two new benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Training 3D visual grounding models for radiology requires large paired phrase-region datasets, which are expensive to create through manual radiologist annotation. The authors observe that radiologists already create implicit supervision during routine reporting by placing 2D annotations (measurements, arrows) on key images.
AI.method: The proposed pipeline has two main stages: (1) Metadata matching to link each 2D clinical annotation to its corresponding finding in the radiology report; (2) Use of a promptable 3D segmentation model to convert the 2D annotation into a volumetric mask, producing phrase-mask-volume triplets.
AI.result: Applied to a single institution's PACS, the pipeline generated 105K phrase-mask-volume triplets from 59K abdominal CT exams. Two benchmarks were created: LocusBench-Onc (240 oncology cases) and LocusBench-ED (260 emergency department cases spanning 13 categories). The LocusCT model achieved hit rates of 0.725 on LocusBench-Onc and 0.773 on LocusBench-ED, outperforming comparator models substantially.
AI.conclusion: Routine PACS annotations represent a scalable, previously untapped source of supervision for 3D visual grounding in radiology, eliminating the need for additional manual radiologist annotation.

title: AgentSpy: Making AI Agent Behavior Observable
summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) run shell commands, read and write files, and reach the network, typically with their user's privileges. However, what an agent does during an execution is difficult to understand: tests assert on the result, and the agent's trajectory records only what the agent reports about itself, which may omit behavior executed by its subprocesses. We present AgentSpy, an approach that observes an agent from outside the agent. AgentSpy runs the agent in an isolated environment, configured by a declarative specification, and records the system calls and network traffic of the agent and of every process it executes. Based on this monitoring, AgentSpy supports two families of analyses: conformance analyses, which measure obligations, i.e., what an agent execution should do, and safety analyses, which check prohibitions, i.e., what an agent execution must never do. We instantiate one analysis of each family. The reliability analysis uses rules to summarize each run by the environment resources the agent uses: the commands it executed, the files it accessed, and the hosts it contacted. The security analysis applies deterministic rules to the system calls of an execution. For reliability, we evaluated AgentSpy on 77 tasks with the codex harness and three recent LLMs, executing each task three times. Sets of repeated runs of the same task are more similar than sets that include runs of another task in 92.2% of the comparisons. Among tasks for which all three runs pass outcome-based tests, the agent performs task-unrelated activities in 18% of the cases, reads the grading files in 7%, and does not use the developers' guidance in 17%. For security, the generic rules of AgentSpy detect four of five attack categories we considered, with no false positives across 50 runs.

AI.tldr: AgentSpy is a framework that monitors LLM-based AI agents from outside their execution environment, recording system calls and network traffic to enable conformance (reliability) and safety (security) analyses. It was evaluated on 77 tasks with 3 LLMs, showing that repeated runs are more consistent (92.2%) but agents often perform task-unrelated activities (18%) and sometimes read grading files (7%).
AI.motivation: The core problem is that AI agents built on LLMs are difficult to understand and monitor during execution. While agents can run shell commands, read/write files, and access networks with user privileges, their actual behavior is opaque - tests only assert on results, and trajectory records only show what the agent reports, missing subprocess behavior.
AI.method: AgentSpy runs the agent in an isolated environment configured by a declarative specification, recording system calls and network traffic of the agent and all its subprocesses. It supports two analysis families: (1) Conformance/reliability analysis using rules to summarize environment resources used (commands, files, hosts); (2) Safety/security analysis applying deterministic rules to system calls.
AI.result: For reliability: Sets of repeated runs of the same task are more similar than sets including runs of another task in 92.2% of comparisons. Among tasks where all three runs pass outcome-based tests, agents perform task-unrelated activities in 18% of cases, read grading files in 7%, and don't use developers' guidance in 17%. For security: Generic rules detect four of five attack categories with no false positives across 50 runs.
AI.conclusion: AgentSpy provides effective external monitoring of LLM-based AI agents, enabling both reliability and security analyses. The approach reveals that even successful agent runs often include unintended behaviors, and can detect most attack categories without false positives. This represents a significant advancement in understanding and securing AI agent executions.

title: Progressive Multi-Ancestor Bit-Depth Distillation
summary: Model compression strategies are widely employed to reduce memory footprint and network complexity, particularly for devices with constrained computational, memory, and energy resources. Prior works that rely on simultaneous conversion from floating-point high-precision (FP32) to integer low-precision (INT4) representations and distillation into smaller models suffer from unstable training and drastic degradation of prediction performance. To address these limitations, we propose a unified framework, known as \textbf{P}rogressive \textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}ncestor \textbf{B}it-depth \textbf{D}istillation (PMABD), that progressively compresses the network while transferring knowledge through a growing pool of higher-precision ancestor teachers. PMABD generates a sequence of intermediate teachers that each learn from all higher-precision ancestors and jointly supervise the final target student. This multi-ancestor, multi-stage design stabilizes ultra-low-bit quantization by lowering quantization noise profiles across training and ensuring stable quantization. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-20/32/18, and Tiny-ImageNet with MobileNetV2 show that PMABD outperforms state-of-the-art compression frameworks, results in 1.06$\%$ increase in performance of W2A2 (ResNet-18/CIFAR-100) student model. We show that a saturation-based stopping criterion contributes to improve the performance of our final student.

AI.tldr: PMABD is a unified framework for progressive model compression that addresses unstable training and performance degradation in ultra-low-bit quantization (INT4) by using multi-ancestor knowledge distillation. It generates intermediate teachers that learn from higher-precision ancestors to progressively compress networks while maintaining stable quantization.
AI.motivation: Prior works on simultaneous FP32-to-INT4 conversion and distillation into smaller models suffer from unstable training and drastic prediction performance degradation, particularly for ultra-low-bit quantization on resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: PMABD uses a multi-ancestor, multi-stage design: (1) progressively compresses network bit-depths through intermediate stages, (2) generates intermediate teachers that learn from all higher-precision ancestors, (3) jointly supervises the final target student, and (4) employs a saturation-based stopping criterion to determine optimal training termination.
AI.result: PMABD outperforms state-of-the-art compression frameworks, achieving 1.06% performance increase on W2A2 (ResNet-18/CIFAR-100) student model. Validated on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-20/32/18 and Tiny-ImageNet with MobileNetV2.
AI.conclusion: The progressive multi-ancestor approach with saturation-based stopping criterion effectively stabilizes ultra-low-bit quantization training and improves compression performance compared to existing methods.
